THE PEASANT AND HIS CHILD. . (From the German of Sturm.) The peasant stands beside his field, ' His brow contracted from displeasure, "I have." he argues, "tilled the land, Have taken pains pure seed to measure, And now, see here, weeds everywhere, The devil must have put there !" Up bounds his boy in high delight, Gay coloured flowers, his arms up-piling, Cornflowers and poppies, cockles too, All from the field, and he shouts, smiling, • k " • "See father! see how rich, how fair, ' The dear God must have put them there r
LADY WILDE ON MRS. BROWNING AND THE

_ QUEEN. And still are with us women who can guide The souls of men to calm, clear heavenly heights Where clouds and mist roll down beneath the feet. Heroic hearts are near, deep-spirit, eyes • Gleam on us in the darkness of our lives As on the shepherds in the midnight gleamed The star that lit them to the feet of Christ. The race can never die. Still on our ears The clear " Excelsior " from a woman's lips Rings out across the Apennines, although The woman's brow lies pale and cold in death With all the mighty marble dead in Florence. For while great songs can stir the hearts dt men, Spreading their full vibrations through the world, In ever-widening circles till they reach The Throne of God, and sons becomes a prayer— And prayer brings down the liberating strength Tint kindles nations to heroic deeds— She lives—the great-souled poetess who saw , From Casa Guidi windows Freedom dawn On Italy, and gave the glory back In sunrise hymns for all. Humanity!

..... And homage must we give to her who wears, With the calm grace of God's anointed Queen, The diadem of Kingdoms on her trow. Supreme above all Women—Empress-Queen Of countless millions and of half the globe, Yet blending with her royal majesty The soft, sweet music of a woman's life. Gentle, while all her armies shake the earth, And seas and oceans bear her lion flag. . Strong, with the sacred reverence for truth, Steadfast for right, and loyaLto her land Through storm and sunshine, splendour, gloom, and tears; For no unworthy act has ever marred The holy consecration to the vow Her child-like lips uttered in that solemn hour When, crowned with sovereignty, she took her place Amid the scent-red monarchs-of the world. • --The Woman's World for Jannary.

Convict (inhal- ing the fragrance of a violet) : "It will be December of next year, miss, before I make my debut." Vestris, the celebrated opera dancer, used to say with the most perfect sincerity, "I know only three men Europe at the present day who are unique in their we, —the King of Prussia. Voltaire, and myself." "If you haven't yet read that book you promised to," said a lady, severely, to her son. 'you show a great lack of principle." "Oh no. mamma,' was the calm reply, not lack of principle: only lack ot interest." The generous man, in the ordinary acceptation, will soon find that he has sacrificed to fools, knaves, flat- terero, or the deservedly Unhappy, all the opportunities of affording any future assistance where it ought to be. —Steele. _ . _

"True !" cried a lady, when reproached with the in- consistent marriage she had made, "I have often said I never would marry a parson, or a Scotchman, or a Pres- byterian; but I never said I would not marry a Scotch Presbyterian parson." . It is very easy, oftentimes, to do a generous net im- pulsively. and on the' spur of an occasion; and as so done —it Imw be both useful and gratifying to the recipient—' may confer a real favour, and merit thanks and the feel- ings of gratitude.—G. A. Sala. A gentleman who was commiserating a consumptive 'waiter standing in the hotel which he was just quitting, remarked to his jarvey. "he looks ill, poor fellow !" "1111" exclaimed the driver. "Sure he's dead these two months, surr ; but he's too lazy to close his eyes." The hand of the generous man is like the clouds of heaven, which drop upon the earth fruits. herbage. and flowers; hut the heart of the ungrateful is like a desert of sand, which swalloweth the showers that fall. burieth • them in its bosom, and produceth Main "Madame, you are growing more beautiful every day," gallantly said a gallant to an actress, now past her prime. "Every day? Oh, Monsieur," protested the very vain and aged party, "you flatter me r "Well," gal- lantly and accommodatingly replied Hasselbrinlc,“ let's Say every other day?' Wife (reproachtully) "Before we were; married, George, you used to say I was very dear to you." Hus- band "Yes, my dear. I did; and now you are dearer then ever to me." Wife (delighted) : "Really! do you mean it?" Husband: "Of course, I mean it. Valen- tines, rings, and all that made you dear enough; but they are nothing at all compared to milliners' and -dressmakers' bill=." THE MACK ARTS.—A REVERIE iat TIEIE Sramsn.:—And truly, putting all likings for old fashions out of the way. it remains certain that in a given time and with simple means, a man of imaginative power can do more, and express more, and excite the fancy of the spectator more, by frank outline than by complete 'work; and that assuredly there ought to be in all our national art schools an outline class trained to expaess themselves vigorously and accurately in that manner. Were there no other reason for such lessoning, it is a sufficient one that there are modes of ,getdous which become richly productive in that re- stricted manner; and yet by no training could be raised into the excellence of painting. Neither Bewick nor Cruikshank in England, nor Retsch, nor Ludwig Richter, in Germany, could ever have become painters; their countrymen owe more to their unassun3ing instinct of inYention than to the most exalted efforts of their his- torical schools. But it must be noted, in passing, that the practice of outline in England. and I suppose partly cantincntal academies also, has been both disgraced and arrested by the endeavour to elevate it into the rendering of ideal and heroic form, especially to the de- lineation of groups of statuary. Neither flesh nor sculptured marble can be outlined: and the endeavour to illustrate classical art and historical essays on it, by outlines of sculpture and architecture, has detne th.e double harm of making outline common and dull, and preventing tWpublic from learning that the merit of sculpture is in its surfaces, not its outlines. The essen- tial value of outline is in its power of suggesting quan- tity, intricacy, and character, in accessory detail, and in the richly ornamented treatment which can be carried over large spaces which in a finished painting must be lost in shade.—J. Ruskih, in" The Magazine of Art" for Januar:g. THE 'FANATICISM OF THE EARLY SCOTTISH REFORMERS. —No one now denies that fanaticism, intemperate zeal, cruel intolerance, iconoclastic excess, characterised the Reformation in Scotland. Is fanaticism good? Are in- temperance, intellectual narrowness, ferocious invective good? Are these the legitimate fruits of a moral and in- tellectual revival? In this sense, again, we have to ask ourselves, was Knox's way best, or was Lethington's? 'Unless the plea of Urgent necessity is admitted, there Can be no question of what the answer must be. For my own part, I decline ta accept the plea. I see no reason to doubt that the Reformation (even in Scotland) might have been successfully conducted obn other lines: that a real reform of abuses, moral and spiritual, might have been brought about without the sacrifice of intellec- tual breadth and veracity, of moderation, of comprehen- sion, of Christian charity. When we are told that Knox's Reformation was the cause of all that is "best and greatest" in the Scottish character, we are tempted to ask whether in point of fact the Scot since Knox's time has risen to arly high moral or spiritual level? It is pro- bable that under any form of religion or government the national caution and the'national shrewdness would have led to material success and worldly prosperity. But Is it just to assert that the severe and gloomy Puritan- ism of the preachers has impre-sed upon the national conscience a finer ideal of duty or a higher standard of 'purity? If this could be truly asserted, then, indeed, the narrowness, the fierceness, the bigotry might be for- gi7en. That the life led by "the Scotiish commons" smee the Reformation has been, as a rule, simple, frugal, and deveut, I Would gladly believe; but that it has been in many respects a maimed and stunted life, wanting in bezuty and attractiveness and the instinctive refinement af Moo favoured nations, as well as hard, narrow, and eaeiteat; in judgment and conduct, cannot, I am afraid, be denied. or do sobriety, purity, and cleanliness quite Cansist with certain unpleasant returns which have been taken to show (rather unfairly,'l believe) that among the nations of Europe the countrymen and country- women of Knox are the most intemperate and the most chaste From Mary Stuart in S'cotlancl,hy John Skelton, CB., in Blackwood's Iffogre:ine. BY HUGH Berm I.—THE FAMILY SAW. f Speak of me as I am; Nothing extenuate, nor aught set down in malice.—Othello. I make bold to state there are not many householders who do not possess a saw. I don't mean a saw after the style of "A rolling stone gathers no moss," but a saw in the strict sense of he word. Never mind of what quality the saw is, so long as it is a saw. If it has been in the possession of the family any reasonable length of time, it is clearly entitled to the name of the "family saw," and if you compare one hundred family saws, you will find them exactly alike. If you feel inclined at any time to persuade one end to come off a piece of wood, you just walk intro the coal-hole, and take down this tool from the wall, and the persuasion commences. The history of the family saw is indeed a chequered one. Grandmother can tell you how John scarcely ever .had it out of his hands, and what useful work • le did with it; but even ;Ike does not know, how it came into the family; so it is quite useless for the young/to:mem- bers to speculate upon its first arrival. It might have been brought here by the Crusaders; it might have been picked up at an auction many, many years ago; or it might have been bought quite new by your grand- father. These speculations are arranged in order, the first being the most reasonable, and the last being worth next to nothing. The thing must have been new some time, but really it doesn't look so. The best point of tbe family saw is, that you cannot lose it. Whenever you want it, it is there; not, pahaps, on its proper nail, but certainly not far away. To describe it would be not (ply useless but silly, when anyone can take it down and examine it. Perhaps, though, you didn't notice that it wasn't very straight. The missing teeth are the consequence of your grand- father sawing through large nails Of course, it is rusty; a family saw that wasn't rusty wouldn't be 'worth calling a family saw, and if anyone shows you a bright one in contradiction to this statement, you can tell them flatly that ymi are not so easily imposed upon. For the benefit of the rising generation, who have not yet had it out to work, it will perhaps be as Well to state the ingredients required to work along with it— auxiliaries, as it were. The recipe ought to be com- mitted to memory by every member of a well-regulated family who has not used the saw. • • "One battle of oil, or a large tallow candle; any amount of patience, and as much muscle as you can raise in a given time. Grease the blade, uncork the patience, ply the muscle, and keep your left thumb out of the way, that's all." The family saw is used chiefly to cut wood, nails, sods, bricks, Sze- To cut a board in two lengthway, you draw a pencil-line on the board, and commence to saw at one end of .the line. (N.B.—Never begin in the middle.) The tendency of the family saw on such occa- sions is to follow the line for about four inches, and then to strike aa iridependent line on its own hook. If the saw keeps on the line all the way through, you have another proof that it is not a family saw, and the sooner it is shown up in its true light the better. In this Itngth of sawing, you will probably come in contact with one or two nails, but, of course, this only makes the difference of a little extra power being re- quired on the saw, and you keep right on until the nail is cut through.: Now this is the main beauty of the family saw. The family sawyer shows none of that nervousness displayed by professional wood-workers, such as joiners, Sze., when their saws come in contact with a rail. At such a time the joinefs.language is certainly not fit to be printed and framed as an ornament in a young Men's Christian Association. The family sawyer sometimes does lose his temper, though, and all through a paltry nail, but it is generally his thumb-nail, and his remarks are directed against saws and saw-makers, in contradistinction to observa- tions of the joiner, which are directed against metal principally, and iron nails in particular. The first time I heard the F.S. consigned to a place that woujd inevitably have melted it was at Uncle Ben's, when I was a very little boy. 'Uncle B•on was patching up an old hencote, and amongst his tools was the ever- lasting F.S. remember standing besi•le him as he started to saw a piece off the end of a hoard. The proper way to do this with the F.S. is, as every- body should know, to scrape gently away with the saw teeth until you get them embedded in the wood, other- wise you are not safe. Uncle Ben spit on his hands, grasped the saw handle, and made a plunging sweep across the board, just scratching the wood, and nearly amputating his left thumb. Uncle Ben the made a short and emphatic speech in praise of nothing or nobody particular, but a pretty straight condemnation of saws and their manu- facturers, and exposing the unworthiness of humanity at large. • This was the first sample of fiery elocution that Uncle Ben was ever known to give, and those senior members

STRAITS. A MIGRATION OF TETE WOODCOCK: BN JOHN PEERS!

Beau Maris is indeed a place from whence we get —by gracious permission of our insular weather—a beautiful view of the sea; for here both land and water lend themselves to form a noble panorama by their blended beauties ;, the castle-crowned woods of Penrhyn are succeeded by the bol&bald front of Penmaenmawr, :the scarce seen valley of the Con- way, and this by the majestic Head of Orme which projects its huge mass rectangularly from the land. and helps to enclose—with the exception of a slight opening between itself and Puffin Island L-a very pretty bit of land-locked sea. The Anglesea side with its tamer, if mote homelike beauties, forms the left hand boundary of this little Mediterranean. When the summer haze hangs its purple mantle in the clefts and vales, and the laughing sea is dotted • by4vhite-sailed yachts, it is woithy to be the dream of the poet or s subject for the painter. •:1 , But we, the Woodcocks, bold Beaumaris ingrate- ful remembrance for more than its pleasing associa- tion of mountain and marine scenery. It afforded us—what after all must be the 'foundation of all

artistic and poetic ai.preciat•on of the beauties of nature—the solid, if more sordid, objects of sensual appreciation, as furnished by the butcher and baker. Nor did we forget to replenish the keg with a sup- ply of the pure element 'as supplied at per yard IneaSure from•the pier. I found little pleasure in perambulating the super-heated streets of the town, and hastened th,e,little busiiress I had to do in order to exchange the arid pavement for the cooler and more grateful, if less stable, footing of the boat. Here too, the passenger insisted on replacing the rang, or peak—down-haul—which had got quite toe' obviously in the ragman's hands, if, indeed, its state of 'attenuation was not too great to excite the cupidity of that useful, if inornate individual. And is not the rang there—and is it not not known by the co ,nomen of its donor even until this day? On the previous evening we hid tntruited to the care and convection of tha• Post- master-General a missive bearing the important shipping intelligence announcing the safe arrival of the yacht Woodcock at this port, all well, thus enabling the skip- per and his mate Simon, and, indeed, the rest of the absent crew, to take advantage of her presence in these waters, and come over to join our aquatic revels. Now Friday morning was the last the P. could spend with Us, business demanding his presence at home. As we were going down the Straits that morning, he deci- ded td accompany us to Menai Bridge, thus giving Win the opportunity of seeing more of the beauties of this narrow sea. the morning was beautifully fine, with just a nice little working .wind. So we roamed about from the steep and wooded Shore of Anglesea, past the mud encumbered harbnr of Bangor, and the school ship Cho on the South Mde, to the stage near the beauti- ful Suspension Bridge. Here we regretfully disensbarked our Passenger, he to return by tho steamer, and we to pursue the ever-fleeting phantom form if Pleasure through the rock strewn windings of the swirling ,

It might perhaps be assuming too much to say that all your numerous readers have+ seen this fine bit of scenery, so perhaps I may be excused by those who have had this pleasure if I try to convey to those of my less fortunate readers some idea of the nature and aspect of this curious water passage. The Straits here become more strait—very much contracted—which natural ad- vantage has been the mese of bringing the bridge-build- ing engiteers to the spot where the approaching shores so much facilitated their labours. The shores here, too. exchange characters, the mainland becoming high and steep and the Anglesea side low, broken, and in places overflowed by the tide. The waterway itself is very ! much embarassed by rocks, which show their unhand- some heads more or .Is according to the state of the tide. The contracted ehamiel causes the tides to rush with greatly acciel- erated speed among, around, and over these I impeding rocks, causing great overfalls of seething; water, swirling eddies, and boiling upeasts from below. 1 The watery commotion• thus created is something won- derful, and, to those unacquainted with it, absolutely awful in its manifestation of contiegent possibilities of death and destruction. Around the Fisherman's Isle, ith its little white cot, the maddened waters rage and boil with aggravated fury, and fill the air with fond oomplainings, night and day, with but slight interniis- sions of its roar when the impetuous current checks its career, but to change itidirection and renew its wild lashings among the rocks. And it IS a sight flattering to our human vanity—as showing the conquest of "mind over the blind but -destructive forces of nature—to See some big schooner manceuvring through the rock-en- cumbered channel, trimming her sails, and guiding her course with nice discrimination to escape the rocks and avoid the giddy-swirling of the eddies. Low water makes the ugly presence of these tangling ! impediments more evident, and brings to light some which, when the tide is in, are only dangerous as shoals. When examining the effects of the current upon the rocks, we are struck by bare places on them where even the qing,ing tang may not find or retain a foot- ing, the oft=fivrept surface being left bare, save for the pointed and fast-adhering habitation of a shell fish, giv- ing these patches a conspicuous appearance among the tang-grown surface of quieter places The persistence of these obstructions to the free passage of the tide is, I think, owing largely to the purity of the water. The sand-laden water of the Merseywould have scoured them away long ago, Turning off from the stage with mutual good wishes, we were soon swept by the swift current under Telford's noble bridge and among the mazes of this much-vexed channel ; here over to the Anglesey side, there Close to the steep rocks on the main land, and under the southernspan of the Britannia Tubular Bridge, and so out into the quieter waters opposite a picturesque-looking water mill on the Anglesey side. A little below this, and on the op- posite' side, lay the coasting flat Perc' Y Captain Plump- ton, of and for Sankey Bridges, slate laden, await- ing the turn of the tide, to take her through the Swellies. Hailing her, brought on deck a young laely, of whom we inquired if that (without indicating which) was the way to San- key Bridges? To which she, with equal vagueness, an- swered, " Oh! yes, straight on !" Accepiug these some- what vague sailing directions for what they were worth, we turned the boat's head towards Caernarvon, and dropped, with the tide through a ra.thher narrow part of the Straits where the water is of that still-flowing, deep- green. darksome depth that gives, withthe overshadowing woods, rather a gloomy aspect to the place. Here, on the Anglesea side is &tine residence with stone steps to the water, and a little dock, with a little steam yaeht in it. Past Port Dinorwic, a cleft in the rocks, up which vessels crowd to load slate coming fromitho Dinorwie slate quarries. Here the Straits begin to widen out, and become sandy., this giving them a more home-like look. The old familiar golden sands appear once more with the winding channels rippling between. Through these Alf. and I, the remnant of the crew,. dropped quietly and pleasantly down to Caernarvon. Here we found the "Ada," of Runcern, Mr. Timmins' steam yacht. They quickly recognised the old "Crocodile," the Runcorn equivalent for "Woodcock," and gave us a friendly hail.

The Straits here very much resemble our own estuary —somewhat the same width—the same extensile sands, but infinately clearer water. After a stroll through this interesting old town and making• a few purchases, we turned off with the flood tide and began to retrace our steps, if such a thing be possible in a boat. When we came to the "Percy" w found them busily getting ready to run the gauntlet of the Swelliea. Now wind there was none, and we were rather curious to see how a laden vessel would be manceuverei through the intricacies of the shoal,' channel. The little boat Was manned and ladled, for our friend of the sailing directions stepped into her and took an oar—yes! and used it manfully, if such an expression be admissible in this case. Anyway, she did good work, and it was vary pleasant to see such willing hands doing suck good work. The day was broil- ing hot and the cup of tea they served out to -those in the punt was well-earned and doubtless very acceptable. In our case we had to go without the tea, having no one to boil the kettle for us, all the crew being actively engaged in rowing. However, we as well as the " Percy" escaped the rocky perils of the place and slowly rowed our slow way to Bangor, in the harbour of which we spent the night.

div.head: OUR LONDON LMER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LMER.
LONDON. THURSDAY NIGHT. The series of Cabinet Councils immediately pre- ceding the opening of Parliament have commenced, . .
and w"ill be ContinUed at regular intervals up to the eve of the session. Since the Government have

boldly decided to turn a deaf ear to popular protest, nothing could be more comfortable than their posi- tion. There is no example of a Government equally strong, for the simple reason that since 'constitu- tional government was established succepsive minis- tries have always been liable to the conSeqiiences of , -defeat in the Hou.sd of Commons. A little more than two years ago Mr. Gladstone, though on the main lines of his policy sUpporta.by a substtintial majority, was on a particular question defeated by it Coalition.of Conservatives and Irish members. He thereupon resigned, a Conservative Ministry came in; and there was witnessed the anomaly of the Liberal Chief, on'all important divisions, sp.ll master of the situation, sitting in opposition, whilst a minority Ministry hung on tremiilously to the Treasury Bench. It was, on the whole, not a very .cont enient state of things. Bu 4 was decreed by Constitutional law that the Minister of the day be- ing defeated on a critical division, should resign, and Mr. Gladstone obeyed the law. Lord Salisbtlry, head and representative of the great Constitutional Party, knows better than that. He has, with a cynicism almost splendid in its audacity, formally declared that if he is defeated upon' a division in the House of Commons he will not necessarily dis- solve Parliament. . .

That being io,.there is no need whithe' ConsPr- vatives should abandon office till ,by the flux ,of time the life of the present Parliament expires. Even 'Lord Salisbury cannot very well decree the suspension of the Septennial Act. But he may upon this new opportunity.avail himself of its utmost limits, and is certainly inclined to do so. The mean- ing' of his announcement on the Dissolution ques- tion is obtrusively plain. He, at the moment, en- joys control of a motley assembly of politicians: He is driving an ill-assorted team and knows tliat at any.moment either the leaders may stop, tiirn round and stare him in the face, or the wheelers may jib.- Lord Salisbury announces that they may do-so if they please, but the coach shall not there- fore stop. If the Conservative section of the Mini- sterial party object to any ,clause in .the Local Governitent Bill, or any proposal with respect to Procedure, they may amuse themselves by voting against the Government without the apprehension of displacing thei,r leaders and bringing in the ter- rible-Mr. Gladstone. A similar liberty isguaranteed to the Dissentient Liberals, and so things will log pleasantly along, Union being found even in pis- union.

This itnportept condition being settled there re- Mains nothing for the Cievernment hut to. prepare a programme that shall to like a geobd deal 'of work, and involve as littldr result as possible.- fhe one thing next to the im, ortarne ,of .remaining in office is to postpone the inevitable question of Home Rule for Ireland. In order A.co do that with decent pretence of conserving the general interests of the Empire, the Local Government question for England will be taken up and pursued with every appear- ance of anxious desire to settle it; ankhere at once is presented the cleft stick in which eGovernment maintained in such peculiar circumstances is sure to find itself. There is a Radical wing of the Dis- sentient Liberal Party which even with the object of keeping Mr. Gladstone out of office could not for shame accept a settlement of the Local Gov cra- m ent question such as would recommend itself to the Conservative country gentlemen. Mr. Chamber- lain and Mr. Chaplain, for eXample could 'never agree upon the elementary basis of elective power. • But what of that, since Lord Salisbury's happy ex- ' pedient will be in force? At a critical period there will be a hostile division, and the Local Government Bill will be lost; but the Government—a Govern- ment which dies in the ordinary course of nature, but never surrenders—will be safe, the session will be wasted; and the Irish question staved Off for another twelve months. That is the Ministerial programme for the session of 1888, and it .has every prospect of being comportably carried out. - Mr. Wilson Barrett seems to be the only' man not amused by the high and finished comedy which has resulted in the transference of his drawing-room furniture to unknown and unauthorised hands. The . .

-- episode recalls the storrof the witness in the Lady Colin Campbell case whose magnificent fur awit was frequently referred to. Some smart member of the unemployed in court mastering the situation posted off to the witness's house, asked • for the fur coat of which he represented the owner was in urgent need, got it, and has never since been heard of. A learned judge has been led to disclose a similar Story personal to himself not yet published. In a case he presided over, a witness swore that he could not fix the time of a particular juncture be- cause he had accidentally left his watch at home. The cross-examining counsel was rather sceptical about this, whereupon. the Judge said—" There is nothing unusual in that. Why, only this. morning I left my watch blithe dressing table,- and did not recollect it till before entering the court I wanted to find out the time." When the Judge got home he found a messenger had visited the house, men- tioned the J'udge's forgetulness, descnihed where the watch was, and asked for it to take,to the , owner. Then the Judge' remembered what he had 'said in Open dourt. . •. • ' In the interesting sories of letters published by a local Paper, in which Mr. W. S. Cain&is describing his journey round the-world, he mentions a domes- tic incident that befeli him 'at Nikko. . Nikko is one of the sights of Japan, not its least attractions lying in the fact that in order to reach it travellers have to undertake a long journey, involving something like six days'-traveqing. When Mr. Caine and his daughter,who is his travelling comptinionoat down to their first dinner in the tea house at Nikko they discovered that wa.zer was served to them in bottles, one of which has-once held Scotch whisky, another being an imperial pint bottle. bearing Bass's well- known name on it. lam not size about the Scotdh whisky. but I know all about the Bes.s's beer bottle, for, to tell the truth, it was mine. 'Travel- ling through Japan four years ago by the route Mr. Came has follevied, we were, through the courtesy of Count Inouy4, Foreign Minister', accompanied by one of his private secretaries. This gentleman's knowledge of the English lesiguage was not pro- found, but his appreciation of the Ilaglish charac- ter was like Mr. Weller's ackuaintance with London, extensive and peculiar, tie accompanied us to Nikko, and seeing us installed in the tea house left to return to obis deities at Tokio. Before going he 'wished to make as a little present,expres- sire of the esteem which had grown up on the ' journey. After passing a sleepless night in cogita- tion he hit upon the very thing. Nothing, he felt sure, would bring such joy to the heart of two Eng- lishmen and an Eng,lisia lady, far from their island home, than a good glass of beer. He had heard of Bass's bottled beer, but it is needless to say it is not sold at roadside tea houses in the interior of Japan. Nor was such a thing ever seen in Nikko. Ile accordingly telegraphed to Yokohama. whence a dozen imperial pints of Bass wore sent to the terminus of the railway, and thence by special messenger on a jinrickshaw. We stayed long enough in Nikko to finish this price- less gift, and learn with tender interest how shocked -So stout a teetotaller as Mr. Caing was to have his table water purveyed under the Ilk of one of the most powerful enemies of the cause. Some weeks ago there appeared in "Punch " a brief poem which 80 tersely and faithfully summed up the character of Mr. Bright that it. has since become a catchword in London. It ran thus— . 4".10hn Bright, Always right." But there is nothing new under the sun. Turning over an old volume of "Punch" I And that eighteen
-iv
it c,l

years ago the-v.6v same-Weal struck another-:COU-- tributor to " Punch," and was expressed in verse differing only in' metre -and length. It is to be foetid in the number of June 14th; 1869. The Home of Lords were muttering discontent with the Irish ,phurch Bill. • Mr. Bright had it that time been scarcely a year installed' in -Cabinet- office, gnd it was vainly expected that the responsibility. per- taining to his new positien: Would modify his or- dinarily But this did not prdve the case. • He took an opportunity. of blillying the peers and threatening them 'With " aceidints un- pleasant to think of." • Notice, was taken in both.

houses of Parliament of this ebullition of temper on the part of a Cabinet Minister, and Mr. Glad- stone was obliged to disavow official knoWledge or reponsibility for it. "Punch " had a cartoon on the subject, with some verses, the first of which runs thus—

"You're an eloquent man; John Bright, John Bright— You're an eloquent man, John Bright— But the tune of your song Is still " nu are wrong; There's but one man invariably • And that's Bright !-- He's the one man who always is right. Z The lobby of the HOlll3B of commons wi,ll &vein hardly itself, bereft of the presence :of Inspector Denning. t suppose there is no public man of the day more widely and, •it may be safely said, more favourably known than Mr. Denning. A generation. of members of .Parliament `have come and gone. since he first put on his braided uniform. He has seen social and political revolutions, has watched -parties grow and decay, Governments come in with vast majorities and go out broken .up by tea-room cabals, cave assemblies, and other sectional forma- tions. Hisposition was one of greet responsibility, full of daily difficulty, which was surmounted by an inborn tact, a natural geniality, that made life pleasant •both for, liiiiiselfPand ;those who!came in contact with him. In and about the, House of Comnions, as far as Inspector Denning's influence went, discipline was strictly- maintained, but in a manner that preVented unnecessary friction. Mr. Denning, by no meang an old man, :has that ruddy complexion that implies excellent health. But he has had hard times of 'late, what with dynamitards *outside aid obstructors inside the House. During the dynamite panic I remember meeting him in the corridor one night carrying a box under his arm, It was addressed to the Home Secretary, then Si; William Harcourt. Sir William did not like the look of it, so sent for• Denning. and blandly asked him to take the box to hie room and open it. —Sir William Harcourt was not the man to be deterred by danger to the Chief Inspector. When the box was opened• it Was found to cOntrtin ft iiisty old pistol, with a trigger,that would not work, and a piece of red• pocket handkerchief that would not explode. If-the Home Secretary bad known that, he probably would have winged the box himself. Ai it was, it was one of the reanY,difficulties'iliat fell to the lot of Inspector Denning.

div.head: SERMON TO. 'YOUNG MEN...
div.p: SERMON TO. 'YOUNG MEN...

„ . In the course of a special Settle:on' to young men delivered in Wycliffe Congregational Church; -War- rington, on Sunday evening, by the Rev. Jbhn Yon,ge, the reverend gentleman, who took for his -subjeet the words, "What be did. when. be beeame a man,” spoke of the difference between'a eorniii of age in the .motal sense and in the legal sentle; A legal infant, he remarked, could not come into pro- perty, or do anything that should alienate it. He could not exercise the franchise, nor be elected to serve in Parliament, during his infancy, yet,- so in- .congruous was the law of the land that, at a much younger age than tvventy-sme ties might be formed, engagements contracted, and even marriages enteod into, which would influence the enti-e subsequent life of a person. In ancient Rome men were re- garded as minors until they had completed their twenty-fifth year, and in our own day there were in various countries different acms at which the minosity expired and legal manhood commenced. He took it that most young men were disposed to put the legal age of twenty-one as tolerably far ad- vanced for the beginning of manhood. Perhaps they might consider the term infant, as applied to them, derogatory, if not insufferable. There was a consider- able tendency, even among lads of fourteen or fifteen, to • claim privileges and assume the airs of young:men. What used to be known at one time as boyhood, the period between childhood and youth, had now become a very-brief stage. A boy was now a youth, and at six- teen he was a young man. To expect a youth of six- teen or se'venteen to mind when his ,mother speaks to him, and to do his father's will, in many caaes would be looked upon ae an undue assumption of authority on the part of the parent, and an unreasonable exPectation of obedience from a young man. It was no doubt a question admitting Of much diseussion,amongst youths especially, as to when manhood commenced, and also a.s to what constituted manhood, but it would not 14 difficnit to, select specimens from life of boys who tried to drags and talk and net as asen—who Spoke with dhgmatism on sub- jects of trade, eommerce, politics, and religion as though they had served half a dozen apprenticeships and were well versed in the ways of the world. They might find them every i day, and See them on every pave- ment, especially n the evening. When' they became men they were apt. to tale a „ereat deal of license and freedom to act as they liked, without con- suiting the wishes of parents, or paying attention to home regulation.'' Apparently it was thought manly to go out. and come In when they liked, to spend their even- ings out of door, and to do as they liked about going to a place of worship on Sundays.. there were some who looked with something like contemptuous indifference and incredulity upon the religiimthat had been themain- ' stay, and the hope and courage of their parents, ~and was the most precious thing that they had. He did not envy the disposition of the youth who had been trained religiously by God-fearing parents, still finding it •con- venient to live under their roof, glad of its shelter and the many•ministrations of fatherly And motherly affec- tion, but who had got to be so civer that when his parents went to church he turned out for a stroll, or lounged in self-indulgence at home. . Very earnestly did he hope that youths and young men who had been brought up in o°d-fearing homes would never pass such slight upon parental training, and inflict such a painful wound on a parent's heart. Some respect was due from the young to the very faith ortheir parents. They might have attained the legal age of manhood, but they should not claim a liberty in this respecti-at any rate at the cost of knowing that they inflict eff grief upon a mother's heart, and disappointment to a father. It was' by no means so customary as it should be. for a youth; when he became a man, to take himself. resolutely in hand; and determine in the highest and noblest sense to be a man: That was what he wished to impress upon them that night. Manhood in its full sense want full responsi- bility—full and direct acakountableness. They must re- member, too, that in this life they had to prepare for eternity, and they must also divest themselves 'of the opinion that manhood was a synony-rn for freedom. Man- hood meant responsibility; it meant stewardship, it meant eternal honour or eternal shame. Mr. Yongethen spoke of the manhood of the Apostla Paul, his sermon being listened to with attention by a crowded cong,rega- tion. .

BRUTAL Wn-n Mtrunms.— Tietvven one and two o'clock on Thursday morning a lablkuring man named George Timms murdered Ins wife in Charles-street, Warwick, by battering her skull with a brick. The,: parties quarrelled on Wednesday night, and While the winnan was asleep, in bed the husband • attabied her 'as described, killing her' instantly., He theist an out• of the houge, and meeting a policeman, seized him, and said "I have; killed my wife." He was 'thereupon arrested. - -

THE THAFALOAR-SqUARE MEETINGS.—The trial of Mr. Graham, M.P. and Mr. John Burns, on charges arising out of the conflict in Trafalgar-square, on Sunday, Nov. 13th, ended at the Central Criminal Court, on Wednes- day, in each of the accused being found guilty of unlaw- ful assembly, but not guilty of .riot Cr of assaulting the police. Mr. Justice Charles, who said he agreed with the verdict, senbSiced each defendant to six weeks' impri sonment without hard labour. - _ _

.... _ THE QUEEN AND THE POPE.—Speaking on Wednesday evening at. the annual meeting of the Manchester anil Salford Auxiliary of the Congregational Church Aid and Home Missionary Society, the Rev. R. B. Brindle,- (Not- tingham) said he thought the action of the Queen in send- mg to the Dbpe on the occasion of his jubilee a jug and plate to be used at Mass was open to criticism. That was a matter which concerned the English church. for the Queen was the head of the Church of England, and was the sworn defender of the Protestant faith. RELEASE OF FATHER RTAN.—Fatheil Ryan was released from Limerielr gaol on Wednesday morning. The demon- stration which it was prqpesed to hold in his honour was not proclaimed, but the Government instructed Major Rella.ston, the magistrate in charge of the police, to dis- perse, by force if necessary, any gathering that-fnight be held. In spite of this a large nuMber of people assem- bled outside the prison, and cheered Father Ryan when he appeared. During the day Father Ryan made three speeches, and he was escorted by a large crowd to Her- bertstown. To THE DEAF.—A person who was cured of deafness of 23 years' standing by a simple remedy will send a description of it free to any person who applied to Nicholson, 15, Camden Park-road, London, N.W.-2144.

div.p: CHAPTER I.

BEIGHT,EYED PHYLLIS. Simon Knight was a well-t 041.6 Man, better to do than most of his acquaintances; and he knew it inn well, and expressed it in his Sleeks Comfortable, and at times slightly insolent mien, though in words he was perpetually forcing 'on general notice that .he was a poor hard-working individual who, with all-his strivings was little more than a pauper. No one be- lieved him. How could they with that well-built substantial red house of 'his staring them in the face as they walked across Wandsworth Common, and the well-set:OW yard lying, behind it; why the brass plate on his door alone, startled ' outsiders into an enormous respect for the man's position as a teades- %man . • SIMON..KNIGHT, I ' Builder. %s • . (Funerals punctually attended.) This latter line Was engraved in larger letters than .the preceding ones; people said this was done to tor- ment his wife, who had an intense horror of all allu- sion to the subject of death, and could not think "why Simon didn't stick to building houses for the living and leave the:dead' folk , get buried without his interference." Simon however, saw things not at all in this light, and as he stood by his own door, clay pipe in mouth, ,in the gloaming of a May evening, lie was chuckling over aa order he had received that day for the burial of a Wandsworth magnate, and reckoning.how fs- larger was the percentage gained by supplying fune- rals than that he could ever lefile for in the ardifutry course of his buildins' business. ' "Folks is always easier let in when they is de- pressed," he remarked to himself, "and when the will hasn't been read• and they ain't. sure who'll have to pay, the hill—give up funerals indeed! , Hannah's a fool—but then she always Was a peer thing—a very poor thin,. Whatever would she make of life if I was to die.. She shan't have much money to squander on • another man. ' lin blessed if she shall. I'll tie it up tight on the gal. The gal ! It was just my, luck to ' have a gal, instead of a boy. Phyllis is comely eriousds and loves me, I make no doubt, butif slits was only a boy as could succeed me in this bit. of business Fein better pleased—succeed me, grade& power. Simon Knight, you're getting maudlin—you'd, best go down to the public for a bit and pull . yourself, together—succeed —there won't be no succeeding you for, many a year yet; by that time we'll see if a grandson can't do it." And having come to the em], of his soliloquy very much to his owrisatisfaction, Simon Knightlasselted the ashes out of his pipe preparatory to a saunter down the roadto the Three Griffins,Where he very fre- quently 9/Pent his evenings andscame back—well, not exactly what might' be called the worse for liquor; but decidedly inclined to he most disagreeable to his wife and daughter.,, Having emptied his pipe, he lint it in his pocket, and, looking round, called out, "Mind the door, Hannah'; I'm 'going out a bit" "All right," answered a querulous voice from a dis- tant room. , ' Simon Knight; though he could well have afforded it, kept no servant, but made his Wife Who was by no means strong, _ and pretty Phyllis' Who was only seventeen, do all the work of the red-brick establish- ment, even to washing and ironing: the '.buildee's shirts and white waistcoats, of which latter he *ore , a considerable number in the :summer months. He thought they added to his importance, he said, and truly he was night, .if he meant that they made his portly figure leek more portly, and,for a man of forty- fivele was Of no mean proportions. Besides a'whiteeraistcoat he indulged in a white hat:which was generally put on rather on one side,and these were the only white things about him, for his well-shaven face was so ,red as 'to be 'almost scarlet, and his cloth clothee, were always seedy-looking and dark. The white hat rather more on one side than usual, he swagg_erecl a few yards along the road and then paused to look over his own. wall. • "IN by, that there timber has never been taken down to Cominingses, and I told Greaves about it this booming. I'll discharge Greaves if I have to sneak about things twice. Hullo, whatever is that moving, in among them planks. No one's a right to be in the yard. at this hour of the evening"—then Shouting out,. "1 say you there, who are ye, and what are ye at?" At first there was no answer. So. Simon Knight shouted again,this time more loudly and angrily than before. One of the planks fell with a clatter as though nervous trepidation lurked behind it, and a curly head, surmounted by • a round brown hat, ap- peared • the rest of the individual's' sperson was' planks forming a sort. of barricade which concealed , Mr. Knight, however, recognised the head at once, -even in the rapidly increasing darkness and called out still in a voiceof thunder, 'Phyllis, why what the devil are you doing there ?" "Conic and help me instead of asking questions," she said, "yon see, I have got into difficulties." Phyllis was evidently not afraid of her father how- ever cross and harsh he might be. Afraid! no, with her winsome ways and bright eyes, she would have been an utter little fool to be afraid of any man. And Phyllis Knight was by no means a fool and she know full well that to manage, her old savage of a father she must meet him more or less on his own ground. To assist Phyllis in extricating herself from the planks among which she had no business, and from which, in the event of their all coming clattering down she stood in some danger of her life, Mr. • night had to go,baels to the house door and through the house to the yard. There was a gate- leading from the lane at the further extremity of the yarde but of this Mr. 'Knight had not the key, as it. was always kept on a nail in the parlour- out of work hours. It took him ' a minute or two them to reach Phyllis, and during that minute or two Phyllis had not been idle, but had managed with an agility„ for which she was re- nowned, to scramble on to the top of a tottering stack of timber. ' "Good God! Phyllis, you'll break your neck," cried Mr. Knight.. " You,are the most audacious gal. Now bide.there,still till I eau reach you." "All right, father ; " hilt the end of the brief sentence w,as a most overwhelming crash that brought peeple withia a quarter of a mile to their wiudows and Made. Simon Knight's red face turn as white as hiswaistesat, while it so paralysed him that he did not attempt to move one step farther. • The last echo of the crash, however, had not finished its reverlseration through the yard,, when a ringing peal of laughter. fell on his ear. Phyllis had jumped from her perilous position, and though she had brought the whole stack of wood down behind her, she was standing unhurt on terra firma in front of her father. "Itds all Greaves's fault," she said. "I heard you tell him this morrdng to load that wood and cart it to Cumming,ses." ' • "Greaves be hanged !" interrupted Mr. Knight. getting angry now he saw his daughter was safe, I"What the: devil businees. had you to get ,there I should like to know ?" , • "Well, I was coming in at the back gate—and it was dark you know—and of course, I thought the wood was gone since I heard—" "Nonsense, ; what were you doing at the back pee ? I've told you fifty times I won't have that there key took off its nail—after dark too. You'd no business , out. Your mother ought to be ashamed of herself. Where have yea been Answer me, d'ye hear." But Phyllisslid not answer him, only tried to get phmasii:tpio(hh:nniei:ainnatto:ng,house. She made a point of never answering hint if She could help it when he was angry, "it only led to words' she sagely decided. appeared M no mood to change that's what you've been after," he knight, however, went on,"and I can tell you, you young hussy, that it ain't no good your starting .lovers. I ain't going to victual none of the lazy chaps as thinks your pretty face and the chance of a ready-niade business ''ud suit 'else You'll marry a well-to-do middle-class respecta- ble tradesman of my choosin', or you won't marry at all."

" Ler', father, how: you do rattle on, " cried Phyllis laughing, and compelled to answer, in spite of herself, ," Who is thinking of marrying or love- making; it ain't me, if that,',s what you mean—l've been to the station with Miss Irene.'

"Miss IlAie, has she been here again ? I'm blessed if she ain't always here, and I'm pretty nigh sick on't Phyllis, that's what I am. -These grand folk always hanging about, and your mother encourages them. Don tdo you no good, gal; they illyour head with their own beastly airs and graces." ' " Why, father, I thought you were devoted to Mr. Stanhope; that it was he or his father tvho first set you lip in life," • • •

"Who told you that, gal ? " asked Simon, his red face turning into a sort of purple. • Phyllis was going to say mother," but even in the semi-clarkne,ss she could not fail to note the expres- sion of the builder's countenance, and in a moment was sorry she had been so imprudent as-to speak. If she shielded her mother he would think it was some member of the Stanhope family who had been gossipping, and considering that Simon seemed to have objected very much of late to the' frequent visits of these people to his yard, and still more to hers and her mother's constant journeys to Mr. Stanhope's house in Eaton-square, she was a little bit perplexed whato to answer; , While she was thinking, he thundered fcrtki the - query a second time. "Poor mother! She'll have to bear the brunt of another storm. But if it wasn't about this it would be about something else," 'Added Phyllis, all in a hurry. And she was right. Many were the vials of wrath poured forth on Mrs. Knight's .unoffending head, when her lord and master chose to be out of temper. • No sooner had Phyllis pronounced in a subdued voiee the simple word " mother" than he strode into the house, straightinto the parlour where his wife was sitting at work. • "How dare you—how dare you say that I'm be- holden to the Stanhopes ?, What do you know 'about the matter, I'd like to inquire?" he asked vphem- ently, the. words almost seeming to choke hire as they came out, and his whole appearance :giving the impression that an apoplectic seizure was imminent. Mrs. Knight laid her work in her lap,and looked up at him quietly and sorrowfully. She was a little woman, bearing on her face the remnants of a great beauty; but she was, oh ! so faded and weary-looking that it made even the .c,s,yest beholder sad for a second or two as he gazed at her. As for Phyllis, she idolised her mother, and her heart often ached for her, while she strove hard to make matters a bit smoother for her ',• she had inherited all her mother's beauty, and a good deal Of her father's spirit, which enhanced it, and made her a brighter and more cap- able Woman than ever her Mother told f " nothing, mother," she broke in now. " Only a foolish remark o mine that has set father

raging." , " Hold your tongue, you hussy," shouted Simon, "and don't ,interrupt. me." fhon turning to his Wife, "Did you or 'did you not say, Hannah, as I was beholden tot hem Stanhope.s ?" "I never said anything but the truth, Simon," re- plied his wife meekly, bat firmly, "You know the truth as well as I do." • "The truth,".lie sneered; ". blessed if I think vost know much about, the truth—if I thought as you aid, I'd break every bone in -,,,our,skin," Mrs. Knight quivered and shut her eyes... Was it only too possible that she did not know all the truth, she wondered, and that last sentence of hers had served as a shot, and hail gone home. She did not attempt to answer him; exeept: on Phyllis's account she would, perhaps, have " been thankful if he had finished her straight off; existence, with this tyrant for household lord, stirring. up -perpetual „donrstic was almost more, than she could endure. Phyllis as usual, came to the rescue. • "Look here, father, if you want to break bones break mine, they are pretty hard---got a bit of your own stuff about them—but you shan't touch mother.' He turned round on his daughter for a moraent,and then something like a smile stole over his harsh features. He loved Ph§llis. She was, as- hie had just said, bone of his hone, flesh of his flesh, and her high spirit generally , had the effect of dannting him. If poor patient Hannah. had sliewn a little more pluck. he Would probably, have respected and cared snore about her, and not been quite such a great bashaw ; but it was too late for a new leaf to be turned over now as far as she was concerned. - Phyllis at once noticed her father's smile and seized the opportunity to turn the conversation, away from dangerous subjects. "Come oh, let's have supper;" she said, "Mother's sat long enough over that endless seam, and I'm that hungry with jumping a. off that stack. Didn't you hear, the crash, mother 71 wonder you didn't come out.' "Was thatyou, Phyllis? I thought it was an earthquake Or summat, but as your dad was there I supposed he'd see to it." "See to it if it was a earthquake," shouted Simon knight, this time laughing, heartily, "my sto- Hannah, well you must have an opinion of nie,and mistake, if you think as I can see to earthquakes. " Well, you're always a meddlin' with tho dead, and burying—one thing leads to another, Simon. t ain't clever, as you know, and it's beyond me to sal wherever you'll stop." , "All right, old woman, you go on a believin' in me, and you'll never get far out of the track, but don't let's have no preachin' about benefits received and a parcel of humbug as you don't understand." And so, thanks to Phyllis, 'good humour was rø established, and since Simon had been balked of his usual visit to the "Three Griffins." it might perchance, with management, last through the evening, especially as Phyllis gave it as her tention. if he was very good that she would crook n little bit-of delicious hot Supper. She left, the door open, however, ' while she went into the ;kitchen for this purpose, so that she might- come to the rescue at any moment if a storm once more blew up between her father and mother. * . Quiet, however, seemed to reign for 'a while. Simon took a paper all sat down in his arm-chair by the windOw ; Phyllis's voice singing over her cook' ing in the kitchen seemed to soothe him. Perhaps she knew that it had this effect for she warbled away most unremittingly as though thoroughly , la.ying claim to the, title of the "Wandsworth nightingale," as she- was called. Meantime Mrs. Knight folded up the white seam and 'busied herself laying the table -for supper, a bit of housewifely 'care which she had just ac- complished When Phyllis came back, and tn, the tune of "Loves young dream," 'set a bog' of gorgeous buttercup,* in the centre of the table, and beside them a' foaming 'tankard of ale. Simon Knight threw down his piper, and drew hi. chair nearer to the- ale. "Well, gal, you can sing—if you -can't de, naught else,'' he said, as lie,took up the tankard. "Yes, and I can cook," she answered, "as yon will see presently, when you get a pig's fry for your supper as would please a king." Another second or two, and it is on the table beside a dish of floury potatoes, and the three Knights are so happy together for the time that it would seem almost impossible that the cloud n( bigger than a man's.ltand is always. there ready develop at any moment into a dangerous and ovo whelming tempest. .Phyllis, whose cheery bright nature detests gloorn ' and storm . hopes they tire going 'to have no more storm for that evening; at all events, and she doe her best, and with great sueeess,to keep the converse. tion as much as possible out of da.ngeroin channels, and is rejoicing over her cleverness, whel a loud knock conies at the outer door. It is not yet locked; in fact, owing to the warmness of the even- ing, is 'still open, so Simon's stentorian voice bids' knocker to. come, in. Another minute, and a man of about six-and- twenty puts hiS head into the sitting-room, and i' received by Simon Knight with the cordial greeds' of, "Well! to 'be sure, who ever expected to see Ti Chilton this ere•blessed May evening t" (To be canti )

LOVE AND LEARNING:.

A well-known, elderly nobleman, of large wealth, wooed and won, a few years ago, a young and very' beautiful girl. Their life has been as happy as it is pos- sible for married life to be, when December is united to May. . His lordship is distinguished in scientific civeles and possesses high literary attainments. Some time after • his marriage he Was foolish enough to think that, his Lovell wife was not sufficiently educated, and laid out a course of reading for her. A month later he inquired about her prowess. and found that she had nntopened a book. He set up hl eye' brews after the manner of old husbands when their young wives have displeased them. Whereupon she looked up at him with d bewitching smile, and said: " I was made to be loved, not to be learned." She won the day, of course. What is learning compared bathe light of a sunny blue eye P Would not a husband rathei be met with a senile and a kiss. then by a wife who assured him that she "knew her lesson ?" Wtsdont Is all very well, but winning ways go further. Laughing eyes beat Greek roots all to nothing. A woman's lovely tresses, waving on the outside of her shapely head, are more precious in a husband's eyes than ever so much learning in- side of it. Therefore. all women should endeavour, to preserve their attractions, and welcome their liege lords, with loving looks, pleasant smiles, and flowing silken tresses, for after all a beautiful head of hair is the crowning charm of. a woman, 9. charm which all may possess by using Mrs. S. A. Allen's World's Hair Restorer, which will keep the hair healthy and strong, restore gray or faded hair to its original color, and make it, soft. silk,, wavy and hmurtnit. MONDAY.—The new bill giving increased stringency to the present anti-Socialist legislation was aublaittea to the Reichstag to-day. The leading feature of the measure is a provision for the expatriation, or 4ntire loss of the right of German citizenship, in the case of certain offences against the law. The preamble of the bill justifies this provision on the ground that under the existing law persons against whom a decree •of expulsion has been issued are in the habit of resum- ing their agitations in their new places of abode, carry- ing it frequently into districts which hitherto have been but little or not at all affected by the Socialist prdpa- ganda. It is further explained that those who deny to the State thesright of existence should have no claim to remain German subjects. Ih order to guard against a too far-reaching application of the new law, the bill Stipt.lates that etpatriation shall only be resorted to when a qualified magistrate shall have declared it to be ad m es ble.

It is stated that over ft hundred. people have' been fruzeuto death. :The.trains have been 'blacked for, days. Yonx. Mornay NTOTTT.—Telograms describe the b'imard throughout Tex" Minneso, a, Docota, AlonfAna,, Nebraska, and Kansas as the worst known. • Within 24 hours the mercury fell from 74 above *.ero to 28 below it. Almost, in a single hour a cloudless sky was replaced by snow as fine as flour, driven by a roaring wind at a frightful velocity. 'Men's voices were inaudible at a dispincs of 61t. , Children perished when coining from school, and farmers returning from the fields died before reselling their houses. One womaii, who stepped from her door to look for; her husband, died at the tbreshold. . . . To majority of those who lost their' litres were: stiffo- cated rather than frozen, it being impossible to breathe agaiest the bl'zzard. Although the list of fatalities is ine.imol3te, the •lodS of life is known to exceed one hundred. . Thirty-five paupers,- who arrived at New York on board .ihe' steamer 'Leerdain, have not been chewed to Lull, and hate consequently returned to Europe.._ -

- THE SNOWSTORM IN AMERICA.-230 LIVES LOST. , Pitiful reports continue to be received in New York from all. the districts visited- by the rEcent, blizzard, and the total number of victims is now 'expected to itench two ,hundred. In addition tp those actually frozen to death, a large nunabjr had their limbs an other parts of the bodye'fioien, while many.lost their way in the blihcling snow and perished, being caught in the storm .owing to the sudden blinding snow, and being, thus ;unable to pro- ceed or seek shelter. Many, in .fact, perished only a short distance from places of refuge, not ,knowing of their proximity, owing to the denseness of the Snow. Whole batches of school children perished on their vfay to their "homes, and a large number of Cattle have been killed by ,lit-frost. The severe cold has also extended to TexaS, where, however, it Was of short duration. LIFE. , LISBON, THUNSDAY - The, steamer Cascapeclia, ' 'of Livespool, .put into pert to-day. She was in a collision 2.'eAterday with .the steamer Oxfordshire, 'which sank, the Ca.scapcdia enlyl,sueceetling in resetting four of her crew. , ALARMING NEWS • FROM CENTRAL 'AFRICA., .". Much anxiety has been 'Caused in Edinburglii, by the receipt of alarming hews from the Livingsbnlia.regiort, in Central Africa, concerning the fate of missionaries of the :Scottish Free Church 'out-there, aWil, tribes, the Angqiii and the Aryonga, were On the eve,of battle when the latest despatch was sent, and the position of the missionary staffs-at Aitgonf and Bendawe was such as ex-. cited the gravest concern. The'war party threatened to drive Dr. Laws out of the country. Dr. Elmslie is nego- tiating: •

The bank rate Of discount ,was On Thursday reduced from 3i't to 3 per cent: . • THE Pin:AMITE PLOTS: A CURIODS I'DOCEEDING.— The Glasgow :police stated on Satgrday that it was quite' true the police have been watching ,the move- ments of a fashionably-dressed Irish American, believed to have come to GlasgOW' op a Fenian missiotl. He visited the railway stations, and met the worst Fenian in Glasgov. Seeing he was witched he hailed a hansom, and the detectives jumped in beside him. The vehicle drove to the police station. After examination the'un- known man washllowed to go. He proceeded to Loudon, where the Scotland Yard officials met hith. It is sup- posed that he is connected with the Paris dynamitards. THE WEISE TITHE DISTRAINTs.— The distraints for ' non-payment of tithes in Flintshire were resumed on Saturday in a mountainous district close to the Welsh seat of the Duke of Westminster. The inhabitants took very little interest in the proceedings, and the 13th Ilussars, who during the week had been engaged in pro. tect inf., the officials at the sales, left Holy well for Man- chester. The ground traversed covered a distance ot twenty miles, but the amount of tithe due was small, amounting in one instance to only sixteen pence. No distraiate were made, but the likrid will be seized by the Sheriff, unless the landlord undertakes in the meantime „ pay the tithes. At a meeting on Saturday night, at Hoywell, at which Mr. John Roberts, M.P., Mr. Abraham, and others spoke, Mr. Roberts described the pro- ceedings of the past week as.an ineffable disg,race to the Church in Wales., A WHOLESALE AfortretnEss.—llungarian papers report' that a woman from csoka, being desirous of joining the religious sect of the Nazareans, went to see one of the priests residing at &ate. Proselytes have to make a full confession of . their past sins extending over, their whole lives. That 'of the new, convert ,ran thus :—" I have had eight children, and have killed them all. My first, a boy. darned Victor, born in 1874, was four months old when he died. Another was born in 1879. I forget what we caUed him; but he did not live more than a few days. On the 29th of February, 1880, I had twins, Peter and Rosa. I killed them a week after their birth. My daughter Juliana was born on the 11th of April, 1881, and was dead two days later. Agnes, of whom I was confined on the 29th • of March,lBB2, also lived only a few days. On the' stt of May, .1883, I again had twins; one was stillborn, and I killed the other a month after- wards. •My lac, lid came in May, 1834. - I disposed of it in t+.4,-, Pat-yr. I poisoned all my children with a decoction of.4l%ipies. They were all previously baptised. I did not want any children. My husband know nothing of what I had done. I lived on bad terms with him, and nted too vex him." The woman was at once handed over to the authorities, before whom she renewed her confession. • _ _ Kim's COMPOUND Essence of Linseed, Aniseed, Senega Quill.
