div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

At the Westminster Police Court, on Monday, the Rev. , George Burcroft Butterfield was remanded nu a charge ' of being- drunk-and begging at South Kensington. was stated. that he once held a good position in the Church of England. The authorities at Scotland Yard, received a cable telegram from New York, on Saturday, announcing that Harry Benson, who was implicated in the turf frauds case, in England, has been arrested for a series of alleged fogeries in Kentucky.

• Sir Geo. Chetwynd, replvtng to Mr. Edwd. Weatherby, says he does not intend tilting any legal proceedings on the subjett of the recently published correspondence. but that he ls most anxious that the .Tockey Club should investigate the question as between himself and Lord Durham. •

SIR WILFRID LAWSON AND EIS TENANTS.--Sir Wilfrid Lawson, M.., has returned to his tenants on the Brayton •estate, Cumbenland, 10 per cent. of their rents. With the view of rendering remissions unnecessary in the future be has invited his tenants to consider scheme by means of which rents shall in future be regulated by the prices of agricultural produce.

MYSTERIOUS DISAFFEARANCIE OF A SCOTCH MINISTER.— The Rev. Duncan Campbell, who was recently appointetl assistant minister at St. Columba Gaelic Church, Glas- gow, has mysteriously disappeared since the 7th instant, when he went to Paisley to attend a meeting. On the following day he was to preach at Greenock. The matter has been put in the hands of a detective. - -

Alderman Duncan, IP., bead of the firm of Duncan and Sons, proprietors of the South Wales Daily News, died at his residence at Penarth, near Cardiff, at three on Saturday morning, at the age ef 65 years. The deceased gentleman succumbed to a bronchial attack. but he had been in failing health for years. The recent foggy weather caused acute symptoms in his malady, and he gradually sank.

An inquest, held at Deptford on Monday afternoon, on the body of William Bate Curmer, aged 41, whose death was alleged to have arisen from injuries inflicted by the police in Trafalgar-square, resulted in a verdict of death from natural causes. Professor Pepper and Dr. Bedford gave evidence to show that death resulted from excessive heart disease, and that the injuries had nothing to do with the fatal result.

TRAGIC END TO AN ELOPENENT.—A romantic story attaches to the late of the young woman, Kate James, who was drowned in the canal near Wolverhampton, under circumstances already reported. In the early part of last year the manager of an extensive liquor vaults eloped from Wolverhampton with his domestic servant, leaving behind him a wife and four children. The com- panion-of his flight was the unfortunate girl, Kate James, whom he had cruelly deserted, and she was returning to the home of her parents when she met with her death. • A STRANGE STORY.—Ati evening paper published on Monday a " romantic story," which has since been copied into other journals, and which has, of course, excited a good deal of notice. It relates that irr a certain family, 'well known in a suburban district, one of them, who had always been regarded as a woman, one day appeared dressed as a man, and was introduced to the friends as a onan. The story is true, and it was consequent on the discovery of the real sex by a medical man in the city. -Bu-, the fact might have been ' allowed to rest thete. Now, for the sake of an attractive "mystery" paragraph. the whole town—and particularly the female portion of it—is set talking over a matter which must Involve sexual topics that ought not to be so diacussed.—British Medical Journal.

FATAL POACHING EXPEDITION.—AbOUt one o'clock on Saturday morning, Richd. France, a wailer, and Michael ' Baker, a labourer' two well-known poachers, went on a ! fishing excursion to the Fitz Stakes, in the iver Der. went, about a mile from Cockermouth, intending to net for salmon. Before the men had been long fn the water they found their net had got entangled with a spile in the bed of the river. The water was very deep, and in trying to loose the net France seems to have lost his hold and was drowned. Baker, thinking his companion had •eot out on'the other side of the stream, packed the not and went home. At daylight a search. was made, hut-' up to dark on Saturday night the body had not beee found. THE YORKSHIRE CoLetans.A conference of Yorkshire miners was held at Rotherham on Monday, the delegates preaent representing , 31.000 men. Resolutions were adopted expressing the opinion that the colliery owners had acted discourteously in not meeting a deputation of the miners, and that if the masters Would not state what they considered to,be an "equitable" sliding scale, the conference could not see its way to suggest any further scheme for the regulation of wages. ,The conference ayes ready to -enter into a proposal similar to one agreed upon two years ago; 'and with regard to the waces question, the meeting determined that it should be decided by ballot at the various collieries as to whether notice should be. given with the view of enforcing an advance of 10 per cent. THE WORK OF A LoNDON PUBLINTIER.—A London cor- respondent writes :—The speech of Mr. George Boutledge at a complimentary dinner VMS certainly the best of the unreported sayings of last week. He teld the story of fifty years of most active publishing; how he began at Carlisle when parcels came by a mail-coach from London; how 30,000 copies of the "Colleen Dawn" were sold during the performance at the Adelnlii ; 100,000 copies of Grant's "Romance of War ;" how in 1852 "Uncle Tom's Cabin" sold at the rate of 10,000 copies a day; how he paid a royalty of '2d. a copy on " Queechy," atid 'sold 60,000; how in 1853 he engaged with the late Lord Lytton "to pay him a sum , of, £20,000 for a term of ten, year," and how "the agreement was carried opt to the letter;" bow the firm ,then .purchased from the present Lord•Lytton "all the copyrights and plant." Mr. Routleclge said, "We have for this author's works nearly paid the sum of £40,000." He spent £l,OOO 0= the illustrations of an editionof Longfellow's poetical Werks. And gave £l,OOO to • Mr. Howard Staunton for editing an edition of Shaks- peare, the plant of the work costing £lO.OOO. He sold • 10,000 copies of atarey!s "Horse Taming," and appears by se dollar, to have spoiled Rarey's ten-guinea: lectures. The copy was brought from New. York by a gentleman, who got £326 for his trip. Mr., Routledge gate Long- fellow £l,OOO for his "New England Traeedies"ind £5OO for his "Dante." In 'conclusion, Mr. Routledga said,. "For fifty years I can say I have published 100 books each year, or two a week." DISGRACEFUL ATTACK or ORANGEMEN.—A, disgrace- ful Scene: was witnessed on Sunday afternoon at the weekly meeting of the Evertort branch of . the lrih Natikenal League, which was held at Netherfield Hall, Liverpool. •It was observed by the Chairman (Councillor Byrne) that a large proportion of those present were not i'll.accord with thafeeling of the Home Rule party, and they were, invited by the Chairman not to inter,rupt the proceeiings of the League, which he said was not hostile to the Protestant party. The proceedings were continued till one of the Orange party seized the collecting box placed at the door. This it was thought was a ruse to 'draw.off the Police who usually are present at the door. lie this as it may, the Act ;certainly had the effect, for whilst the'oonsfible was .pursuing the thief the Orange roughs first of all attacked the chairman, Mr. P. Byrne, beatin„ii- him unmercifully' with belts and sticks. He re- sisted them as long as possible, but eventually was over- powered by numbers, and now lics at.his residence in a dangerous condition. Not content with this the faction, seized the furniture in the hall, and with brickbats broke the windows, leaving the place a mere wreck.—On Mon- day, a man named Burnett wa:s%charged at the Liner- !ol Police Court with stealing five shillings. It was stated that in the confusion the accused ran away with the contribution plate at the door. He was remanded. DESPERATE ATTEMPT TO MURDER A .....nET,ECTIVE.—At Bow-street Police Court on Saturday afternoon, before , Mr: Bridge, the man who on Saturday week attempted to shoot Inspector Lansdowne, of the Criminal Investiga- lion Department, Scotland-yard, was brenglit up on remand. At the last hearing he refused his name and. • address, but he has ginoe given the name of Saml. Prince. It appeared from the evidence already given that on the :might of Friday week Earl Compton's luggage was lost from a cab between the St. Pancras station of the Mid- land Railway and Lennon.: Gardens. On the following day the prisoner presented a -cheque for payment- at Messrs. Drummond's bank, which WKS amongst the stolen property. The clerk at the bank communicated ; with the police, and inspector Lansdowne saw the pri- soner at the bank. When questioned he said that he had I received the cheque from his partner, Mr. W. Clements, I a jeweller, of 145, Barnsbury-road. He was taken to .1 that address in a cab, when it was found that his state- ment was false. Inspector Lansdowne then arrested him, and was about to take him away in the cab, when lie endeavoured to shoot the officer, who grasped the receiver with his thumb between the hammer and the cartridge, by which his life was saved, although his thumb was injured by the hammer.—The prisoner was • committed for trial up= the charges of attempting to murder, of forgery, and of stealing the portmanteau. GREAT FIRE AT BIRMINGHAM : DAMAGES, £150,000. —At an early hour on Saturday, a great conflagration broke out on the premises of Messrs. Morris and Norton, furnishing depot. Corporation-street, Birmingham. The ; building, which was one of the most handsome in the town, had been built upon land in Corporation-street from the design of Mr. W. H. Chamberlain. The pre- mises were demolished, and the adjoining buildings placed in considerable danger. The fire seemed to gain complete possession of the building almost instantly, and considerable difficulty was found in rescuing the occupants who were sleeping in the adjoining blocks. The Daily Post and the Daily Mail, printing offices were placed in imminent peril, and the publication of the Daily Peat was for some hours doubtful. The destruc- tion of Morris and Nort,en's establishment was absolute. The building has three frontages, namely to Corporation- street; Cannon-street, and a narrow thoroughfare called Fore-street. Upon a site of si 1,000 square feet, not a wall remains, the only portion of the structure itanding being some of the leading granite pieces and a few of the girders. A fire of such dimensions and spreading so rapidly has not been known, in Birmingham for many years. The telegraph office which adjoins was placed in great danger. The Central Arcade—the first arcade built in Birmingham—was destroyed, together with the Central Restaurant. The Daily Post office did not take fire, but the glass roof of the composing room was shattered by the heat soon alter the fire broke out, and the printers bad to leave work. The damage amounts to £150,000. .
A GIRL IN A TRANCE FOR TWO MONTHS.

- - For some fevr weeks pastcousiderpt4A excitement has been caused in.diattersea-and the immediate neighbour-," hood, owing to a rumour that, a young girl was in ,trance. She is a young girl, 16 years of age, and her .name is Florrie Chisnell, hying with her parents, NOho tare-very poor, at Green-lane, Battersea, London_ The ipoorgrrl has now been exactly two months in a state,of unconsciousness, and is stin about the same condition as when she was first at en dowF- Medical gentle- men from all parts nave been to see hor, including three well-known physicians from the Westminster Hospital, and all are of the opinion that her case is beyond their skill. On first entering the room 'where she was lying, one would think she was m corpse, her face being deadly pale. On a closer ,examination you can plainly 'see her breathing, her eyes being half open, and very watery, the top eye. hid every now and again dropping and opening. Her arms are folded across her chest, each hand grasping the upper part of the arm, and it has been found impossible to move them. Her legs lie straight down and close together, the toes having a tendency to curl.under. She is sensible at times which are few and far between, and then only momentarily. In the lower part of the body and legs she has no feeling whatsoever, this having been eknerimented by thrusting needles into her flesh, with- out making the slightest impre*.imn.' She is supplied with nourishment with a feeder, her food consisting of brandy, beef tea, eggs, and milk. Her mother, who is her sole attendant, is constantly with her. Hundreds of people have been to see her, and the case is creating quite a sensation.
TWO WOMEN BURNT TO, DE:ArIT: A
HUSBAND'S COWARDICE.

A' fire broke out early on Monday, in a private house at St. Margaret's-bank, Rochester; and before the inmates could be re,,,euecl. a woman named Turner, the wife of a basket-maker, and her mother, were burned to death. Two dwelling-houses were burnt down to the ground. A policeman had his attention attracted by shrieks of "Fire," which he discovered came from a man at the upper window of an old-fashioned, over Capping gabled house, near Winch's distillery. The man was gesticulating wildly, and shouting for help. At the some time, the constable noticed that the rear of the premises was in flames. Forcing (Ten a side door, the 'constable endeavoured to 'go upstairs, but was driven back by dense smoke and heat Meanwhile, the man, whose name was Turrier„by trade a basket-maker, again appeared at the wincloA • and jumped to the ground, without sustaining much injury. The fire brigade had by this time arrived; and soon afterwards, it was discovered that two or three other people were in the upper part of the house, and that the building was one mass of flames. The firemen endeavoured to rescue the people, hut their efforts were imsneeessful. An hour afterwards, the bodies of Mrs. Turner and her aged mother (Mrs. Horne), in a terribly • charred condition, were grit out, and removed in a basket. A child ' was saved by Mrs. Turner, who dropped it into the arms of the constable, after Turner had made his escape.

div.head: ..MORE SHIPPING DISASTERS.
div.p: ..MORE SHIPPING DISASTERS.

• SAD LOSS. OF LIFE. The steamship Belmont, of. Sunderland, collided 'with a pilot cutter, in the Bristol Channel, on Monday. The cutter sank and all her crew were drowned before the steamer could give assistance. The steamer Milan, from Alexandria to Bristol, laden with cottonseed, has gone ashore at Oveston, and Alin become a ;total wreck. The crew was saved-10 by the life-saving apparatus, and 12 by the lifeboat. ; Fears are entertained at Cardiff for the safety or the steamer Darien, of Newcastle, which left Cardiff with coal for Leghorn on the morning of the 26th of December, and has not since been beard of. It is conjectured that she encountered the disastrous gale of the 28th ultl, and foundered in the Bay of Biscay with all hands. • She was built in 1881 at Jarrow, and was 1,779 tons register. The owners are 'Messrs. Nelson, Donkin, and Co.. of New- 'castle, and the captain John B. Mackie, of Sunderland, who had a crew of 27 hands.' The Norwegian brigantine Isbarden, from Cardiff for Pira, Was towed into Falmouth on Saturday afternoon by the steamer Armine, the vessel's crew being in a deplorable condition,, and having lost overboard the - captain, named Jorgensen. ''he brigantine encountered a gale on the last day of the year, and terrific seas broke over her, doing gretit damage to all the deck fittings. One sea washed away the captain, a fine fellow of 35 years old, who was at the time standing in the doorway of his cabin. No assistance could be rendered to him on account of the violence of the sea and storm. The mate and crew for three or four days had a terrible experi- ence, being unable to go below, and labouring con- stantly at the pumps, fearing at any moment the foun- dering of tie ship, which was unmanageable owing to the loss of her topmast and gear. 4n effortwas made to reach Falmouth, but for some days variable winds and high seas prevented progress. The crew were, how- ever, gallant and stalwart men, and at length 'made the Woolf Lighthouse, and in the mouth Of the Channel were picked up by the steamer, the crew being thoroughly exhausted. . . . .

The men saved from the Juana Nancy state that their vessel was sawn out of the ice in the Lulea Rimer; and drifting down among the ice floes was ultimately re- leased. On Christmas night a -violent storm erase, dur- ing which the captain fell from the bridge and was in- jured. The vessel was altogether driving before Pie wind for three weeks, and on the 11th inst. the 'provi- sions came to an end. Four of the crew arc suffering from frost-bite, having been three days on thelco, and are now in the hospital at Gamla Carleby. The Juana Nancy had on board a cargo of rails fin- Lulea, and her crew numbered 18. 'The entire Crew of the Juana Nancy could hayetaeen rescued on Thursday last, but the cap- tain, who was awaiting telegraphic instructions from London, refused to leave the vessel. 'len of the crew re- mained with him.

div.head: COMING EDUCATION CONFLICT.
div.p: A COMING EDUCATION CONFLICT.

It has been publicly announced that the Royal Com- mission on the Working of the Education Acts lids .concluded its investigations, and is now considering its report. The announcement has, remarks a London journal, been received with a flutter of anticipation in clerical and ecclesiastical circles, • and confident hopes are expressed that the report will mark the beginning of a new era in national edu- :eation. The , Royal Commission was intended. as a check to . the rapid development ,of . the School Board system. It is the last and most promising strategical movement in the eighteen years' war of the clergy and the squires against the Education Act of 187.0. The aPpointnient of 'the Commission was one of the latest acts of the TOry Governinerrt-of 1885. Sir .Richard Cross, now Lord Cross, was' then 'Mine Secretary, and in granting the Commission he avowed its object. It was a Government bid for the vote and interest at the election of the friends and sup- porters of sectarian education. It offered the opponents of the national system of education the opportunity of J., final, attack on Mr. Forster's Act. The working .of that Act was to be ostentatiously investigated by a body on which its most active opponents were in a clear majority, while enough of its prominent sup- porters were present to give an appearance of fairness to a foregone conclusion. • Sir Richard' Cross, in an- nouncing the inquiry, expressed the opinion-that. the Act of 1870 had not worked well, and' that the "voluntaryschools ought to be. placed in the same position as the Board schools. As Lord -Cross is Chairman of the Commission, this declaration •WaS• eqnivalent to the giving of a verdict and sentence by a judge before the jury had been empanelled.. The judge, being . thus pledged, proceeded to nominate a jury which should agree with him; and the word has gotv., forth to the Whole army of clericalism in education to ' be upon the move, so'as to secure the predominance of the right spirit.in.the Report. The friends of unsee- tarian education ought at once• to be up and doing. They must•not allow the Education Commission to say that public opinion as represented by the memorial's addressed to them is all on one side. There is no fear of reaction if the alarm already raised is duly heeded. The battle is one which has been often fought, and has been as often won. If it is forced upon us we shall Light it with the same energy as before, and with the l same result.

FATAL DYNAMITE EXPLOSION IN GLAMORGANSHIRE.— According to a Cardiff telegram a fatal explosion of dynamite has occurred at Llansainlet, in Gramorgan- Shire. A number of miners were engaged in blasting the slag at the bottom of the cupola at the old zinc works with dynamite, when a charge prematurely exploded. Two miners, Wm. Bellalick andogob Thomas, were killed on the spot, and another bad a narrow escape. A POLICE SERGEANT DRIVEN TO SIIICIDE.—An inquest was held at Dartmouth, on Monday night, upon the body of Police Sergeant Allee, who committed suicide by swallowing strychnine. The de&ased's superior-officer complained to the Chief Constable of Devon that he had neglected his duty in not making, an arrest in connection witli a fire. For this Allen, was ordered to be reduced snd removed. It was pointed out that he was engaged elsewhere, and that the officer had made no arrest him- felf. The jury expressed their opinion that "Allen's mind was upset by the arbitrary, cruel, and unjust manner in Which his superior treated him." TIIE NEW BREWERY COMPANT.—The limited liability company of Bass. Rateliff. and Gxettnn has been regia- ',ered, with a capital of £2,720,000, divided into 13,600 preference shares of £lOO each and 13,600 ordinary shares of £lOO each. The object is to acquire and.take is a going concern the undertaking, earned on at Bur- Gowen-Trent and elsewhere, by Bass. Rateliff, and Gret- ton, Limited, incorporated in 1880. The first subscribers are Lord Burton, Mr. Richard Ratcliff, Mr. John Gretton, Mr. Robert Rateliff, Mr. Charles J. Clay, Mr. Hamar Bass, M.P., and Miss Fanny Oretton. The number of directors Is not to be less than five nor more than ten The first five directors are to be Lard Burton, Mr. Richard Rat- cliff, Mr. John Coetton, Mr. Robert Ratcliff, and Mr. Marks J. Clay. . .
CURRENT POLITICS.

On Saturday, Mr. Parnell left 'Kingstown for England, §nTblis way to .London; Ig r Sir Wm. Harcourt wiA be the guest of the Eighty Club, on February 21st., and will deliver an address. It is stated that Lord Charles Beresford has placed his resignation in Lord Salisbury's hands, and that other changes at the Board of Admiralty are probable. The reorganisation scheme is reported to have fallen through.

The Pall Mall Gazette states that Mr. W. J. Evelyn, M.P. for Deptford, will not immediately resign his seat. He was elected in 1886 as an anti-coercion Conservative. Other Conservatives have swallowed all their pledges, but he has written to Lord Salisbury. stating that he will be unable any longer to vote with a Government which is pursuing a policy at variance with the pledges of so many of its supporters. Mr. Gladstone -wrote to Monday's Daily News from Florence I have once more to trespass on your in- dulgence with a request that you will permit me, through your columns, to return my cordial thanks to the numerous persons and bodies who since my quitting England have been so kind as to convey to me their con- gratulations on the completion of my seventy-eighth year, usually in conjunction with the further gratifying assurance that I am permitted to retain their unabated confidence in public affairs." CONFERENCE OF LIBERAL UNIONIST LEADERS.

A meeting of the Executive Committee of the Liberal Unionist Association was held at the offices of the asso- ciation, Great George-street, Westminster, at noon on Saturday. Lord Hartington presided, and there were also present Lord Stalbridge, the Earl of Camperdown, Mr. A. Craig Seller, M.P., Viscount Wolmer, M.P., Mr. Biddulph, M.P., Sir John Lulabock,•M.P., Mr. Finlay. Q.C., M.P., Mr. Walter Morrison, P&P.. the Hon. H. Brand, and the Hon. A. Elliot The proceed- ings, which were of a confidential character, lasted three hours. Lord Hartington on Fri- day evening •attended an ordinary meeting of the executive of his party at Great George-street, West- minster. The meeting had under consideration the general plans of the work for the coming session • and among other things Ninsidered was the action a the party regarding the vacancy created in Liverpool. It was resolved that Mr. Mattison should have the aid of the Liberal Unionists. Lord Hartington later in the day left for the country, but will return to town tp-day, and will have an interview with the leaders of his party dur- ing the week in reference to the Government measures for the next session. The relations between the Govern- ment and Lord Hartington's party continue amicable. BARON HENRY DE WORMS ON FAIR TRADE.

Baron Henry de Worms, the Secretary to the Board of Trade, having been asked to state his views on Fair Trade, has written as follows :—" I consider Fair Trade and Protection to be, in reality, synonymous expressions; and I believe the re-establishment of Protection in any shape to be impracticable. Free Trade has made the cost of living in Great Britain lower than in any ether important country in the world, and, as 'wages have risen considerably since its period of introduction, it is evident that the condition of the mass of the population of these islands has improved under tho existing regime. The recent speech of President Cleveland shows that the introduction of Free Trade principles into the United States has become a question of the immediate future; and I am inclined to' the belief that if means could only be found to enable the great. Continental Powers to reduce their cologsal armaments, and thus improve their financial position, the general abandonment of Protec- tion and the ultimate untversai adoption of Free Trashe might not be the Utopian idea that many people imagine." THE PROSPECT OF A DISSOLUTION.—MR. PARNELL

div.head: INTERVIEWED.
div.p: INTERVIEWED.

Mr. Parnell. M.P., in conversation with a representa- tive of the Freeman's Tonreteil, on Saturday. said he was going to England far a few days; but if his health con- tinued good, he hopod to return in time to summon meeting of the Irish members in the Dublin City Hall just. before the opening of Parliament. Otherwise, he should invite them to meet in London. He believes that. Lord Salisbury's statement that in the event of a hostile vote in the House of Commons, the Government would have to consider whether to resign or dissolve, indicated - the existence of grave dissensions, perhaps in the Cabinet. certainly in the party. He expected that a Ministerial crisis might occur at any time during the session. aris- ing rather Out of some-English than- the- Irish question. it would be politic, I think," Mr. Parnell said, "for the Irish and English Radicals to do everything they possibly can to facilitate the Government business during the coming session, so that no cry of obstruction can be got up or alleged against us for avoiding the entertai,p- ment of great matters of English policy. Nothing could be more fatal than to give the Govern- ment an opportunity of saying that owing to . obstruction, they had not been able to find time to at- tend to pritish interests. It is in such matters that the germ of disintegration of the so-called Unionist. ranks- lies hidden. They may be able to agreeebout hnliying or dragooning Ireland. but they will undoubtedly part company over their English legislation. 'Let the Gover- nment get to work upon their English bills as soon as pas- sible,' would be my s advice to the freelances of the Liberal party." Upon the question of the schedule of land rent reductions Mr. Parnell said : "I consider that the reductions in judicial rents only amount to one-half as what the fano prices alone entitled the tenants to, leaving out of the question altogether the reduced yield from the effects of the drought during the past year.. I think it would he good policy for the Irish members to press for the shortening •,f the judicial term from fifteen years to five,,or, at nll events. the Scotch term of seven years; so that the whole question of judicial rents may again corim under notice of the Sub-Commissioners, free from the ineenious mathematical problem contained in the Act of last Session." Mr. Parnell remarked that- the results of the recent revision by the National League have been favourable to, the Nationalist party, and there was little doubt that whilst holding their own in other constituenaies, they would gain North and South Tyrone and South Derry at the next

div.head: VW COMING SESSION: CABINET COUNCIL
div.p: VW COMING SESSION: CABINET COUNCIL

The Ministerial Christmas holiday terminated on Tues.' day, and by noon nearly all the Cabinet Ministers were in town to take part in the Cabinet Council, which ,tssembled at 12 30. Lord Salisbury was the first to • irrive at the Foreign Office. Lord Cadogan attended at Downing-street during the morning, and Mr. Matthews was engaged at the Home Office; whilst Lord Cross, who arrived from Eccles itigge on Monday, transacted busi- ness at the India Office. The only. Ministers absent were Mr. 'Balfour and Sir Michael -Hicks-Besch. • Stanhope appeared to be suffering from severe cold. The Council rose at half-past two. , Soon after Ministers had separated, Lord Hartington _dreve In? to Downing-street, from Devonshire House, anl had an interview with Mr: W. H. Smith,'Whicfi Tasted a eonsiderabletirne: . ' The Central News says :—The first of a series of Cabinet Councils, at which the Ministerial programme !Or the toming Parliamentary session will be finally arraaged, was held on Tuesday, at the Foreign Office, and was attended by all the Ministers, except Mr. Balfour. alio cannot at present conveniently leave Dublin, and Sir Michael Hicks Beach. The council opened at half- past twelve, and the proceedings lasted just two hours. We have reason to believe that tho chief. , subjects of discussion were the proposed alterations in the rules of Parliamentary Procedure, and the Local Government Bill, which the Government are pledged to bring forward early in the session. In regard to the question of procedure Ministers have dc' aided to press forward their proposals at the earliest oessible moment, and, if necessary, without Waiting for the completion of the debate on the Address. Mr. Ritchie was Able to inform his colleagues that the Assistant Comtnissioners appointed under the laiwers conferred by the Boundaries Act of last session has made great progress in their work, which it was hoped would be finished in about six weeks' time, although they had met and are still meeting with considerable difficulties, owing to local jealousies, prejudices, and rivalries. Minister's having been placed in possession of the views of the Liberal Unionist leaders upon the leading features of the Local Government Bill, considerable discussion took place at the Council in reference thereto. We under- stand that it was decided to meet these views on several important points, notably, in regard to the proportion of ex-office members on the new County Boards. The concession which the Government have decided to make to their Lilieral allies will, it is thought, remove all serious differences of opinion, but neither Lord Salisbury nor Lord Hartington will under- take to fetter the freedom of action of the rank and file of their supporters in regard to matters of detail: ....When..tbe Council broke up at half-past two o'clock Mr. Smith remained for a short time in conversation with the Premier, and then proceeded to No. 10, Down- I lug-street, where he subsequently received a visit from I Lord Hartington. The interview lasted over an hour, and Mr. Akers Douglas was present part of the time. It ia understood that Lord Hartington expressed himself satisfied with the communication made to him by Mr. • aith..

Mr. Shaw-Lefevre will, if the Clanricarde evictions are continued, address a meeting in the district. A telegram was received in Cork, on Monday, from Mr. Douglas Pyne, M.P., stating that he had arrived at Ply- mouth, having successfully eluded the police authorities. Six ,of the rddare hounds were found deal from poison in their kennels on Sunday morning. At Satur- day's meet six coverts were drawn blank. It is stated that in consequence of this poisoning of hounds the hunt will be stopped. Mr. Pyne, M.P., has again escaped from Lisfinny Castle, where for some months he has been besieged by the police. It seems that on Friday evening, while a large number of cattle were being driven round the castle, he left his hiding place without attracting attention. On Monday, a Add was made on the house of a man named Gallaher, residing within three miles of Sligo, ostensibly for the purpose of obtaining arms. Miss Gallaher was the only person at home, and she gave the monnlighters a sum of £6B, with which they decamped. Berry, the hangman, his written a letter to Cork ex- plaining why he did not attend the Cross inquest. He states that, although he has performed 130 executions, he never performed his duty so satisfactorily as in Cross's case. In conclusion, be hopes this explanation will satisfy the morbid curiosity of the jurymen. An application, on Monday, in the Queen's Bench Divi- sion to admit to bail Peter and Michael Murphy, who were tried at the Wioklow Winter Assizes on a charge of Whiteboyism on the occasion of the murder of Head. constable Wilelehan at the house of Thomas Sexton, County Clare, was refused. The jury disagreed at the While police, uuder District Inspector Brett, were as- sisting on Saturday in the execution of warrants for the collection of rates at Menaclacky, near Gweedore, they met with very determined resistance by the people. A . conflict occurred, and in the encounter one woman was stabbed and a girl was badly injured in the head by a blow from a truncheon. A policeman was also wounded, and all are under medical treatment. Two prisoners were arrested.

Mr. Valentine Ryan, J.P. for the counties of Kildare. Limerick, and Tipperary, and an extensive landlord, was fired at, on Monday, at his Tipperary residence, Chad- well House, near Limerick Junction, but, it is stated, 'escaped unhurt. A man, who is-unknown, called to see Mr. Ryan, and an angry conversation took place, in the course of which the man suddenly pulled out a revolver, and fire4but missed his aim. Mr. Ryan recently sum- moned several tenants for non-payment of rent. Mr. William O'Brien, M.P., will be released from Tea- more Prison to-day (Saturday), on the completion of his sentence; but the conviction is strong among his friends and Parliamentary colleagues that he will be re-arrested on a charge arising out of the midnight meeting at Wood- ford. During his incarceration United Ireland has regu- larly published reports of the suppressed branches Of the !fish National League, but as Mr. O'Brien has been in prison since they were proclaimed he cannot be held responsible for the conduct of the journal. His re-arrest might interfere with the proposed demonstrations of welcome.

Early on Saturday morning the post office at Killarney was broken into, and about £250, which was in various drawers and an iron safe, stolen. The building was .re- cently erected for the special purpose of a post office. and was supposed to be secure from attacks of this kind. No one slept on the premises, but it is supposed that tilt, postmaster was about to do so. The robbery was first. discovered about five o'Clock by one of the clerks who attended °to sort the morning mail. The police are actively investigating the matter, but no arrests have been made yet. The thieves entered the post office by an unsecured window from the yard. The thieves must have been well acquainted with the plan of the office. Bishop Nulty, referring to his refusal of admission to visit political prisoners in Tullamore Gaol, says he in- fdrmed the Prisons Board that they were all members o! his flock, and he had a divine right to visit them in their exceptional trouble, and would not abuse the privilege through ignorance or design. The Board replied that Mr. Sullivan could select him as a visitor any day; but in the case of Mr. O'Brien, he was not entitled to any tith visit, and they could not comply. He accordingly complains of being impeded in the exercise of his divine right and the discharge of his diiise duty, and hopes that some member of the Irish party will bring petty irritating bigotry before Parliament Judgment was given at Ennis on Saturday in the appeal from a sentence of five weeks' imprisonment pro nonuced by two resident magistrates at Tulla on a trader named Thomas White, tor refusing to supply goods to, and on a blacksmith named Bryan Brazil for refusing to shoe horses for, the Rev. Mr. Grier, who was boycotted. Mr. Hickson, the county court judge, confirmed the ruling of the magistrates. The Crown, through Mr. Mahoney, said that as an improvement in the habits of the people in that district was visible, he would sanction that the parties be admitted to bail in their own recogni- names of £243 each to come up for judgment when called on. A second appeal, by Denis M'Namara, who was sentenced by the Ennis justices to two month,' imprisonment for selling (kited Ireland, containing F.. ports of suppressed National League meetings, was als, affirmed. Whamara was sent to gaol.

Correspondence was published on Monday between tile Lord Primate of Ireland and Prof. Galbraith, of rriniti- Coßege. Dublin, on the subject of' the latter's member- ship of the National League. The Primate says very painful impression has been made on lii mind, and on the minds ot many collrogues, this connection with a body hostile to the right. of property, and it was their painful conviction that was not for the financial interest of the Church of In- land that he should continue a member of the finanir. committee of that body, and remain at the same time a member oT the National League. --ne-tert the solution o' this painful question to Mr. Galbraith's sense of honour. The Rev. He was unable to see that his having joine,i the National League had unfitted him for the ;faithful discharge of his duties on the Finance Committee. joined the league for conscience sake. as a pretest the unconstitutional action of the Government in sup- pressing public liberty, but it was not his present in- tention to take any prominent part in its councils. ‘, MR. BLUNT IN PRISON.—EXTRAORDINARY • STATEMENTS.

Ald. Dillon, solicitor, having obtained the permissi of the Prisons' Board to pay a second visit to Mr. Blunt on legal business, he travelled to .Galway on Friday nieitt for that purpose. • Mr. Dillon-etes_not allowed,to see Mr. Blunt, the governor saying that eircumStances lv arisen which prevented Mr. Dillon from seeing the I.r. soner. Mr. Dillon telegraphed to the Prisons' Beatil iii reference to this refusal, , Mr. Blunt was on Friday de- prived of the overcoat which he brought with Mtn, an.; which was absolutely necesFary for warmth. To resent this action Mr. Blunt thereupon flung off the prison clothes and: demanded his own suit, which, of course, was refused. The priidnet then gathered a blanket abent him, and paced the -cell thus clad for the remainder of the day. Major Wilson Lynch, • the first of the justices called on Frilay. prisoner was subsequently seen by Colonel O'Hara. A meeting of the visiting justices was held on 'Saturday. and subsequently Mr. Dillon received permission to visit Mr. Blunt. Colonel Nolan, M.P., had seen the prisoner earlier in the day, And hens then in bed. While Won't Nolan was conversing with tm the visiting justices, hav- ing adjourned their meeting, went to Mr. I3lunt's and the hen, and gallant member at their request, with- !drew. Mr. Blunt then made a lengthy statement respect-- ing his treatment, and complained of the action of the authorities in taking away his overcoat •He also insisted upon relating an interview which, he said, he recently had with Mr. Balfour, upon which occasion the Chief Secre- tary declared to him that his method of settlinc, the Irish question was to imprison six of the Irish leLlers,lho were physically weak MOO, and who would not sunive six months of prison treatment. Mr. Blunt was mot anxious to put his declaration in writing and upon oath:. but the justices felt they could not receive it The justices present were Colonel Dale, Major Lonsell, Mr. Marcus Lynch, Mr. Roche, and Mr. Lambert. The visit- _ine justices made the following recommendations : " That the prisoner be removed to a better room with a ,fire, that his overcoat be restored to him, and that he be Supplied with a table and writing materials in his own "oom." Inquiry having been made of Mr. Balfour whether there was any ground for the extraordinary assertions which Mr. Wilfrid Blunt is reported to have made against him. the Chief Secretary for Ireland replied by teleglaph,--eflidiculous lie, I ao not believe Mr. Blunt ewer made the asserkon.—BALFOUß." If the chae-e is true, it brands Mr. Balfour as unfit to have any part in the government of a civilised nation. No one I ey-1 env that Mr. Blunt would deliberately concoct so ;hi t-otti an accusation. His defence fund has reached

SAVED BY A NEWSPAPER PARAGRAPH.
The following statement, made by a well-known General, besides the =usual matter of value which it contains, will be found most readable and inter-

efei-ng _ „ , Messrs. Editors,—l have always believed most firm- - ly in,the Brotherhood of Men, and think tvery human- being is in duty bound to assist his fellow-man to the fullest extent of his power. The relation, therefore, of my personal experience will, I trust, prove of benefit' to many thousands in this country and India. "For thirty-six years previous to 1875 I had been a resident of India. During this period the performance of my duties frequently exposed me, for months at a time, to the malarious and poisonous emanations of the jungle and the fevers and diseases incident to a hot, moist climate. These repeated exposures finally resulted in a chronic disorder of the kidneys and liver, so com- mon to the inhabitants of that country. This was some twelve years ago, when I finally became so seriously ill that I was obliged to return to England. Upon my arri- val I took to my bed, enduring untold agonies. My medical attendant was puzzled as to the nature of my ailment until I commenced to pass small stones. From this I secured temporary relief, but relapsed from time to time, having the most distressing spells of sickness imaginable, with high-colourled water, fickle appetite, bad taste in the mouth and completely prostrated at frequent intervals with.the most agonising attacks from congestion and the passage of gravel, obtaining but tma- sient relief from talented medical man. I was complete- ly broken down physically and firmly of the opinion, which was shared by my. friends, that I should never regain my health as during my long residence in India the kidneys and fiver had become so diseased that I was beyond permanent relief. , "While in this desponding condition, I was one day talking with my friend Mr. D. L. M. Moore, of 3, Hill Street, S.W., when he called my attention to a para- graph in the Christian Union, a paper at that time edited by the late Henry Ward Beecher, which recounted a cer- tain investigation which had been made regarding a reme- dy for the cure, of kidney and liver diseases, at thatitime attracting a great deal of attention in the United States. I decided to try the medicine, and procured -it at once. The first dose gave me relief, and under its continued use I rapidly improved. In ten months Ifully recovered my health, and am to-day in its full and perfect enjoy- ment, never having had a particle of trouble since my remarkable recovery. As this was five years ago, I can safely say that the wonderful cure was permanent, and that it is all to be attributed to Warner's SAFE Cure, a medicine which I consider has no peer for all diseases of the kidneys and liver. It has given me a new lease of life., It is a remedy, I think, particularly designed for climates such as that of India, and I hope soon to hear that steps have been taken which will enable the inhab- itants of that country to receive-benefits from its use. "Yours faithfully, W. F. NIITHALL, General. "10, Edith Terrace, Edith Grove, _

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, JANUARY 21, 1888.

_ The Allotments Act of last year was heralded by a flourish'of trumpets. It was described by the 'Tories and by Liberal Unionists as little less than a revolution in favour of the agricultural labourer, and Mr. JESSE COLLINGS, in particular, made it a matter of reproach against Mr. GLADSTONE that he did not deal with this question rather than with Home Rule. But the act has already proved to be a failure, and the word has gone forth, among those who have been honestly trying to bring it into operation that it will have to be amended considerably before it can be made really useful. We ventured at the time the bill was be- fore the House of Commons to comment on its structural defects. It was impossible that it could succeed, so far as we could perceive; and we are now inclined to conclude that it was 'never inten- ded to be of any benefit except for electioneering purposes. An allotment measure to be really ser- viceable must make allotments easy of attain- Ment. It should be .remembered that those for whom the allotments are intended are poor, and, relatively speaking, ignorant. They do not know how to go about the setting in motion of cumber- some and complicated machinery, and, if they did know, they have not the means required to over- come the opposition they might have to encoun- ter. Let us suppose that a number of Cheshire labourers, say in the neighbourhood of Walton, were anxious, as no doubt many of them are, to rent an acre of land each for their own use. They would have to formally notify the Sani- tary Authority that they were desirous of obtaining allotments, a'Nd that, as there were no voluntary offers of land, they wished the Authori- ty to take immediate steps to bring the Allot- ments Act into operation. It would then be the duty of the Sanitary Authority to satisfy them- selves that allotments were not to be obtained "at a reasonable rent under reasonable conditions by voluntary arrangement," and, having done this, to set about acquiring land for the purpose, either by hire or purchase. But if the landowner, who .in
this instance would be Sir Gilbert GREENALL, was

mit willing to sell, what then? There are, to be Sore, compulsory clauses in the act; but it is not for the Authority to apply them, until they have exhausted all the arts of the Circumlocution Office. They can do nothing further until they have peti- tioned the County Authority, who will then take the matter in hand and proceed to make full in- quiry into the case, after which, if they are satis- fied that the right course has been taken ali through, they will make a provisional order auth- -orising the Sanitary Authority to put the Act in force. The order, it will be noticed, is provisional, and the matter does not end there. The next step is for the County Authority to apply to the . Toc4 Government Board, who, in turn, "shall introduce into Parliament a bill confirming pro- visional orders made by the County Authority and the Sanitary Authority." Was there ever such beating about from pillar to post, and all in order that a few labourers may have authority to rent a bit of land? The Sanitary Authority, being poor weak lot, are required to refer the business to the County Authority, and those gentlemen, being in the eye of the law little or no better, have to apply to • the Local Government Board, which, having no power of its own, must actually appeal to Parlia- ment to settle the trumpery question of the letting of an acre or two of land! The Legislature in the exercise of its wisdom has done some singu- larly foolish things; but we challenge anyone to name anything more foolish in the way of a busi- ness arrangement than the setting up of the , machinery for the working of the Allotments Act. In saying this, we are looking at the matter from , the point of view of the professed object of the Act— that is providing labourers with allotments; but if we look at what is probably its real object—a piece Of profession which is not intended to result in Performance—we are constrained to admit that it is admirably adapted to its miserable end. Like most Tory enactments, it is a piece of class legis- lation; the framers of the Act have been thinking not of the labourers, but how to protect land- owners who may detest the compulsory clauses of the measure. The Act, if it is to be of service, will require tobereconstructed. It must be stripped of red tape; the machinery must be simple and effective; and, in order that Sanitary Authorities may not have a prejudice against its working, pro- vision should be made whereby the costs of 14ing- ing the compulsory clauses into operation shall be borne by the Consolidated Fund. This must be • the Work of the Liberal party; the Tories will never set about it. The Liberals had to remodel a sham Agricultural Holdings Act; and they will next be called upon to remodel the sham Allot- ments Act.

WE have received from Messrs. STEVENS and Soxs a goodly volume containing "The law rela- ting to Public Libraries and Museums, and Literary .and Scientific Institutions, with the Acts of the' Session of 1887." The treatise is from the pen of Mr. GEORGE F. CHAMBERS, barrister-at-law, and author of" A Digest of the law relating to Public Health," &c. • The work was recognised when the firstedition was published as the standard authority on the subject, and has proved invaluable to the conductors of Libraries, Museums, and other kindred institutions. All the statutes are given lfl full, and there are brief notes of leading eases. We have looked in vain for a case on all fours with the point which has been raised at Warrington— that is as to whether the Library and Museum Committee have any warrant in. law for making a charge for the loan of books. Everything in the • Acts, as we have again and again shown, points to

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 21, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 21, 1888.

the opposite conclusion, namely, that it is a breach of the law to make a charge; and, after conning carefully the latest Acts on Libraries as issued in the work before us, we can well understand why the Library and Museum Committee have not carried out the resolntion which was arrived at to take counsel's opinion on the subject. They have not done s.o, because, as one member of the Com- mittee has observed, they are "afraid that it will go against them." Every advantage has been taken of obscurities'in the Act of 1855 to make it appear that the law makes no provision for lending books, and this has been done by members of thei Committee in sheer disregard of the fact that, if their contention was sound, they stand self-con- demned for having lent books out under a sub- scription. But granting, for the sake of argument, that there may be a doubt as to the strict legality of lending booksunder the Act of 1855, there can be no question as to the authority to do go which is conferred by an amendment act that was passed on the Bth of August last. Clause five of the new At says :- 1 The power to erect, establish, and maintain a library, given by the Public Libraries Act, 1835 (herein-after called the principal Act) shall be ex- tended so as to empower the library authority to establish and maintain a lending library, without providing any separate building for containing the 'same, and to enhble them to place such lending library under the care and superintendence of such person as they shall think fit, and in a building or room not appropriated for the pqrposes of the said Act, or erected, purchased, or rented by the library authority, and all the powers of the said Acts shall 1 be applicable for the purposes of this section. It will be seen that "the Library authority" (which in the case of Warrington is the Library and Museum Committee) has its powers extended so as to enable it to maintain" a lending library." In view of this Act, which the Committee have hitherto ignored, it is absurd to contend that there is not now, whatever may have been the case in the past, specific authority to lend books. So de- sirous is the Legislature of encouraging the estab- lishment of libraries, that, as will be gathered from the clause quoted, the way is made easy for having a lending library without being put to the cost of "providing any separate building for con- taining the same." This means that villages such as Penketh and Grappenhall shall be put in a position to have a "lending library" as well as towns like Warrington, Widnes, Runcorn, or St. Helens. Surely, after this, we shall hear no mbre as to whether Lending Libraries are recognised by law. The phrase is used in the Act of 1887, and it is now no longer possible to deny its exist- ence. _

I With regard to the question of the power to make a charge, we have all ,along contended that, since the Act of 1855 taxes the ratepayers by /helms of a penny rate, any f urther charge is in the na- ture of black mail levied by the Committee, see- ing that it has not so much as a shadow of authority in law. The words used are :--" The admission to all Libraries and Museums established under the Act shall be open to the public free of all charge." In other towns, this has been taken to mean that books, too, shall be lent out free of charge; but Warrington has stood alone, to its shame, in insisting upon a subscription. Now, what is called a concession to the ratepayers is being brought into operation, and that is .by permitting a book to be lent out on the payment of a penny by those who are not subscribers. But the injustice is not so much in the amount of the charge as in the fact that there is any charge at all. Unfortu- nately, in amending the Libraries Act for England, our law makers were not cognisant of the absurdi- ties of the Warrington Library Committee, or, by a stroke or two of the pen, they would have put an end to them. In canny Scotland it has been otherwise; instead of passing an amending act last session, they set to work in the right way, and secured a consolidation of their Public Libraries Acts. The result is that every clause has been sub- ject to criticism and amendment, including the clause which said that admission to the Libraries and Museums should be "free of all charge." They have foreseen, and, perhaps, had experience of the way in which, here and there, a Committee will go wrong, and so they have put it beyond the rower of anyone to say that "free of all charge" does not apply to books. The Consolidation Act for Scot- land was passed on the 16th September, 1887, and the clause, as amended and as it now stands, reads as follows :

" All libraries, museums, or art galleries estab- lished under this Act, or to which this Act applies, shall be open to the public free of charge, and no charge shall be made for the use of books or maga- zines issued for home reading." A clause like this would reach the Warrington Library and Museum Committee—that is, if they are made of " penetrable stuff ;" and if they will not do the right thing without compulsion, it will, perhaps, become necessary to compel them.

PREBENDARY GRIER SPEAKS THE PLAIN TRUTH. —The annual meeting of the Burnley Temperance Society was held in the Mechanics' Institute, Burn- ley, on Tuesday night. The Rev. Prebendary Grier, ALA.. who was amongst the speakers, recommended Conservatives and Liberals to join hands to get rid of this gigantic evil. At the present time this was out of the question, and both Church and State were bribed not to touch the great evil. He was not going to blame statesmen and leave men of his own cloth untouched. He said distinctly that the Church of God and the religious bodies of this country in general were bribed to he silent upon this great question through the large gifts that they received from the ill-gotten gains of the brewers. He proceeded to deal with the con- nection of a celebrated brewer and the Bishop • Liverpool respecting the new cathedral. lie sa, the brewer gave a handsome donation to the new cathedral, and received an acknowledgment from the Bishop. Ile (Prebendary Grier) said he wrote a letter to the Bishop and the brewer; and he re- ceived the same reply—a simple acknowledgment cif the letter. He did not expect any more from the brewer, but he did expect a- great deal from the chief pastor of Christ's flock at Liverpool. It was disgraceful of the Bishop of Liverpool. He had waited noW for some months for the Bishop to take ac- tion; but he had taken no action. He cared not for one single moment. It mattered nothing to him. The Bishop might go on flooding this country with tracts, but he was not an evangelical Bishop if he , did not denounce vice and uphold the cause of Christ in the place where he was made chief officer.—Pre- bendary Orier's remarks were received with tre- mendous cheering.

One of our contemporaries has been hoaxing its readers by purely imaginary details of a purely imaginary Lazy Club. The journal in question has evidently great faith in the gullability of its supporters.

Now that the Tories are at dagger's point with the Nationalists, they do not hesitate to show the old hatred of Catholicism. At the Holy Trinity Debating Society, on Monday evening, the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton occupying the chair, Mr. H. J. Long- ton, solicitor, pointed to Roman Catholicism as one of the causes of pauperism. As Mr. Lcygton is a Tory election agent, it may be presumed that he knows how to follow the party cue. '

The Liberals of Birmingham, finding a Liberal Unionist in the way in a municipal contest this week, withdrew their man, and voted for:the Tory candidate. They thus ran the Tory in with a large majority. This will be a lesson for Liberal Unionists; but it should be a lesson to Liberals too. It is a game which they cannot afford to play at except, say, once in a century. "Do shouldn't worry dog when there are wolves and foxes to be found."

Oman Digna must have as many lives as a cat. He has been "killed," according to telegraphic despatches, about half a dozen times. But he is still alive—and kicking. His camp was attacked at Handoub by the English the other day, and he was driven off. But, after his wont, he came back, and this time turned the tables on the aggressors, who were compelled tojetreat. Why not leave the Arab chief to himself ? ,There is an adage about letting sleeping dogs lie.

The farmers of Somerset have been saving hunts- men a deal of trouble; they have been trapping and killing foxes. But the huntsmen don't like it; they are shocked at such unsportsmanlike pro- ceedings. As to the foxes, it will matter little to them how they are killed, and, seeing that farms improve in value as foxes disappear, it is to be hoped farmers will go on trapping them. The world would be no worse if there were neither foxes nor fox-hunters.

The rack-rented or evicted Irishman may well be excused for trying to stop hunting in Ireland. Pride in their port .dellarkee in their eye, He sees the lords of human kind pass by, and he is by no means happy at the sight; for he knows that what is sport to them may be starva- tion to him. Sport under the present circum- stances of Ireland's suffering is inconsiderate, not to say cruel; it is a case of Nero fiddling whilst Rome is burning.

Mr. Parnell is generally well-informed, and there are others who agree with him in concluding that there are dissensions in the Cabinet. In giving the advice to avoid anything which might look like obstruction, he evidently thinks that the Ministry are most likely to get into trouble by attempting to legislate on the local government question. The Tories will not support a really Liberal measure, and the Liberal 'Unionists will scarcely dare to support anything that is reaction- ary. There are rocks ahead, and there may be a shipwreck.

The Scptch Crofiers have taken a lesson from the Irish Nationalists. They have set the law at defiance in asserting what they believe to be their rights; and a jury of their countrymen have brought in a verdict of not guilty. It would be a poor prospect for England if respect for the law should lose its hold upon men ; ibut there is no fear of that. It is noteworthy that these cases of resistance relate to the land, and there is no deny- ing that our land-laws are in a barbarous state. In other matters, tho Crofters show themselves to be honest, God-fearing men.

On Monday, at the Warrington Police Court, several dealers were fined one shilling and costs under the now Margariae Act for exposing mar- garine for sale without attaching the requisite labels. Margarine is surely as sweet as butter— that is as to name; and the law is the law. Such a small fine as was imposed is merely by way of warning. As soon as it is seen that the offence becomes wilful, the bench will do well to enforce a substantial penalty. In matters of food supplied across the counter, we are believers in Fair Trade and Protection.

• The terrific snow storm, or "blizzard," in America by which two hundred people have been frozen to ; death is a most appalling catastrophe. It is difficult in this country to conceive of such a storm, for we havehappilyhad no experience of such storms as affect the United States. One woman who had turned out to look for her husband lost her vray close to her home, and was found dead within forty feet of her own door. It is stated that it was fine and warm before the storm arose ; and it would seem that, in accordance with the law of wind movements, there has ,been a rush of cold air to restore the equilibrium.

The question of overcrowding tramways has excited the attention of the police at St. Helens, as at other places. An adjourned case of alleged overcrowding came the other day before the St. Helens magistrates; but the solicitor for the de- , fence of the Tramway Company took the stand that his clients were not responsible, inasmuch as, by the instructions they had given to their servants, they had done what they could to prevent over- crowding. The Bench acknowledged the force of this contention; and fined the conductor instead of the Company. If this course be taken in other towns, there will soon be an end of overcrowding in tram cars.

At Newton Petty Sessions' oa Saturday, a grocer named Carrington was fined ss. and costi for selling barm which, on analysis proved to be adulterated with potatoe Fetarch to the extent of ten per cent. It transpired tilat the offender ob- tained the birth from a dealer at St. Helens, and knew nothing of the adulteration; but his Ignor- ance was no defence in the case. Still, it is not satisfactory t 9 see the small offenders pounced upon, whilst the big sinners are left untouched. There ought to be some better means of getting at them. The law with regard to adulteration should be strengthened; it ought to be so string- ent as to make wholesale offenders realise that the game doesn't pay.

Mr: Shaw-Lefevre has, by quoting Mr. Justin McCarthy, let daylight into the Tories in the matter of their connection with the Home Rule and anti-coercion proposals. in 1885. It seems there were two sets of negotiations; one with Mr. Parnell as to a Tory Home Rule measure for Ire- land; the other with Mr. McCarthy as to getting a pledge against coercion'. Sir Henry Wolff writes to deny th-at he made any proposal as to Home Rule; but that has not been charged against him. What, Mr. McCarthy says, he was concerned in was the negotiations as to dropping coercion; and everybody knows how the Tories did drop coercion for a time. Their "counterfeits "on the subject are like bad shillings, and are being nailed down.

Even now Mr. Digby Seymour, Q.C.; who was the Tory candidate for South Shields in 1885, is trying his 'prentice hand at a Tory Home Rule Bill. He calls it an Irish Federal Union Bill; and propounds a scheme for establishing four Pro- vincial Councils. Dublin Castle is to be abolished; certain Irish representatives are to sit in the Imperial Parliament at Westminster; and there is besides to be an "Irish Federal Assembly," with a Senate and a House of Delegates, which is Mr. Gladstone's Rome Rule Parliament with 'another name. Indeed, in some respect this new Tory proposal goes further than Mr. Gladstone's Bill; for it leaves the control of Customs and Excise in the hands of the new authority. Mr. Seymour is only a straw perhaps, but straws show which way the wind blows.

Prince Bismarck is trying to coercethe German Socialists out of existence. Repression requires more repression and the latest move is a bill to put down Socialism. The penalties are to be very severe; for a second offence, the culprit may for- feit his right of citizenship, In this way the man of blood and iron hopes to clear Parliament of the Socialist leaders. This might serve as a hint to

Air. Balfour; he can put Irish members in gaol; but what an advantage if, at the same time he could deprive them of their title to sit in Parlia- ment! It would be nothing to the 'purpose to tell our poor imitator of Bismarck that Socialism is increasing in Germany in consequence of coer- cion. ,Mr. Balfour does not take reason into his counsel.

The Bridgewater Navigation Company have been in the happy position of having too much money after selling their undertaking to the Man- chester Ship. Canal Company, and so there has, been a contention in the law courts as to how the surplus funds should be divided. It was held, curiously enough, first, that the holders of prefer- ence shares were not shareholders at all; and, secondly, that if they were shareholders, they were entitled to the live per cent. only which had boon paid them. But Justice North made short work of both contentions. Ho ruled that the preference shareholders should share with the rest in propor- tion to the amount paid up as their shares. And now, it is expected, there will be peace, and a full purse all round.

CLAIM FOR WAGES IN LIEU OF NOTICE AT RUNCORN Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. Henry Reynolds and Mr. James Reynolds, a young man named Joseph Cannon was suenmoned by Mr. John Nicholas Lello, tanner, of Halton-road, for the sum of 17s being a week's wages in lieu of a week's notice. Mr. Lello said the defendant was employed by him as a " hairer," and he suddenly and without intimation left his work, and did not return. An inexperienced man had had to be placed to his work, and he (Mr. Lello) might suffer con- siderable damage in consequence. He did not wish to press the claim against the defendant, but it was neces- sary to take these proceedings in order to enforce law and order in his works. The defendant alleged that Mr. Lello had on several occasions dismissed him at a mo- ment's notice, but this statement Mr. Lello emphatically denied. The Chairman said the magistrates considered Mr. Lello was very lenient. The defendant must have known the great amount of damage that might have been done by his leaving work, and he must also have known that he should not leave without a week's notice. IWIDDING AT OVERTON.—The quiet village of Ovetton, near Frodsham, was on Thursday the scene of some ex- citement, the occasion being, the wedding of Miss Han- nah Cr orst, youngest daughter of the late Mr. George Gorst, of Bradley, to Mr. John Pollard, son of Mr. John Pollard, of Frodsham. The marriage took place at Overton Church, the service being read by the Rev. Alfred Grier, B.A. The church was crowded with a fashionable congregation. The bride was attired in a dress of terra-cotta silk, trimmed with plush, and was given away by her uncle, Mr. Thomas Gorst. The brides- maids were Miss Lydia Gorst and Miss Ellen Pollard, sisters of the bride and bridegroom. Their dresses were of electric blue cashmere, trimmed with plush, and hats to match. The bridegroom was accompanied by Mr. Richard Gorst and Mr. Edward Pollard. Miss Cissy Outram and Miss Annie Holland attended as maids of honour. The children from Overton School were drawn up by the side of the road, and on the bridal party driv- ing past they were greeted with a volley of cheers. The breakfast, to which about fifty sat down, was served at the residence of the bride's mother. The , bells of the church rang a merry peal in honour of the occasion. The presents were numerous and costly. LECTURE ON "SHAMS," AT RUNCORY.-011 Tuesday evening a fond audience assembled in Bethesda Lecture Hall, to listen to a lecture on "Shams," by the Rev. T. Hallett-Williams of Buckley. In the absen,se of Mr. James Handley. J.P., the chair was occupied by Mr. T. Handles,. The lecturer, who dealt with his subject in an interesting and humourous manner, described this as the age of tinsel. Gilt carried the day. WIFE DESERTION AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Ses- sions, on Thursday, before Mr F. H. Gossage and Mr H. ALLEGED UNLAWFUL WOTINDINO AT WIDNES. —On Thursday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, Thomas Kelly, a labourer, of 2, Milton-road, was brought up on remand charged with unlawfully wounding James Lawton, labourer, of 23. div.head: TRIPLETS AND DEATH OF THE MOTHER.—On Tues-
div.p: TRIPLETS AND DEATH OF THE MOTHER.—On Tues-

day morning, Mrs. Ashton, the wife of Thos. Ashton, a mechanic employed at the Cheshire Lines engineer- ing works, and living at 71, Orford-lane, Warring- ton, gave birth to three children—two boys and a girl. All the children were btrong and well up to last night, but, sad to say, the mother died from exhaustion on Thursday morning. After her confinement she was attended by Dr. Foxy The : Rev. S. Wilkinson. vicar of St. Paul a parish, is ' interesting himself in the matter with the view of securing the Queen's bounty usually presented on such occasions. There is naturally much sympathy in the neighbourhood with the bereaved father. A COMPLIMENT TO ALDERMAN CROSFIELD.—Mr. John Crosfield, the Liberal candidate or Warring- ton, has just received an invitation to become the Liberal candidate for Monmouth District. This constituency hfts a population of 46,033. and its re- gister in 183.5 contained 6,485 electors. The 'present member, Sir George Elliot, is a Conservative, elec- ted without a doubt in consequence of the dissen- sions existing in 1886 in the Liberal party, owing to the Unionist split. The ranks of the party are now, however, fast closing up, and, as the Liberals secured the representation of the district in 1880 and 1885, there is little doubt that, on the first op- portunity, with a good and advanced Gladstonian candidate, Sir George Elliot will have to "bite the dust." Mr. Crosfield has, we are glad to say, de- clined the flatteriiig invitation. He is wanted, we need hardly say, nearer home.

. . THE WILL OF THE LATE MR. W. L. EVANS, .T.P., OF PnEsCor.--Probate has been granted of the will, dated 20th November. 1878. with a codicil made 27th May, 1881, of the late Mr. William Lees Evans, of Prescot, who died on the 23rd October last, and the value of whose personal estate has been declared at .£55,720 Os. 64. by the executors, the testator's brothers, Mr. Thomas Evans and Mr. Artkur Frederick Evans, to each of whom the tes- tator bequeaths fifty shares of .£lOO each in the Garavvood Coal and Iron Company, and his brother- in-law, Mr. William Lockwood, to whose wife the testator bequeaths £l.OOO in trust; and for his sister, Mrs Anne Whistler, J:3,500. with remainder to her children; to his sister Elizabeth and his brother Alfred, £l,OOO each; and to his brother Joseph Henry, twenty shares of .£lOO each, in the Garswood Company The testator bequeaths to his wife, Mrs Elizabeth Evans. .£l,OOO, and all his plate, pictures, hooks. furniture, and household effects, hortlPs and carriages, and the use and enjoyment for her life of Fazakerley House. and he devises and bequeaths all his real estate and the residue of his personal estate to pay the income to her for her life, ! with power of appointment to her of a sum of X 15,000. and on her decease to distribute the ultimate resi- due in equal shares amongst his brothers and sisters. —Mrs Anne Whistler, Mr. Thomas and Mr. Joseph Henry Evans, MisS. Elizabeth Evans, Mrs Mary Jane Lockwood, Mrs Francis Boon, Miss Sarah Evans, and Mr. Arthur Frederick and Mr. Alfred Evans, the children of any brother or sister who may have de- ceased taking their parent's share.

WARRINGTON DISTRICT HIGHWAY DO.IP.D.—A general meeting of this Board was held at the office in Sankey-street, on Wednesday afternoon, there being present Messrs. R • Houghton (chairman), William Royston (vice-chairman), John Fairclough, George Lawtesi Henry Bate, Edward Marsh, James Harrison, Joseph Pennington, James Houghton, John Grounds, H. B. White (clerk), and Thompson (surveyor).—The Surveyor reported that he had looked over the district for the purpose of finding oat the roads which were without names. In Ken- yon the road leading from the tunnel in Kenyon- lane to the station was without name, and he sug- gested.that it should be called Station-road. In Penketk the road leading from Mrs. Tinsley's to the Crown and Cushion Inn; that leading from near Mr. Bolton's house on the Widnes-road to Sankey Chapel; and that leading from Meeting-lane End to Bolton's-brow on the Widnes-road, were also with- out names. He suggested that the first should be , called Hatton's-road, the second Greystone-road, and the third Heath-road. The two latter were situated on what was originally the Greystone Heath, which is now enclosed, and consequently the roads had a local derivation. The report was confirmed.—lt was reported that the claim of Mr. Bennett for com- pensation fer injuries received by the upsetting of al trap in consequence of a heap of soil having been I left in the roau had been settled on satisfactory terms.—The Clerk reported that the balance in the bank at the end of last year was .£1,025 17s Bd. Since then Penketh had paid £67, Kenyon 078, and Cuerd- ley £44. The calls for the remaining townships were yet outstanding. On the recomthendation of the Finance Committee a number of cheques were I ordered to be signed for the payment of accounts.— This was all the business of public interest.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board as held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday afternoon. There were present Colonel Ashton (chairman), the Revs. J. Lockwood and J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Mclntyre, Speakman, Taylor, Grice, Aaron, Light- burn, Hadfield, Knowles, Parr, Whitlow, Stokes, Brandreth, Hewitt, Turner, Pickering, Appleton, Campkin ; H. Linaker (clerk), and W. 11. Linaker (deputy clerk), CALLs.—It was stated that since the last meeting £l4O had been paid to the treasurer. THE DEPUTY CLERK'S APPLICATION. Mr. Hadfield rose to submit the report of the Finance Committee as to the application of the deputy clerk for an increase of salary.—The Deputy Clerk remarked, however, that he had decided to withdraw the application so that there was no need to go further with it.—The Rev. J. Lock- woos said he for one had been strongly in favour of some advance of the deputy clerk's present salary being made, and he thought that if every member of the Board had the facts and figures placed before him in the way they had been placed before the committee the deputy clerk would not be allowed to withdraw his application. —The Deputy Clerk said that after his long connection with the Board he would rather not have any feeling raised in the matter, and therefore he withdrew his ap- plication.—Mr. Hadfield, however, read the report of the Finance Committee on the matter. This report stated that it had been moved by Mr. Speakman, secon- ded by Mr. Whitlow, and carried unanimously, that the consideration of the matter of the increase be deferred for one month. He (Mr. Hadfield) did not see any- thing in that to make Mr. Linaker withdraw his ap- plication.—The Rev. J. Lockwood thought that it was only fair for the information of the Guardians that an explanation should be made. When Mr. Linaker, the clerk, applied in June, 1872, for the appointment of a deputy clerk, there had been no deputy clerk be- fore. The clerk's duties had become so multiplied that that he could not attend as well as he would like to do, and he therefore applied for the appointment of a deputy, and he stated that whatever sum that Board should name as a suitable sum for the deputy to receive, it should be taken from his salary. As £lO was named as the salary of the deputy, and as the clerk received £9O, the latter's salary was reduced to £BO a year. It would be seen therefore, that the Board had never been at any extra cost through the appointment of the deputy clerk. Further than that, in 1867, Mr. Linaker, the clerk, made an application for an increase of salary. He then obtained £9O, and he asked that it should be in- creased to £l5O. The Board of that day decided to offer the clerk £l4O, but Mr. Linaker, feeling that he should not receive less than £l5O, and from that time he had continued to receive only the £9O, which, as he (Mr. Lockwood) had mentioned, had been reduced during the last 16 years to £BO, owing to £lO a year being paid to • the deputy clerk. As a matter of fact, then, the clerk had during the last twenty years foregone something like £4O or £5O a year, which he might have had.—Mr. Whitlow said, with regard to the remarks of Mr. Lock- wood, that the appointment of the deputy clerk was made wholly for the convenience of his father, the clerk. As regarded the raising of salaries, these were not times for that to be done.—The Chairman remarked that the matter had been withdrawn.—Mr. Whitlow: Very well, if Mr. Lockwood had said nothing, I would not have said anything.—Mr. Parr: I am dissatisfied with my salary —coming here and getting no .pay. (14aughter,)—The subject then dropped. / This was the principal busiue as.
