div.head: RUNCORN SAVINGS BANK.
div.p: RUNCORN SAVINGS BANK.

The annual meeting of the Trustees and Managers of this bank was held at the Office in High-street on Wednesday afternoon. Mr. J. Brundrit, presided, and amongst those present were Messrs. J. Simpson, W. Hayes. J. Handley, J.P., W. Whittaker, Dr. McDougall, F. A. Lake, J. R. Frith, W. Littler. James Pritchard. W. H. Rogerson, T. Handley, W. Mellor, and W. Handley (actuary) The minutes of the last meeting were read and con- firmed. The Actuary read the annual report, which stated that during the year the number of depositors was 1.558, and the number of withdrawals 709—making the total transactions 2,267. The total amount deposited during the year was £7,725 9s 6d, and the total amount with- drawn was £8,349 8s id. Of these sums the various ' friendly sonieties had deposited £1,937 17s 7d ; charitable societies £205 us 5,1; penny banks £llB 15s 10d; a total deposit on behalf of these institutions of £2,262 4s 10d. The withdrawals for the various societies had been : IFriendly societies £1,616 2s 6d, charitable societies £59 13s 8d; penny banks £325 18s 3d; a total withdrawal of £2,00114s sd. Excluding societies the average deposit had been £3 19s 74d, and the average withdrawal £8 16s 11d. At the commencement of the bank year, Nov. 20th, 1886, the amount in the ledgers to the credit of de- positors was £26.365 10s3d. The amount now in theledgers was £28,471 lOs 3d. To meet the indebtedness the National Debt Commissioners held on Recount of the bank £28.183 3s 2d; balance in the hands of the treasurer was £330 7s 3d; total, £28,513.105 sd, showing a surplus in favour of the bank of £42 Os 2d. The interest allowed by the National Debt Commissioners on the amount of stock held by them was £Bl4 4s 3d; dividends in stock, £3; sale of pass books, £1 Ds Bd, being a total income of £BlB 4s 11d. The interest and dividend allowed to de- positors amounted to £729 18n 7d, and the expenses of management amounted to £B4 9s 11d, leaving a surplus on the year's working of £3 16s sd. The summary of the ledger balances was as follows :—Personal depositors 794, amount £22,358 2s 6d; Friendly Societies 47, amount £5,318 lOs 2d; charitable societies 13, amount £446 is lid; penny banks 2. amount £348 15s ad; being an increase of 19 depositors and an increase in amount of £2,106. The certificates of the auditors and of the National Debt Commissioners had been produced. The Chairman proposed, and Mr. James Handley seconded, that the report be adopted, and that an ab- stract or the accounts be advertised in the local news- papers. The motion was carried unanimously. The best thanks of the meeting were accorded to Mr. Simpson for his services as treasurer. on the proposition of Mr. W. Hayes, seconded by Dr. McDougall. The following gentlemen were appointed auditors : Messrs. J. H. Salkeld, E. Marwood, W. Williamson, and C. Pownall. The customary routine business having been gone through, the proceedings concluded with a vote of thanks to the Chairman.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday. Mr T. S. Timmis presided, and there were present the Rev Dean Finegan, the Rev Father Clarke, Messrs Bradshaw, H. Wade Deacon, Imison',. Waring, Davis, Heyes, and G. H. Danby (clerk).

div.head: DISTRICT ' EDUCATION.
div.p: DISTRICT ' EDUCATION.

The District Education Committee reported that dur- ing December there were 75 applications for school fees, which were recommended to be paid in 70 cases. There were 170 cases for contravention of the Education Act, and 45. persons were summoned and convicted by the magistrates. One boy was committed to an industrial school. The committee recommended that on the com- pletion of five years' service, the salary of attendance officer P. J. Rowe be increased according to the scale of the Board, the increase to commence on February Ist. —The minutes were adopted on the motion of Mr. Deacon.
WIDNES GYMNASIUM. An application for the use of the infant school at Simms Cross School by the Widnes Gymnasium was con- sidered, and it was decided to grant the application on the usual terms.

div.head: FURTHER EXTENSIONS.
div.p: FURTHER EXTENSIONS.

The Sites and Building Committee recommended that subject to the approval of the Education Department, plans for the increased school accommodation, the plans for the increased accommodation required at the Simms Cross and West Bank Schools, and of the School for Cookery, at the Warrington-road Schools, be approved; and that the Committee be authorised to obtain tenders for carrying out the same. Adopted on the motion of Mr. Davis. ,

FINANCE-AN INCREASED. RATE. The Finance Committee reeommtnded for payment accotmts amounting to £568 Bs 7d. The receipts amounted to £l4l 18s 6d, including £139 Os id. The Committee also submitted their estimate of expenditure of the Board for the year ending September 29th, 1888. The School Management Committee estimated their ex- penditure at Simms Cross School at £2,230, and their receipts at £2,036, of which £836 is school fees, and £1.175 is Government grant; thus leaving £194 to be provided. At Warrington-road Sghool the estimated ex- penditure is £1,182, and the receipts £790, of which £320 is school fees and £460 is Government grant; leav- ire, £392 to be provided. At West Bank the estimated expenditure is £1,980, and the receipts £1,565, of which £6OO is school fees and £950 Government grant, leaving £415 to be provided. The School Management Com- mittee therefore require £l,OOl from the rates; the District FAtlucation Committee £462; Sites and Building Committee £552; and Finance Committee £2,330; total £4,345. The Committee recommended that a precept be served upon the overseers for the sum of £4,300, being the estimated deficiency in the Schoel fund up to the 29th Septemper next.. Mr. Heyes moved the adoption of the minutes. In reply to Mr. Deacon, the Clerk said the amount ot the precept last year was £3,600. Mr. Deacon remarked that they therefore wanted £7OO more.
The Chairman said that on a rateablevalue of £120.000 they would require a rate of Bid. in the £to meet their requirements. Mr. Wareing replied that that was the gross rateable value. _

.-.—.. . The Chairman stated that £120,000 is the nett rateable value. He asked why did they want so much mort money. The Clerk replied that they were overdrawn at the bank. Last year the District Education Committee were within their estimate £2l 2s 4d; and the Sites and Building Committee £261 6s 3d, while the Finance Com- mittee were £2OO and the School Management Committee £3OO bev nd their estimates. The rate last year was about 7d. . , The Chairman said that some of the expense was I caused by removing into the present offices. Had last year paid its own expenses, the rate then would have been about Bd. The average rate for the two years rould be about 71d. The chairman also stated that the school extensions this year w4nild make a hole in £4,000. The Clerk said he did not think the cost would be much over £2,000. After a pause. the Chairman said: I am afraid look- ing at the precept won't make it any lees. (Laughter.). The minutes were ado pted. .

,-THE SHIP CANAL WORKS, AND HOW THEY WILL AFFECT _ WARRINGTON AND THE DISTRICT. NO. I—EsaItODUCTORY:

• It is probable that most of those, and they are to be numbered by hundreds of thoueands. who have felt interested in the construction of the Manchester , Ship Canal have formed a more or less distinct con- ception of the general features of the canal and of the larger and more obvious changes its making I will involve. Most people know that the great waterway is to skirt the bed of the Mersey for a cer- tain distance, that is to say, from Eastham to Run- corn, and then to take an almost straight line to a - point a few miles on trie inland side of Warringtdn, and afterwards by a more circuitous route to reach the outskirts of Manchester, whore it opens out , into huge docks. But only comparatively few people have realised with any degree of clearness to ' what an extent the local features of each district through which the canal is to run will be modified and altered. It goes without saying that a wide and navigable channel is not to be cut through a busy and populous country without old arrange- ments being upset on every side. Old landmarks will be removed and new ones set up in. their place, railways will be deviated and in part recoastructed, roads intersected, paths and bye-ways blocked up or demolished, to say nothing of the numberless other modifications these larger alterations must entail. It is, therefore, with a view to forecasting these changes over what may be called the local sections of the canal that we purpose to give a sefies of articles in our columns, the information con- tained in which will be carefully culled from detailed' and authentic plans, and from various other sources. ' At few points of the route of the canal will so marked a transformation take place as in the ARPLEY FIELDS • at Warrington. Anyone standing on the footway at the southern side of the railway bridge which spans the Mersey near Arpley station will, on a moderately clear day, have well within his view an area of land, or at all events the greater portion of an area of land, not very large in extent. in which, within the next five years, operations will be con- ducted on 80 vast and diversified a scale as to com- pletely change the features of the landscape. At ' present—still taking the footway referred to as the point of vantage—the river, after sweeping under- neath the railway bridge, makes a gentle bend to the left, and is hidden from sight by the projecting houses of Arpley View. It, however, continues in an almost straight course, parallel with Wilders- pool Causeway, till at a point directly opposite the towering and conspicuous structure of Wilderspool brewery it swerves sharply to the right, and after running a slightly round-about course, forming, so to speak, a small segment of an immense circle; flows under the massive pile of Walton Arches. To the Aght the view, so far as terrestrial things are concerned, is cut off by the long railway embanke merit which runs practically all the way from Bank Quay station to the further side of Walton Arches On the northern side the boundary is formed by the railway from Bank Quay station to Arpley station, and the short length of line between the latter station and the Lancashire bank of the Mersey. ' Those familiar with the locality know that at pre- sent a person desirous of walking from Arpley railway bridge to Walton Arches has the choice of two or three different paths. He may, if he chooses, take the footpath which runs close to and parallel with the Lancashire bank of the river, or he may take a nearer cut by the road and path which inter- sect the fields. Still within this area of which we speak, there are also, for thosewhofind no terrors in' quagmires of mud in winter, and gales of dust in summer, the devious windings of " Slutcher's "-lane, 1 which lead from near Bank Quay station to Walton Arches. This, then, is a rough configuration of the Arpley Fields as they are to be seen to-day, • In what respects will'the scene be changed by the „eime the Ship Canal is finished? In order to answer this question let us in imagination attempt to view "the landscape o'er" as it will be five orl six years hence. The river which now, after passing under the railway bridge, continues to shape its course in a direct line for Wilderspool,, will then, • after having passed the bridge by something like one hundred yards, branch sharply off to the right into the new bed which is to be cut for it across the fields, and will regain its old channel just at the near side of Walton Arches. This new "cut " of the river will run in a straight line from the point at which it leaves the present bed of the river at Arpley till within a short distance of Walton Arches, • when it will describe a slight curve to the right in order that the waters may flow more easily into their old course. This river diversion will sweep away the further corner of the grounds of the Warrington Cricket and • Bowling Club, and another of ita consequences will be the complete demolition of the present road -across Arpley fields which for part of its length runs alongside the southern fence of the Cricket Ground. In place of this old ioad, however, will be a new and improved one, but on the south side of the new river bed. At the present time when a per- son passes over the railway crossing on Wilderspool Causeway he has to his right the short street, called River-road, which runs down to the bank of the Mersey, and there of necessity comes to an end. After the river has been turned into its new course, however, something like 120 yards of the old and empty channel opposite the end of River- road will be Ailed up to the level of the adjacent land, and, on the solid foundation thus erected, a new road will be formed which will be contimied parallel with the soueh bank of the new river bed until the latter curves, as already stated, to the • right, when the new road will 'form a still more sudden curve to the left, cross the Ship Canal and finally open out into the Chester main road at a point near the Stag Inn. Lower Walton. This new road, it is needless to st.y 'will very considerably shorten the distance which a pedes- trian has now to traverse in order to reach Lower ' or Hitr,her Walton, Daresbury, or any of the towns and villages in that direction. It will, so to speak, cut across the base of the triangle formed by the present highways between the level crossing on Wilderspool Causeway and, Lower Walton. It will be noted, however, that it is only a small part of the disused river bed whiclr is to be filled • up; the rest of the old •Mersey, channel is not merely not to be filled up, but is to be deepened and extended by the excavating of a considerable' portion of the Arpley Meadows so as to,form WARRINGTON DOCKS. In length these docks will extend from a point of the river as it is at, present opposite the Warring- ton sidaof St. James' Church to a point opposite the cottages which lie midway between Wilder- spool brewery and Tom Paine's Bridge. At the Wilderspool end, the docks will toyer a much larger surface then at the Warrington end, so as to allow the necessary space for the turning and passing of vessels which, it may be expected, will be continu- ally leaving and entering the canal. 'From the south-western end of the docks, there will be a means of entering the river through locks. By this arrangement vessels of suitable draught which may have come to Warrington from Manceester on the one hand or Eastham on the other, or indeed from any intermediate place on the canal, can be passed into the river in order to load or unload a cargo at, say, Bank Quay, or, by ceming along the new chan- nel, at any place higher up the river which is at present navigable. Other works which will tend to greatly alter the general features of the view from Arpley bridge, will be the construction of a NEW RAILWAY and the deviation of the old lines. The new rail- way is projected to branch sharply off from the Warrington end of Walton Arches and to take a direct route to the docks where, doubtless, it will branch out into many sidings for the convenience of traffic. In its course it will have to cross the river in its new bed, end this it will do by a bridge. At present there are two railways running over Walton Arches, one the Birkenhead, Lancashire, and Cheshire Junction Railway, which carries pas- sengers and goods through Daresbury and Frod- sham to Chester, and the other the Grand Junc- tion Railway, which runs through Moore and Preston Brook to Crewe, ana the farther south, the latter being on the westernmost side and running direct into Bank Quay high level station. Both of these tines will be deviated, in order that they may he raised to sufficient alti- tude to cross the canal at a high level. The devia- • tion of the Grand Junction Railway will begin near the arches in " Slutchefs"-lane—the first of the series of arches crossed after leaving Bank Quay Station--and the line will rise from this point on i huge embankments at a gradient of one in 135 crossing the river by a new bridge-a sort of second and heightened edition of Walton Arches--and con- tinuing its upward course will finally reach its highest point on the new viaduct' that is to span the ship canal, when it will gradually descend till it regains its old route. The trains leaving War- rington-by the Birkenhead, Lancashire, and Che- shire Junction Rifilway will continue as at pre- sent to run over Walton Arches, but directly they

cross they will turn t ) the right on to the deviated I line that is to be constructed. and which, owing to the much shorter length of this deviation, will carry them by a steeper gradient on to the great ship canal viaduct, after leaving which they will, as in the other case. desc4nd on to the old line. ' (To be contineted.) ' A WALE ALONG THE LINE.

div.head: BY BOOKER-ON.
div.p: BY BOOKER-ON.

The men employed at Latchford are kept busy for- warding materials and machinery to the various sections of the canal works, awl the wharf by the old canal near the railway bridge is laden with timber, &c. Another steam navvy,has arrived, and is being• transhipped to Haystack Bridge Wharf, Norton. The powerful 10-ton crane which has been erected is found, jnst the thing for lifting heavy weights. Mr. Morris Jones is the engineer in charge at Latchford.

At Acton Grange a. new engine, called Dunham,is at work removing earth from the cutting to form in embankment, which is required for some dis- tance along this section, and a. goodly number of men are employed. , At Bobs Bridge, about a mile further down, some two or three hundred men are busy excavating. A smith's forge, and a circular saw worked by a 10-horse engine, and a. pumping engine are at work here. The engine Warburton has been' got on the rails, and a large number of waggons are ready and wait- ing for the German navvy. a wonderful piece of mechanism, to be got to work. It is in charge of Mr. C. Helmig, Lubeck, Germany. A powerful crane has also arrived, and offices, &c., are about to be erected. Proceeding farther down the line of the 'canal near Astmere, bettor known as the big field, Norton, we come to Haystack. Bridge Wharf, where the locomotive Runcorn is at work, taking away the earth which is thrown into wagons by the Ameri- can steam, navvy. This steam navvy will lift and remove two tons of earth at onde, and can work at the rate of five tons per minute. This soil is being conveyed over the old canal by way of a wooden tressel bridge, which has been constructed by Messrs. Kirkham'. Runcorn. It is then tipped on the marsh between the old canal and the river Mersey, where some million of tons of earth can be disposed of to the improvement of the low-lying ground. Here a goodly number 0 joiners, brick- , layers, blacksmiths, &c., are engaged in the erection of sheds, &c. Another locomotive—the Ince—has I arrived this week from Ellesmere Port. A sawing mill is at work, and cooks' house and carpenters' sheds, tS;c., are in course of construction. Mr. C. Fincham is in charge. The various parts oLanother American steam navvy have arrived, and ?t will be got to work as soon as possible. On Wednesday evening what might have been a very seri us if not fatal accident occurred while the work al a bridge was being pushed ' for- ward. A labourer named William Berry, of Shaw- street, Runcorn, fell from the top of the bridge with a heavy piece of timber inta.the canal beneath. He was got out as .quickly as possible, and taken to Runcorn, where medical aid was proc'ared. 'lt Was found that he had not received . any serious injury beyond shock to the system. Upon inquiry, on Thursday, it was reported that he. will be ready for work %gamin a day or two. - CADLSHEAD. ,

A visit to Warburton on Thursday .afternoon showed that the prelithinary 'Works .in connection, with the Ship Canal are being rapidly pushed forward in the meadows north of the Irwell near Warburtoribßlidge. About 100 yards from the bridge one of Dunbar and lliishten's powerful steam navvies has been erected,.and, is being adjusted preparatory to commencing cutting,operations. This week sixty ballast waggolls have been conveyed by beat along the river to Warburton. A ballast line about a mile in length has been laid in the direction of Irlani and Warrington, and three locomotive ballast engines— the Trlam, a four-wheeler, And the Irlani and Mersey, six-wheelers-"--are being got ready for work' next week. Carpenters are busy erectink sheds for stones, and brick- layers are putting in the fonndations for the contrac- tor's offices and the first block of huts to accommodate the navvies. Thelines of the canal have been marked out; and a large number of trees have been felled and , brush and underwood cut. At Irlarn„ a , ballast,line is ' being constructed to meet that which is beina laid at TR, Warburton. _ _

, It is stated that the committee of , the Lyrnm Local Board have come to Satisfactory arrangements with the representatives of the Manchester Ship Canal Company respecting the -sale of the sewage farm belonging to the Board, and also the transfer of land of a quality more suitable to the requirements of the'Board from the com- pany. The full details will probably be laid before the

next meeting of the Board. ' The first flat load of timber was discharged on the, river bank, a little beyond the Statham Pool Bridge, on Tuesday. This is the first instalment to the Lymm section length. Three truck loadsoarf barrows have also arrived per train, and are being removed to, the site of the works. A foreman has arrived. It Is ,thought that work will be found for all suitable men in this neigh- bourhood in the course of a fow days.

div.head: MOORE.
div.p: MOORE.

_ Considerable progress is being made in the work of conitructing the, canal in the neighbourhood of Moore, and the men are, kept at work late and early. For . several Sundays past large numbers of visitors from Warrington have gone over to inspect the works., SALFORD ,DOCKS. The first locomotive of a number which will be em- ployed wen the Salford section of the Ship Canal was' at work on 'Wednesday on the Mile Field, Trafford 'Road. beers'the appropriate title of "Manchester," and is enga,d in dray-ring waggona to and' from- the • cutting `which has beeh started near the Racecourse. About 300 navvies are engaged in excavating on the site of the ha- tended Salford dock, which will be about 29 acres in ex- tent. Several steam cranes are on the ground,. and two or three sets of railway lines have been • constructed. Eitensive offices are also in course of •.erection on the ground.' Until the arrangements connected 'with the ' purchaks*of the land are completed the full number of hands rennired-cannot be taken on. • • • PAYMENT OF SECOND INSTALMENT. , For four days alarge.staff of clerks employed' by the National Provincial Bank of England has been busy re- ceiving payment of the second instahnent of a ' on the holders of ordinary shares in the Manchester Ship Canal Company. ..Te faW.litate the work, which it would , have beau unicessible,to Conduct with this expedition on any bank Premises in Manchester, a branch of ,the National Provincial Bank of England was opened last Thursday,in. St.,Jarnes's Hall, here a large body of shareholders might have been seen every hour that the brancll h'as 'remained open paying. the amounts due ,from them. On Monday thefe was an exceedingly large at- tendance of shareholders, that being the day Ihien for the Payment of.the . irstaiment. Twenty five clerks were kept for several . hours hard at Work receiving' money ;and filling, in, the forms of receipt:, and when the time • came for closing the doors hundreds Of,' persons were • waiting to make the contributions , required Vom them towards the capital of the Ship Canal Company. Such a spectacle has 'never before been seen in Manchester, except in' connection with the Ship Canal .undertaking. The large amount of money representel by the transac- tioms which have taken p/acein st. James's Hall during ,the last, few days brought on the scene on Monday several persons whose movements were somewhat. suspicious., On being asked what they wanted they replied that, they simply desired to have a look at stich an extraordinary spectacle and," see what was going on." .It is believed that their object was a much more serious one. It is thought that they intended to rob a number of the shareholders by means of some rzise, but their plans were frustrated by Mr. Goodier (of the Ship Canal Com- pany's staff), who sent a message to the Town Hall ask- ing for the presence of one or two 'detectives. When these gentlemen niadetheirappearance thepekons about whom suspicion had been aroused deemed it prudent to take an early departure. , - We understand that hi order to meet the convenience of shareholders who were on Monday unable to wait long enough to pay the calls on the shares held by them part of the staff of the National Provincial • Bank again attended on Tuesday at St. James's Hail to.receive in- stalments of share capital. The public will learn with some interest that three clerks were. engaged &ring the greater portion of Monday receiving money from share- holders who desired to pay up their shares in full.

THE OPERATIONS AT EASTHAM. (From the "Manchester Examiner and rimes.") At Eastham, a thousand men have now been at work for over two months. The first sod of the Manchester Ship Canal was cut at ,this point on the 11th November by Lord Egerton of Tatton. Since then remarkable progress has been merle. For the length of about sixteen hundred feet the channel of the canal is marked out, not in its full width and depth, it is true, but in a way sufficient to give a fair idea of the work which will ultim- ately be accomplished. The work begins with day- light and does not even end with darkness. From seven in the morning till about five at night the main part of the great army of labourers are toiling either in the canal cutting or at the large dock, or are engaged in miscellaneous occupations. At night, s, smaller body of men take up the wondrous tile of organised endeavour, and by the light of immense camp fires continue the path of progress, working from Liverpool towards Manchester. Aivisit to Eakthatn just now is full of interest. The journey, however, is a matter of greater time than per- haps many Manchester people imagine. In the summer the ferry boat runs frequently each day from the Liver- pool Landing Stage to Eastham, conveying chiefly crowds of pleasure seekers. But in the winter there Is no service at all, and a visitor has to cross first of all to Birkenhead, and has thee to proceed

by train either to Bramborough or to Hooton. The former station is more than two miler fronnyther BOOM operations, and the latter Markt than three knitted . Ega' in winter, however, the walk through the country lanes is delightful. The walk takes one threugh, the lovelie.st part of Cheshire. -Fair green fields stretch on either hand, with pleasant villas cosily bowered in Weedlands and many a white satbstantial farmstead. Sometimes I the lanes are long avenues qf trees—the oak; the fir, the birch, and the sycamore—the bare arms. meeting. and embracingoverhead, The fir more particularly is promin- ent- -in the . latidscape„standing high- . in its lean, prim uprightness above its , sturdief' and more 'expansive neighbours. Long before Eastham Ferry is reached the sight and :mounds of labour are heard. The whistle of the lacomotive; faintly caught at firsts, becomes mare and more Piercing to the ear as the journey nears its end. Thick wreaths of dun smoke are seen rising above the distant trees, expanding and dissipating in their gentle upward course. Next, a. little colony of wooden housers, on the hillside above the river, comes in view, and by no means adds to tha charm of the landscape. Finally, with the indtistty of, a thousand workmen filling the ear.' we come to green fields through which a rough road has been improvised, and see belcaw range upon range of wooden buildings— cots, offices, stables, and Sheds for miscellaneans pur- poses, with a score of labourers scattered about placing planks, digging the earth, or giving hoarse. signals' to the drivers of the screeching locomotives. Altogothee it is a scene full of bustle and of labour, Apparently confused; but in reality, as inquiry soon shows, in a state of per- fect organisation, each man's taak 'a faetor in the com- plete unity eventually to be achieved. The Eastham section of the .canal extends some four and a half miles frem a point just beyond the ferry. Far a geed part of this distance the lovely Cheshire' landacape is both deformed and transfoemed by theloreparations for our great undertaking.- Rut Eastham Ferry itself, the paradise of Liverpool plekstire seekers, is untouched by our vandal hands. From the 'Cliffs over the river, the pontoon pier, the square grey-looking hotel, and the noble background of woods, stand pleasantly out. Though Manchesteahas its Will; Liverpool is not to be robbed of its joys. Picnic parties may stilt mime Up the river to enjoy the pleasures of the tea gaidend, tb find what solace they may in the 'Zoological Gardens or to wander under the noble oaks of Eastham wood.' The wood may still be the chief Saturday afternoon 'summer haunt of the Mersey. Here, as in David • Clipperfield," Red Whisker may make his atrocious salad, and David and Dora wander out in a seventh heaven under the treas,, and Miss lills chant her lugubrious melodies of blighted affection. , It is a lovtly- holiday groirid and will not be less so when the canal is: brollOht to COMOUS-- ,a thin. When that day comes, why should not Eastham be a common, centre for •the picnic peopli; of both Man- chester and Liver Pool, where they may shake' hands, as it were, in common enjoytrient, and cane:Rho tea gar- dens .to flourish mightily? The Mersey estnari at this point- is a Magnificent • stretch- of Water, some three or four ariles"-probhbry in width. It, requires a clear day to See the smoking chimneys away on the other side at Garston ; for same' days -past the eutline, of the Opposite shore has been but dim 'and hazy. Ju.st.now the river.is busy with boats and tugs bringing material up the river for the canal works. Although Eastham wood is totetain Its charms, two smaller woods higher up the river, have, it should be fetid, passed away under the hands of the spoiler. Scarough Wood and its neighbour, Heston 'Wood, are now things of the past: The trees have been uprooted and borne away, for they impeded the path of progress. Chiefly; the trees were the oak, the birch, and the sycamore.' The .elm tree's shade,- fortalking age and whispering- lovers made, was wanting : This is a fat which the builders of the canal regret, not from the sentimental but from the utilitarian point of view. The oak is of a perverse and stiffnecked generation, whereas the' elm -would have gently yielded itself to shaping hands, and been-valuable for railway- . wagon pUrposes: The men and steitm navvies are at work on two of the three Eastham lerflaa-and on the main cutting of the canal. Work on the third and smallest of the -locks will not begin for-some time bi come. The site of this lock.is on the rivet bank, near the wooden huts, on the: right which will have to be cleared away when operations be- gin. The greatest of the locks will be 600 feet - long by 80 feet wide. THP cutting already made is some 50 feet wide and ,24 feet deer. 'There is a sufficient dam, of course, between'the lock and the river. a In the striver, quite neat' the lock; will be seen a group of tug boats, nand it is at this point that the canal will have ita-autlet in the Metseg: The second lock, the cutting of which is a1..50 in rapid progress, has dimensions dr 350 feet by 5i feet, while the third will-be 150 feet by 30 feet. In each case the leek is parallel with the river cliffs: The, main cutting of the canal ex`endecla k -day or two ago,- to I,Booft. and the -depth was some 21 feet, Linea of rail- way have been laid--for' three miles in the' direction of Ellesmere Port, at -which place- what is known as -the Eastham seetion ends. It -' is eonv'enient to state' here that the minimum-width of the canal- willtsbe- 120 feet,- and the depth 26 feet. - -Where the reek has been touched some blasting will Too neceksary to secure the proper depth. No less than ten locomotives are at work on the 'railway, panting' all -day Under' heavy burdens, Cad , night' bringing- the men from distant outposts to 'their wooden huts near the ferry. 'The steam navvy is a gigantic-engine for the saving of human labour. It has a great keen tooth, which works from the bottotri of the cutting upwards, and - at each effort atort and 4 half of soil isplaced intheironbticket or -B.4ge.' After each Mobration theeiahe swingsthe-tage round overltatagon; and by 4 dredger-like .appliance: the bot- tom 'doors are loosed; and the soil is; deposited in the wagon. The navvy is hi the-care of -three: men. "A (River has full tentrol Over the hoisting and lowering of the bucket and the jibbing of the crane. The wheel- -man's duty is to see that the tooth of the 'navvy I.s. pressed far enough out into the soil as,it is being -pulled up by the crane, and when the bucket is full 'to, allow it to • run back so. that the crane • meat • jib --Mund. The wheelman alao pulls the string. by- which- the bottent of I the buclget is releneed over the empty wagatias-The third "man connected with the Working of theMaVvyis the fire-- man; The navvy clears away from 700 to 800 cubic a-ards a day, each cubic yard being 'estimated Its :weigh:. ing Aleut a tort4nd*half. At- the present time three. of theataenormously poweilniengines are at work eic,a.v- ating on the Eastham section, but in the Num& of a few weeks more aid-or this' sort is eOpected, so -that quicker proer, iths may-be made:' • '

. aivtib small eolonieg of -,Vtooded Ilqueas built by the Ship. Canal CcinrOnny'foi their workers at Eastham. One tfronp stands-high: oir the cliffs above, the, river; the other is on a meadow slope, not far removed from the Main' reiadi bud towards Easthain pier. These rough wobden walls Scarcely add to!'the bea.uty.Of the landscape-, and, to an irreverent eye have something the look of large •bathing vans. But though-the outside is utipromisibg; indoors If. is; fairly comfortable. . Mantel- pieces, it is true; and other fittings ofatie,houSehold, are rather conspienonsly absent, 'and thereis arstsspicio,n of draughts: but then the houses are only .three wcel* old as vet, and the inmatefi *ill soon inake' good: these little defects. Several inindlidd men, semetimetwith ;families, 'are se housed: the ,rest aro' saattered about the diatrict and find temborary lodgings in the•neighbouring It must not be imagined thateach hdusehold is isolated and complete.' One faThily rents a tenement at a moder- ate rate fmm the I.!ompany.-•and then as a ,Nule takes in as • ' many • lodgers. fansilies Or sin&le • :men,• as

. , . can be acconsnofiated: •On the cliff above the.. river is a gremt. • boaoding - : house. • -managed by an ohilady, and here no lees than 50 lodger have a. home, with the•bo2rding-house luxuries otßlaCkpotd.,o; Douglas. Quite a family look many of the hots have, • with women and ccitnely:girls.talking at the doorways. The laboimers'arb not at all the sort of people the East- ham people fearekl they would be. ' •Fine;. big, stalwart fellows" manv.of them are, capable of ;•aill, amount • Of hard work, buthir nal-trans the.rough and brutal pay- viesl whose incursion was so much ieared.., The men are behaving admirably, an, tiviiig no trouble at all. - '.Mr. Walker's sub-aeent has a very-comfortable one-storeyed house, rough outside; exactly as the rest, but pleasant and cheerful indoors. There are four os.flve rooms; the plain Walls of which.are either covered with homelyvie- tures or concealed: by well-filled/book shelves. One .of the pictures. istir fine engraving of Garibaldi's stern vis- age. Another house visited contained a family and several lodgers. It was net unlike in Ordinary: English' Workman's cottage. Downstairs were the usual living rooms, and cooking preparation 4 were • in !pro7• progress. Several men were seated round the fire, the day's werit being just over and working clothes not Yet thrown off. Upstairs were the bedrooms; with bed- steads, the framework of which had been supplied by the . Ship Canal Company. In one bed a young man was lying suffering from cold or, as he feaied., from a tinsel of ague. Inthis house the 'white -walls had been painted by the occupants delicate green; but the mantlepieces were still panting. - A few pictures, chiefly of a sacred character, did something furthei to :lighten thepTain- ness of the dwelling. So.' although the little • colon* of houses is rather hideous from an artistic point of view, life within its borders is by. no -meats -dismal, nor does it lack the Cesineas and healthful variety which Many in Manchester are • ;Striving to carry to !such quarters as 'Ancoats and Bra,dfmid.. A fair country of green Yields and pleasant woodlands is also open to our Ship Canal- toilers for week-end recreation. •

Another steam naVvyvras sotto work onMonday on the Eastham Section of the canal, making the third now in operation. While the two first are employed in digging, or more strictly speniting scooninrz'out the basin of the docks which are to form the Eastham terminus of the canal,-the new 'digger is placed at a point half way to Ellesmere Port. The centlactors' railway line skirathe shore of a bay abotff beyond the terminus, and crows Pool Hall Brook (which MA been bridged) at about the termination of the second mile. Just beyond this the line of the canal A,es through the fields ag,ain, and it is making the neeessary cutting • that the new steam digger is emPltnicid. In advance of the steam' digger massive embankments of sods and earth are being piled up by•spade and barrcnv work, a thick "pit" (over afoot in depth) being' taken off the ad- joining grass land by the navvies. At Pool Hall Brook also navvy huts are being erected covered with tarred felting. The contractors' line is laid about .half a mile further, and has reached to within about a mile and a half of Ellesmere Port. THE BRIDGEWATER NAVIGATION COM- PANY, LIMITED. DIVISION OF THE SURPLUS.
Judgment was delivered on Monday in the nmiion which was argued on the 16th December before Mr. Justice North. •

His Lordship said the question raised by the motion was on what principle the surplus moneys arising from the sale of the Bridgewater Navigation Company to the Manchester Ship Canal Company was to be divided be- tween the ordinary and preference shareholders in the undertaking. The surplus to be divided after repay- ment of the share capital invested was estimated at be- tween £850,000 and £900,000. The Bridgewater Naviga- tion Company was formed in August, 1872, to acquire the Mersey and Irvrell, the Manchester and Salford, and the Runcorn canals, the original capital being £500,000, divided into 5,000 shares of £lOO per share. Article 4 pro- vided for the increase of capital by the issue of pref- erence' shares; article 92 provided that no dividends should be paid except put of the net profits; article 93 proviaed for the formation of a reserve fund, and article 94, that the entire net 'profits should belong to the holders of ordinary shares. On the 29th September and the-rith October;lB72, 'special- resolutions were formed to the effect that the capital of the Compinv should be divided into £lO shares instead of £lOO shaolts, and that the ca.pital should be. increased by the issue of 80,000 new £lO shattes to Z 1,390,000. In August and Septem- ber, 1874, the articles were slightly modified' by ' Roecial resolutions. Before 1880 £2 lOs pershare had been paid on the 30,000 shares issued,arel £BOO,OOO lad beenborrowed on mortgage, and in 1880 the Directorg'resolved to pay off the mortgage by applying the proceeds from the sale of eurplua lands and by Issuirtg 30,000 preference shares bearing 5 per cent, interest, in priority to the ordinary shares, and then to rank with the ordinary shares in the division of profits after 5 per cent, had been paid on , them. The scheme was succeesfwl, and the whole of the 30,000 shares were- taken, up. When tho Manchester Ship Canal Company was formed, that Company agreed I,to, purchase the whole undertaking of the Bridgewater Navigation Company for £1,700,000, the purchase to . be completed within two years from the date of the agree- ment, which had been done. Nothing remained now to be , done but to wind up the company, which had gone into voluntary licitiidation. pay off aU debts and liabilities, and divide the surplus between the ordinary and preference shareholders. The question before the Court was then raised. The holders of the 30,000 preference shares on which the whole £lO per share had been paid claimed ' that the surplus should be divided pro rata with the llders of the ordinary shares on which £3 lOs pei share had been paid. The holders of e ordinary shares con- tended that the holders of the p ference share were en- titled to only 5 per cent, and that the surplus capital I belonged exclusively to the ordinary shareholders—first, because the issue of preference shams being 'ultra viral,' the holders of preference shares were not shareholders at all; secondly, if they were shareholders then they were limited to 5 per cent. interest, With regard to the first 1 point his Lordship held that under the articles the 'preferettesliares were validly issued, and that their holders were entitlecito rank as shareholders: and secondly, that , in the division of , the, surplus they were entitled to be treated equitably. To limit them to -5 per cents interest otrtheir shares' paying at the date of the winding up of the Company at 8 per cent., would be manifestly unfair. After' citing aathorities, his Lordship said he should de- clare that the balance of the proceeds of the sale of ' the undertaking remaining after satisfying all the debts and liabilities of the Company and the costs of the liquida- tion and repayment to the shareholders of all the capital paid'up ought to be avided amongst all the shareholders in proportion to the amount paid up on their shares. The costs' ef Messrs. Scholfield and NO), appointed to represent ' the preference and ordinary shareholders, otieht to be paid by the liquidator, as between solicitor and client, out of the &seat of the Company. - ' Mr. Cozens Hardy, -Q.C.4 representing the orditim7 shareholders) asked his Lordship to insert the words "'without prejudice to any question with refeience to the reserve fund and other questions which may there- after arise." The Manchester Ship Canal Company took over the whet, of the Bridgewater Navigation Company's undertaking, including this reserve fund. . His Lordship: I don't intend .to' prejudice any qt testion. Mr. Hardy : Before the preferettee shares were issued 'surplus lands were sold to railway companies for large RUM, which were appropriated towards the paYment of Inans. • - -
Mr flig„ains, Q.C. (for the liquidators) suggested that somo limits should he itderted in the order to the time ii which claims to the suriAtle could be sent in. After a long diScusSion

His Lords* amended the form of his declaration as follows :—The-balance remaining after the satisfaction of all the debts and liabilities of the. Company, and after adjusting the rights of the 'creditors inter se (other than their rilhts-hirespect of such balance), and after satiS- fying tr costs or the, liquidators, and repayment, to shareholders of all "Rie ' capital, paid 'up, ought to 'be divided among all the: shareholders in proportion- to the amount paid up on their shares. ' • Ordcr accordingly.

In answer to the Clerk; the WORKHORSE Mime said that there had been nothing done with regard to the Workhouse Infectious hospital.—The Cum remarked that as the subject of accommodation for infectious cases hadbeen zaised it would .be better to deal with it. The Worklibtse hospital had been erected at a considerable cost for the express purpose of receiving infectious patients, but for some years past it had been used for cases that could not easily be removed, and the fact waa that if they needed the hospital for the purpose for which it was built it would be of do use, and he did not know what they would do as Board of Guardians. He observed that at several places there had been an out- break of epidemics.—The CHAIRMAN thought that was• a matter for the House Committee.--The CLERK: They do not seem to have done anything.—Mr. JOLLEY said the House Committee were of opinion that the hospital would biqoonal to all requirements that would come under their hotice: The hospital had been used because they. had been rather short of space in other parts of the house, or because they had utilised other parts of the house in other ways. The House Committee considered they-were perfectly justified in using the hospital in the way they were doing in order to prevent the hecessity for an ex- tension of the Workhouse. If any epidemic arose the House Committee would be fully prepared to meet it, whether it was of scarlet fever, of smallpox, or anything else.—Mr. &Amman thought the matter might be safely left to the House Committee.—Mr. PENNINGTOH said he should like to ask the-Workhouse master if in the event of an infectibus case-being brought to the house the present inmates of the hospital could be removed at onre.—The Wei:3Ellol7Se MASTER: I should remove them. —The CLERK said that if the hospital could be made available at any moment that removed the difficulty.— The matter then dropped. •

Neither team was fully , represented, Widnes being the greatest sufferers in this respect, being minus Hughes. Hardman, and Morris, whilst Wigan were only short of Slevin. The groundwas very slippery—an un- fcirtunate event for ,the losers; who never play up to form on a wet field. A start was effected soon after three o'clock, Smith kicking off for Widnes. . The ..return fixture between the above pjubs was brought to a close on Saturday, On the enclosure at Wilderspool, Warringtan. It will be remembered that ' Warrington visited Walfieldl 'on December 31st, and suffered defeat by one try, and it was thought by many that the local club, on their own ground, wOuld Manage to reverse this Verdiet. This calculation proved correct; for tho home team an Utrdtidly contested game by one goal, one try, and ' twO iMnors, to one goal and, eight minors; Referiln,g to the past meetings of bbth eh:lb% it has neyef, previous to Saturday; . been the WatTingtOni- ans good fortune to 10,54 r the colents of the Trinitarians, they having met ,four times, Wakefield winning throe , games to Warrington one. On Saturday, neither side I was able to place their full strength in the field, lnit „ • Trim ty certainly suffered most in this reepect, being ' without several of their advertised team. It waS esti- mated that close on 8,000 spectators assembled to witness , the match, admirers of the Rugby game journeying from Runcorn, Widnes, and-even Manchester. Each team on making their appearance came in for hearty applause, and nO time was lost in commencing operationi. Banes having lost the toSs, Fallas (the Wakefield cap- ' tain) took sAlvasitige sof the slight breeze.' Frank Turner !•. ' •

set the ball in motion, and Bertram "made his mark " from, the kick off. The Wakefield captain kicked to centre flag, and the first to make any movement was J. Dawson, who put in a dashing run to the Warrington quarter flag. From the first scrimmage formed Dunn passed neatly to Bertram, the latter kicking over the line, the ball rolling dead.; From the drop outFallas ' re- plied to .centre, and shortly after Bartram again kicked a dead ball. Good play by the home backs now settled the game in neutral territory. Gradually but surely the Warringtonians svorked tiien; way by some fine passing into the visitora! 25, and train a pack at the quarter flag W. Dillon mine through'and, dribbling' inSplendid style, scored a grand try close to the quarter, flag, Loud cheers' greeted this effort,, but the place was too difficult for Fair Turner to increase its value, the leather falling lust short of•the bar. Bartram restarted, Barnes returrung in touch at centre. Nevins was conspicuous by saving a rush of the Trinity forwards, And deick passing by the Yorkshire hacks ended in Ash taking his drop at goal, scoring the third minor. Speakman restarted, and the Trinitarians pressed the home team back on their' lines. Hume was now awarded a free kick for a fair catch, but Bartram failed at the place. Jolley put in some sterling work frem the drop out, and a free kick availed the Yorkshire men but little, as Massey returned well into neutral • territory. Bertram almost landed a, goal from a mark of. Davies just .saving, and little relief was brought from the drop out. From a pack at the Warrington quarter Warren tried to, get Asiva,yi, but 'Latham safely held. him. Neat passing by the home baelts was now indulged in, Fair. Turner and Barnes mulling a certain chance of scoring. The game raged fast and furiouS. in . neutral ground, each side striving to obtain the mastery, until a grand kick by Ash scored another dead ball to the already , long list. Ash was again to the fore by a long kick over the line, art'd Bar- tram shone with ardodgy run soon • after the .diop out. Considering that the horn° team • were forced to play on the defensive,this half, they played grandly, never fag-, ging to; one moment, and it was miraculous how they kept the Yorkshiremen from 'crossing their lines. This they did, and the only, special point of interest from now' to the call of half-time was pretty exchange kicking•by Ash, Bertram, fslassey, and Barnes. Half-time was called with the score—Warrington, 1 try; Wakefieldl Trinity, 7 minors. Bertram restarted from midfield, play resting inmeutral territory. Dunn'saved a rush 91 the Warrington' forwards in daring style, and Ash negatived a dribble of the " wirepullers "by a neat run to half-way.' Massey responded by - huge punt to th. Trinity' quarter-flag, but Detin was again the favour,of, his side by a brilliant run and kick to midfield.. The Warringtoniatts would not be 'denied : they Wended their way slowly to the visitors'goaL and a rush-by the home: forwards, headed. by Dillon and Littlewerad,'ended in, Fotherby saving just 'when Dillon was -ready to add another, tangible point. Nevins responded to the drop- out and gained raturd of applause by a fine kick to the Trinity line. The leatber was doomed not to stay here long, for the • rYorkshiremen played up with renewed' vigour, ad Are.spa,ssed on Warrington • soil. , Prettyi passing by Dunn, Fallas, and Bertram ended in a Scrim- mage being feirriatlat the 'WarringtOn quarter-flag. War- ren now called forth cheers from the excited spectators •by a marvellous run to .tlr opposing line, Fotherby just stopping him when ecbring, seemed a certainty. Ash negatived this brilliant run 'by a huge kick to half- way, and . after,some play of a give-and-take nature, Dunn Passed (lure* to Bertram, WhO lowered the War- •1 rington Citadel". On the reemntnencemerit, from:centre, ' J. Dawson again threatened danger, =id got past all position with the eXcePtion of Davies,' Who had retired for a few minutes, but who brought down his man in line „style. .'Ashton. Peve.yo and .Fair. Turaer, dribbled back to centre,, and Spoakman kicked across to Jolley,. the litter gaining 'ground by a strong run to Wakefield quarters The Warrington men now, seemed to get cheer= ganised, and the only point. of interest to chronicle wag grand exchange kicking by 'Ash, 11a/iron-I, Massey, and Nevins. Both, teams tried Shard to , add, Vs the score, Warren getting in another brilliant run. This run seemed to infuse fresh life into the Warringteninns, for Fotherbyiwas forced to adopf the eaving clause. It only wanted alear minntes from the, call of time and people were to be seen Wenditik their way from the ground; thinking that all was' aver;and that Warrington had again to submit to the prowess of the famous Yorkshire cupholders. But the gloriouguncertaintythat is attached to the favourite' winterPristiine was not slow in making itrs appearance: From some loose play in neutral ground*, Jolley got possession, and, threading his way' through the thick of his opponents, placed himself in A favoura- ble position for his drop at gaol; the result being that, he snateiaed tjm victery. from the Wakefield team just when defeat seemed inevitable. 'The Scene' which 'followed cannot'dasily be deseribed here,. suffice it to say that the cheersarecre renewed again and again. After seventy minutes of a pleasant and interesting, game, beth for spectators and players, Warrington•re-;' tired *tors as above. The Warrington team are to be congratulated on their victory. During the first half they had equally asrmuch'of the game as their oppenents, al- though the minerswerein favour of the Wakefield teem. This can only be accounted for by the huge kicks of the j Yorkshire backs. The second half 'yeas h splendid exhi- bition, but after Bartraln had placed the visiting team in the majority the Warrington men se.emed to lose heaat, and if, was niit until Warren, by his untiring ehergy, put fresh life into them and urged the team onrfortherr final effort that they pulled themselves' together. Of indivP. dual , play„ Nevins played splendidly at Nick., whilst Jolley *AS the best of the three (platters. Barnes played a- dashing game; Massey, having -little work; Warren_ surprised everyone brhis hrillip.ut -,play and certainly ought to ho creclitod with high honours. COLLISION OFF HOLYHEAD. ' THIRTEEN LIVES LOST. The Norwegian barque Freidis (Captain Larsen) left the Mersey on Tuesda.y morning for Savannah with a cargo of salt and caustic soda. On Wednes- day afternoon, the Dominion steamer Toronto ar- rived at Liverpool, and landed the chief officer of the Freidis, who is the dole survivor of the crew, the remainder having gone down in the ship, which was sunk by collision with the Toronto. It appears that when the Freidis was off the Skerries a few miles off Holyhead, on Tuesday night, a collisioa occurred between her and the Toronto. The Freidis "sank like a atone," disappearing in a few minutes. The mate, whose name is Larsen. and who Waft the captain's brother, managed to clamber on board the Toronto at the moment • they were togetnerk and thus saved his life. The 'crew of the Norwegian vessel had not time to lower any of their bops be- fore their barqueloundered. With all speed the cati- tain of the Toronto launched fear or five a his boats, and set about looking for the shipwrecked men. Unfortunately none of them .could be found, and after cruising about for some time ' the Toronto was forced to come on to Liverpool with only one of the unfortunate crew. - The Toronto was bound from Portland. It is understood that the crew of the Freidis consisted of 14 hands, so that, only one being saved. there has been a loss of 13 lives. The Men are said to be all , foreigners, mostly Norwegians.. ,The FrOdis was a vessel of 620 tons register, and V7/18 owned 15y Mr. Jacobson in Norway. The mate LOSent received a great Shock, and had to be medically treated on arrival at Liverpool. Captain Larsen was a married . mamma belonged. to Norway. , Larsen, the survivor, alleges ' that the To-ronto steamed ahead for about a mile before her engines were seopped, when the boats were lowered, but no • survivors were discovered. Captain Bouchette, of the Toronto, however, states that his engines were stopped almost instantly, and as soon as the serious nature of the disaster was realised: Larsen states that most of the crew of the barque • were below at the time, and she sank so suddenly after the collison , that there was no time for them to escape. ' The • .steamer sustained but slight injury considering the 'force of the impact, the principal damage being the driving of one of her anchors into the liowplates.

" Burris' Letters" is-issued in the Camelot series by 'Mr. Walter Scott ; and a capital volume it makes. Those who are familiar :only with the poetry of , Robert Burns will do , well to give themselves a further :treat by reading his letters. They abound in hppyphrases, and strong masculine sense, and 'there is not a single letter that could be .reckoned ,4trll by the ordinary reader. The letters are se- lected and arranged With an introduction, by Mr. J. Logic Robertson, M.A., who Writes in a sympathetic vein and throws a good deal of light 'upon the cir- cumstances under which some of the letters were written. . , Amongst the "Great Writers "published by the same firm, *e have, for -the current month, "The Life of Goldsmith" by Mr. Austin Dobson. ,We have read this new life of the author of "The , Vicar of Wakefield" with 'especial pleasure, Mr. Dobson deals with his sub- ject and with the reader so fairly. It is evident that he has a kindly regard for Goldsmith—and who has not that @as studied his delightful works F—but he is careful td give a 'plain unvarnished tale so that Oliver May be recognised not at his best oK at his worst, but as he real- ly. was. Related as Goldsmith was to the great writers of his day, it is matter of course to say that the. book abounds with anecdotes of Johnson, Burke, "Jacobite Songs and Ballads "is tha title of the Can- terbury Boots issue.. The selection is edited by Mr. G. S. IVlacquoid, Who furnishes an introductory chapter which is invaluableto those' who. wish to thoroughly understand the songs. He says :--" Jacobite songs may bo said really' to date from the Revolution of 1688, and the flight -of James the second' (from whose name in Latin, Jacobus, the word Jacobite is derived) although there are many songs before this period which might be 'classed as Jacobite." The volume includes, of course, the ballads.k.c..relatin‘g to the risings of 1715, and 1745 when the. Young Pretender made his attempt and failed•-. Kull ' for the most part of party spirit, the songs are In no wise lacking in go." They are arrangod, as far as possible, in chronological order, and there are,*nnerouSo notes to explain.tho text..:

HE EXPECTED IT.—A gentleman at the funeral of his wife, was annoyed •to' see the cartisges containing the friends get terribly mixed: "I knew perft•Aly well," he said, with a tone of disappointment, "that this day wouldn't go off without some unpleasant incident." INFEamE.—When you see a young .man sailing down street shortly after midnight,„with collar mashed down his neck, you can'maki, •up your,. mind there's a young girl crawling upstairs no far distant•with her shoes under her arm and an extinguished lamp in her

hand. 'A LOVER'S TEST.-" I cannot live without her," said a young man to a friendly adviser, ",and I an going to test her." Ile pulled out a pistol, and added, . I shall go to her with this, and say, 'Here, shoot me down; I cannot live without you: ", "Yon had better not," said the friend; "she might pull thatrigger." "I don't care for that," replied the heart-broken lover. ".1 have filled the weapon with blank cartridge." A PAINTED-% Bru.L.--An. American farmer, on reading that a bull patnted by Rosa Bonheur sold for five thou- sand dollars, remarked to his wife that he didn't see how a coat of paint could so greatly enhance the value of the animal; but, if Rosa didn't charge more than ten dollars, he would get her to paint his bull in the spring. His wife replied that she thought he might paint it him- self, end save his ten dollars. -This hint he took, and on driving the bull to market in the spring his disappoint- ment was great at finding his artistic efforts not appreciated. Brown, who had married the eldest of seven daughters, tried to quarrel with his mother-in-law the other evening. "Brown," she said, "Larn.not going to ruin my reputation by quarrelling with you. Wait till my other girls are married. At present as a mother-in- law I am only an amateur.'. Uncle: "Why .did you fail to pass the examination ?' Nephew: "On account of a mere digerence of opinion between the fellow who examined me and myself. Uncle : "How was. that ?" Nephew : " Qh, I thought one side gained the battle in an anCient war, and he fancied it was the other." Durnley had accompanied a friend home to dinner, and as they seated themselves at the table, the hostess remarked, 'I trust that you will make allowances, Mr. Dunrley. My servant left me very unexpectedly. and I was compelled to cook the dinner myself." "Oh, cer- tainly, my dear madam, certainly," rosponded Dumley, with great emphasis ; " I can put up with anything !" AN ENIGMA.-Not wishing to be outdone in literary enterprise by those publications which have tractions especially designed for the pleasing of the fancy and the strengthening of the intellect of youth, we nave con- trived and built up the following enigma l at great ex- pense of time and labour :-I am a word of 13 letters. My 7,9, 4,4, is a village in Europe.. My 7, 14, 5,7, is a kind of dog. My 11, 13, 13,9, 27.2,3, 6, 1,13, is a.] peculiar kind of stuff. My 2, 6,12, 8,9, 4, is the name of a great general of ancient times (have spelt it to best of ability, though may have missed the bull's-eye on a letter or two, but not enough to signify). My- 3, 11, 1,9; 15, 2,2, 6,2, 9, 13, 2;6, 15,4, 11, 2,3, 5,1, 10, 4,8, is the Middle name of a Russian philosopher, up .whose cognomen fame is slowly but surely rising. My 7, 11, 4, 12, 3,1, 1,9, is an obscure but very proper kind of elephant. My whole is-but perhaps a reasons ble amount of diligence and ingenuity will reveal that. „ A CHEAP MARRIAGE.-TIIP other day, while a registrar sat warming his feet by the fire, and his nose by a cigar, a stranger entered; and Inquired " iw much will you charge me to read over about 15 lines of printed matter from a book I have?" "Why, can't you read them ?" replied the official. "I can, but I want to hear how the lines sound when read aloud. I'll give you a shilling to read them to me." "Go on, I can't earn money any quicker." A woman opened the door at that moment, and the stranger put down the book on the desk, disped her hand, and said-" Begin at the pencil-mark there, and read slowly till I give the word for ybu to stop. The registrar's chin dropped as he saw that the reading mat- ter was the usual form of marriage, but he didn't back down from his word, for he said, "I am an honest man, and might have lost money by refusing." He read the service and pocketed the shilling, and the man and woman left the office, rejoicin'gat having accomplished one of the cheapest weddings on record., BACHELOR'S Hath..-A gentleman who is rather given to story-telling relates the following :--When I was a young man I spent several years at the South, residing for awhile at Port Hudson, on the Mississippi River. A great deal of litigation was going on there about that time, and it was not always an easy matter to obtain a jury. One day I was summoned to act in that capacity, and repaired to court to get excused. • Upon my name being called. I informed his Honour the Judge that I was not •a freeholder. and therefore not qualified tO serve. "Where dO yoti reside ?" inquired the Judge. "I am stopping for the time being at Port Hudson." "You board at the hotel, I presume ?" "I take my meals there, but have rooms in another part of the town, where I lodge." "So you keep bachelor's hall ?" "How long have you lived in that manner ?" "About: six 13101411 s." "I think you are qualfs.ed," gravely remarked the Judge, "for I have never known a man to keep bachelor's hall the length of time you have who had not 4usf enough in his room to Make him a free. holder !" A RUSTIC COURTSIIIP.-A Green Mountain boy fell in love with a pretty girl who lived in his neighbourhood, and determined to "court her." To that end he dressed himself, in his " Sunday-go-to-meetin' clothes," and went to her father's house, where he found her alone. "How dew yeou deir?" timidly enquired he. "I'm nicely. Take a cheer, Jonathan." Jonathan I seated himself in the farthest corner of the room. Ain't yeou cold-hadn't you better set up tew the fire ?" says Sally. No, thank yeou; I reckon I'm com- fortable." " Yeow is your marm ?".asked Sally. " Wal, sht's ccmplainin' a little." Here a -Wise of ten minUtei, during which time Jonathan whittled a stick. "There's nothing new up yeour way, is there ?". in- quired Sally. " Wal, no-that is-yes, eour spotted ceow's got a calf!" replied Jonathari. Sally would have undoubtedly laughed at this queer piece of information, only she was too much vexed at the speaker. At length, after another protracted silence, Sally got up a small edition 9f a scream, and in a loud voice exclaimed, "Let me al6ne." "Why," says Jonathan, dropping his knife and stick in astonishment, " why,l ain't touchin' on yeou.'' "Vat," says Sally, in a voice which might be indicative of fear, but sounded like a request- " Val, am n t yeou goln' tew ?" Jonathan thought a moment on this equivocal reply; and after placing his knife in his pocket he drew his chair by the side of pretty Sally, gently encircled her waist-and the next week-they wgre married.

CATCHING COLD AT THE COUNTY COURT. Sir,—Will you kindly allow me in . your columns to draw attention to the heating, if it can be so called, of the Warrington County Court during this severe weather. I had oce.asion to spend some hours at the court yester- day, and, although I was pretty warmly clad, the result is that now I ara suffering from a severe cold. There is one stove in the room, but as the building is a very large one, only the fortunate individuals who happen to be near the fire get any benefit. lam not alone in this complaint, for I heard many people express great dis- satisfaction. do not know who is responsible for this state of things, but it is one that should certainly be remedied. Perhaps a word from his Honour the Judge, or from the Registrar, would improve matters ?—Yours truly, Warrington, January 20, 1888.
A SUFFERER.

" ANTI-QUACK " AND "FAITH HEALING." Sir,—l do not propose to defend the faculty from the attack of this mis-named "Anti-Quack ;" they are quite able to give him his dose, did they: think him worthy of their steel (with or without quinine). My prescription would be cinder tea, that being the specific usually re- commended for his complaint. If he seriously wishes to discuss the question, let him throw aside the pusilanim- ous nom de plume, appear in his own name, and give a reason for the faith that is in him. As it is, I regard the not too refined criticism of " Anti-Quack " as I should thel aimless blundering of a. purblind cockchafer who had made his unwelcome presence felt by flying in my face. I have a pin with which, on a repetition of the offence, I shall impale him as a literary and psychological curiosity. If this un-" fair anonyma." does not make a practice of exercising his reason more—even if his faith be less— he may find himself at last in "further straits" with a waistcoat attached.—l am, Bm.,
JOHN PEERS.
ANOTHER TORY JOB

Sir,—At a meeting of the Trustees Of the Warrington Blue Coat School, on Thursday, at which seven out of twenty-four trustees were present, Mr. Henry Greenall was appointed Clerk to the Trustees in the place of Mr. James Nicholson, who has resigned. Mr. H. Greenall had no previous connection with the charity, but had three near relatives at the meeting. Mr. Henry ' Brown White, the other candidate, had been connected with the charity for nearly twenty-seven years, for the greater part of which tune he had entirely managed the trust business on behalf of the late clerk; but hs had no relatives on the Boa-d of 'Trustees. This is the third appointment Mr. H. Greenall has secured through the influence of relatives; first, Clerk to Income-tax Com- missioners; second, Clerk to the Magistrates of the Daresbury Division; third, Clerk to the Blue Coat School Trustees. Mr. Grsenall is the Tory election agent. All the Trustees of the Blue Coat School are Tories.—Yours truly, FAIR PLAY,

div.head: CALIFORNIA,
div.p: CALIFORNIA,

Sir,—The old adage is still true that they who live in glass houses should not throw stones. Mrs Parker asserts that my letter was written in a trades union spirit, and as there is evidently some kind of union in connection with her emigration scheme I am sure she has no cause to throw stones. It is only by means of union with her friends on the coast of the Pacific that she is enabled to carry on her work of disinterested philanthropy. Will you allow me quietly to assert, that my motives were as pure as hers, being simply a desire for the truth respect- ing this garden of Eden over which there is such an amount of gushing sentiment. People who view things from a winning side are apt to look very differently on the same object than their neighbours who are among the losers. It has been Mrs Parker's happy lot to be entertained in California by people to whom this sunny land has been truly a mine of wealth; therefore to them all is golden sunshine. But as no picture is complete without its dark shades, I sha" be glad if Mrs Parker will give us a little of the darkside. —Yours, Ike., J. W.
19, Mill-lane, Warrington, January 19th, 1888.
THE SHIP CANAL.--RUNCORN AND WESTON.
Ia the. Runcorn district affairs are assuming a

more active and progressive aspect. In the town- ship of Norton, at the Big Field, Messrs. Kirkham and Co. are fast completing their contract for the construction of workshops, &c. The buildings, which are most conveniently situated to each other, are of wood, and comprising commodious offices, store-room, mess-room, engine shed, fitters' shop, blacksmith's shop, and an erection for a saw mill, In which work is already proceeding. A considerable number of watchmen's huts have also been made. I A novelty in this part, of the country, and one that excites the interest of the visitors is a mud cabin.

_ intended to be used by the navvies at meal times. From the workshops in the direction of Runcorn lines have been laid for several hundred yards, and navvies are busily employed in preparing the ground for a large extension of the metals. The line branches off along the bridge constructed over the Old Quay Canal by Messrs. Kirkham & Cc. This bridge is substantially built of wood, and stretches on the other side of the canal a distance of about three hundred feet. Its chief pur- pose is for tipping the excavations of the Ship Canal. Machinery is daily accumulating at the Big Field. There are now two engines, the " Run Corn " and" Ince," the former being in active work, three moveable steam cranes, three steam navvies and a considerable number of wagons. Hundreds of the townspeople have been attracted to the spot this week through the rumours of the extraordinary accomplishments of the steam navvy. As yet only one of these machines has been fitted together, and operations were commenced with this one on Wednesday. When in proper working order it is capable of removing 1,200 cubic yards of earth per day, equal to about 1,500 tons. Three men are required to control one machine, which works with great rapidity, considering its ponderous nature. At Weston Point Mr. Walker has rented an office from the Weaver Navigation Company, and a start has been made in the construction of workshops necessary for carrying out the scheme in the neighbourhood. So far, however, the preparations are not on a large scale. It is interesting to note that the Manchester Ship Canal Company have bought the old Sprinch Works. at Runcorn, from Mr. W. 11. Kershaw, of Widnes. Formerly, the works were used for the manufacture

of glyceiine, and latterly a portion has been occu- pied by a firm of lard manufacturers. It is pro- bable that this purchase has been effected with a view to improving the Bridgewater Canal by cut- ting off the awkward bend that occurs at that point.

div.head: "MARVELS OF THE HUMAN FRAME."
div.p: "MARVELS OF THE HUMAN FRAME."

At a meeting of the Penketh Wesleyan Mutual Improvement Society, held in the Wesleyan Day School, on Wednesday evening, the Rev. Frank Ballard, president of the Liverpool . Microscopic Society, gave a lecture to a large audience on the subject of the "Marvels of the human frame." Mr. C. E. PARKER occupied the chair, and remarked that such matters as the lecturer was about to speak upon, and, in fact, every forward movement, found an earnest supporter in Mr. Ballard, whom he introduced to the meeting with great pleasure. The reverend lecturer, by way of preface, said that in ORO lecture it would be impossible to do justice to even a limb of the human body, so great and so com- plicated was the construction of our frame. It was, however, possible to take wh at he termed a landscape view. What he proposed to bring before his audience was some of the marvels of the human frame, because it was

impossible that they could take the whole of them. Every part of the body was equally Marvellous, and every part was wonderful in itself and in its relation to the whole. If he put a pin into any part of a person's body, the person would at once cry Oh !" What was the reason of that? It was that the nervous system was so marvellously arranged all over the body. Every- where there was some marvellous portion of a mar- vellous whole, and that night he must ask them to be content with a landscape glance of the whole. One great lesson h 3 wished to emphasise was the lamentable and profound ignorance that seemed to exist amongst almost all classes of society regarding the structure of body. Probably. with the exception of doctors, not one person in a hundred had any common sense idea of the con- struction of their own bodies. It was a marvel that people were so well, and that things went on so well, in view of the amount of crass and dreadful ignor- ance that appertained in this matter amongst almost all or- dinary. individuals. This in itself was one of the great marvels of the human frame---that it went on so well as it did. Br was a strange fact that the people who thought least about their bodies got on the best. The greatest task a medical man had to perform was some- times to persuade people to let their bodies alone. After having spoken of the advantage of a painstaking investi- gation, and consequently an ample knowledge, of the human body, Mr. Ballard said he should first speak of the boney system—the foundation of the whole. Next he would touch on the muscular system, then on the vascular, the digestive, and the resprative systems, and also on a few of the sense organs. By means of a magic lantern views were then thrown on a screen, thus enabling Mr. Ballard to give a practical illustration of his subject. The lecture was listened.to with, great at- tention, and at the conclusion the lecturer was heartily thanked for his services.
