CLAIM -AGAINST A WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCILLOR. At Warrington County Court, on Thursday, his Honour Judge Ffoulkes and a jury were occupied nearly the whole of the day in hearing a case in which the London and North-Western Railway Company sued Councillor Francis Dixon, Arpley- street, for a sum alleged to be due in respect to the carriage of goods on the railway of the plaintiff company. Mr. R. M. Preston appeared for the company, and the defendant was represented by Mr. H. L. Riley, of St, Helens. The original claim was for £32 3s, but the defendant had paid the amount into court less £l3 2s sn, which represen- ted an abatement to which he alleged himself to be entitled on the ground that the company had charged lOs 5d per ton for the carriage of certain goods from Wolverhampton to Swansea, whereas the rate should have been 7s lid for that class of goods.---Mr. Preston, in stating his case to the jury. said that the defendant was a dealer, in oxidised ashes, &c. The railway company had carried for de- fendai4 105 tons of what was described as fur- nace refuse, but which turned out .to be oxidised zinc, carriage of which was charged at the rate of lOs 5d per ton, whereas furnace refused for 7s lid per ton. The difference in cost between these two rates-was £l3 2s sd. which the defendant, believing himself entitled to the lower rate of carriage, had declined to pay. Hence the action to recover it. Mr. Preston, after pointing out that furnace refuse was carried without much trouble, while zinc ashes and similar materials had to be very carefully handled, said that it could not be expected that both would be carried at the same rate. He then read correspondence that had passed between the par- ties relative to the matter, and called evidence in support of the claim of the company. For the defence it was contended that oxide of zinc was commercially known as furnace refuse, which the railway company quoted at 7s lid per ton, making the difference in question-between the two rates, and the charge of lOs sd, it was submitted, was an overcharge. His Honour, in summing up, said that according to the evidence of one of the witnesses, an analytical chemist, furnace refuse was not composed of any particular commodity, and it was for the jury toy whether oxide of zinc could be distinctly described as furnace refuse. After retiring for a few minutes, the • jury found for the plaintiff company for £l3 2s sd, being the difference between the two rates of charges.

AT.T.FOED MISAPPROPRIATIONS BY A LETTER CARRIER. At Lymm Petty Sessions, yesterday, John Walker, postman, of Millington, was brought before the magistrates in custody on a charge of having on the 2nd January, feloniously stolen £4 in money, a sheet of paper, an envelope, and a penny stamp, the pro- perty of Samuel Burgess, blacksmith, Millington. I Mr. Burgess said the prisoner was postman for the Millington disttict, Knutsford. On Monday, the 2nd January, he saw him in the road about a quarter to six o'clock in the evening. Prisoner was called into the smithy, and witness asked him to get a post-office order at Knutsford for £3 I9s 6d, and then handed to him an envelope addressed to Mr. Clarke, of Alderley, agent of Lord Vernon. The envelope was stamped, and contained a letter written by witness's wife, stating that an order was enclosed, and asking for a receipt to be. sent. Wit- ness gave prisoner four sovereigns, and a shillirz for himself. Prisoner had previously obtained orders for him' which turned out to be all right. As no receipt had been received, witness's wife wrote to Mr. Clarke, who, it turned out, had not receivedthe order. Witness consequently inquired of the prisoner what he had done with the order, and the latter alleged that he sent it away the day after the money was given him. Witness afterwards went over to Knutsford Post-office, and there prisoner was asked about the order in the presence of Mr. Hulme, the post-master, and he then replied that he had left the letter on the counter along with other letters, and had forgotten it. Mr. Hulme, however, said he did not be- lieve this, for he would have seen the letter.—Corrobora- tive evidence was given by Mrs. Burgess, Thomas Bryce, and Mr. Hulme.—ln answer to the Chairman, the latter stated that postmen were.not compelled to get orders for other people, but they were not prohibited from doing so.—P.C. Jones, of Rostherne, said that when he appre- hended prisoner the latter said that he had left the letter in question with other letters on the counter, but he afterwards said, "I might as well tell the truth; I had the money, and spent it in drink."—A remand was asked for by Mr. James, who represented the postal authorities. It was stated that there had been a number of other letters found, with regard to which it was desired to make investigation. The prisoner was remanded till next Friday, when he will be brought before the magis- trates at Altrincham.

div.head: FATAL ACCIDENT AT GRAPPENHALL.
div.p: FATAL ACCIDENT AT GRAPPENHALL.

Yesterday afternoon an inquest was' held at the Dog and Dart Inn, Grappenhall, by Mr. H. C. Yates, coroner, as to the death of a young man named John Perdue, who, it is supposed, met his death on Mon- day night by falling over the parapet of the bridge which crosses the canal near Grappenhall village. The first witness called was Thomas Perdue, of 67. Legh-street, Warrington, who said deceased was his brother, and was 31 years of age. Deceased had been employed as a groom by Mrs. Greenall, at the Old Rectory, Grappenhall. The last time witness saw him was on Monday afternoon, about half-oast four. He was all well and hearty, lie had notliing to drink then, and was perfectly sober. Deceased was on good terms with other people, and witness did not suppose that anybody would throw him over the bridge.—Charles Eaton, landlord of the Barry Arms, Grappenhall, said he knew the deceased by sight, but not by name. He came to witness's house on Monday night, about nine o'clock and had two pints of beer to drink. He remained about half-an-hour and then went away, saying that he had a letter to post at the general post office, Warrington, and he wanted to be there befere 11 o'clock. When he left witness's house he was per- fectly sober. He went out with Mr. John Tinsley's coachman .—Richard Barker, farmer, Grappenhall, said that on Tuesday morning, about half-past eight, he was going over the canal bridge with his horse and cart, when his attention was drawn by a boatman to the body of a man who was lying underneath the crane at the foot of the bridge. Witness gave information to the nearest constalle.—The police officer stationed at Grap- penhall said that on receiving information from Mr. Barker, he went to Stanny Lunt Bridge and saw the dead body of the deceased, whom he did not know. De- ceased had only been in the village about a fort- night or tb.ee weeks. The body lay parallel with the canal, with the feet pointiwe to the bridge. Deceased's right leg crossed his left, and his right arm was on his chest, the left arm being stretched out. Witness raised the body, and found a quantity of blood under the head. The body was removed to the Dog and Dart, and on being searched there were found upon it 20, a pipe, and matches, and a letter addressed to a soldier. The top coat was buttoned up to the neck. There did not appear to have been any struggle. The letter, witness had since ascertained, belonged to one of the servants of Mrs. Greenall.—The Coroner remarked that he did not propose to open the letter, as it did not concern that inquiry.—The witness, continuing, said de- ceased must have fallen a distance of 14 or 15 feet from the bridge. The bridge belonged to the Manchester Ship Canal Company, and it had only 18 inches of parapet. If a man walked against it and tripped, he could not save himself from falling over, as there were no railings or protection of any kind. Monday night was dark but not foggy. He (witness) stood on the bridge about ten minutes past one o'clock on Tuesday morn- ing, but did not hear any groans. Dr. Joseph, of Warrington, gave evidence as to a post- mortem examination he had made. Upon tne right side of the head he found a wound to the scalp, and on re- moving the rcalp he found a large quantity of ex- travasated blood resting on the bone. Beneath the blood the skull was extensively fractured, the injury to it being so complete as to be more correctly described as a smash. On exposing the brain he found a large quantity of blood between the bone and the ,brain and to the pressure of this on the brain he ascribed the fatal results. There was nothing more likely than a fall from the bridge to cause the injury. Death was more likely to have been caused by this than by a blow with any in- strument he could think of. After the fall deeps ged had probably lived a few minutes, not more than a quarter of an hour. He would be unconscious from the first,— The Coroner having recapitulated the evidence, a short discussion took place amongst the jurymen as to the dangerous condition of the bridge, and it was resolved to recommend to the Ship Canal Company that a railing ought to be put up.—A Solicitor, from the office of Messrs Grundy, Kershaw, and Co., of Manchester, appeared on behalf of the Canal Company, and promised to convey the recommendation. At the same time he remarked that as the bridge had stood in its present condition about 120 fears, the danger of pedestrians coming along the footpath from Grappenhall walking against the parapet of the bridge had probably been caused by the setting back of the fence of the road. A verdict of " Accidental death'? was returned.

ASSAULT AT EARLESTOWN.-At the Newton Petty Ses- sions on Saturday, before Messrs. R. Houghton and T. J. Gillespie, Joseph Littler, of Earlestown, was sum- moned for assaulting a youth named Charles Walton, on the 11th inst.—Defendant, who did not appear, was re- presented by Mr. Stuart.—The complainant stated that on the date named he was passing the defendant's shop when the defendant came out and assaulted him by striking him a blow on the face and making his nose bleed.—Mr. Stuart applied for a remand as the defen- dant had not turned up, but the Bench decided that the ease should go on.—ln reply to Mr. Stuart the complain- ant said the defendant only struck him once. He used to be in the defendant's employ, and was discharged be- cause he took a holiday on Bank Holiday.—The Bench fuied the defendant 5s and costs.
:WYCLIFFE ANNIYAL, TEA TARTY.
SPEECH 33Y TILE REV. G. S. HEANEY.

The annual tea party in connection with Wycliffe Church, Warrington, was held in Wycliffe Hall, Bewsey-street, on Thursday evening. In the after- noon, prior to the tea, a sale of work which had been promoted by the ladies of the sewing class was opened in the Infants' Schoolroom, and was largely patronised. In connection with this sale of work there was also Christmas tree, which was hand- somely illuminated. The stalls were presided over by Mesdames Armitage, Yonge, Westgarth, and Wal- ker, and over .£l5 were realized. To tea about 450 persons sat down' the tables being attended to by Mesdames H. Roberts, Pearson, Lane, Wylie, Garland, W. Roberts, Barker, Legge, T. Wallington, W. Wallington, G. Wallington, R. Travis, Dick, J. Knowles, J. Owen, Harrison, Coutts. Farrar, Podmore, Howard, Bristowe, and Harrison; Misses Roberts, Porritt, Paul, Murray. and others. A remarkably good tea including meat sandwiches and dessert, was provided for sixpence, the arrange- ments for which had been made by Mr. Haynes, Mr. W. Roberts, and others. The hall, as usua', had been very tastefully decorated with curtains, banners, pictures, and various other ornamen- tal articles, the effect being extremely pleasing. The decorations had been done under the super- intendence- of Mrs. Pearson, Mrs. Lane, Mr. S. Naylor, Mr. T. Wallington, and others. Around the platform and in other parts of the hall there were a large number of beautiful plants which had been lent by Mr. J. G. McMinnies and Alderman Crosfield. In front of the platform were a model of a water- wheel in operation. and a fountain, these objects being the source of great attraction and admiration The water-wheel was the handiwork of Mr. C. Roy- lance, of Butterraarket-street, the fountain being furnished by Mr. A. Kaye. of Peter-street. It should be mentioned that the platform, the fountain, &c.. were illuminated with fairy lamps, whose bright and various colours contributed very largely to the pleasing effect of the decorations. After tea an excellent musical programme was rendered. The Rev. J. Yonge officiated as chairman, and the others on the platform were the Amy. G. S. Heaney, of Cavendish Chapel, Manchester, Rev. W. R. Parry, Mr. Z. Armitage, Mr. W. Rigby (Bowdon), Mr. W. Beswick, Mr. J. S. Garland, Mr. J. P4.4more, Mr. R. Roberts, and Mr. B. Farrar. The CHAIRMAN said he need not tell them that it gave him the most real pleasuke to meet them there that even- ing, and in fact he thought the first thing which he ought to say was that he was very glad to see them, that they were very glad to see one another and that they were all glad that they were there. (Hear, hear.) They had had many tea meetings in that room during the years which it had been his pleasure to spend in their midst as their minister, and some of them could go back a very much longer periOd than that, and remembered with pleasure—and were especially reminded by a face that was there that night—of happy meetings when Mr. Reaney was the minister of Wycliffe Church. (Applause.) He was quite sure that they felt with him a very real pleasure that it so happened- Mr. Reaney had once more cast his lot in the best county in England. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Somehow or other Mr. Reaney became enamoured of the city which had the distinguished honour of being his (Mr. Yonge's) own birthplace— (laughter)—and after spending a season of very hard and wearying work in London, he had come into the bracing atmosphere climatic, ecclesiastical, political and social—of Lancashire, in order that he might once more be braced up for new work and new enterprises. He Ins sure they all wished him very heartily "God speed" in his ministry at Cavendish Chapel, Manchester. (Applause.) He was sure it would have given them all very great pleasure if it had been possible not only for Mr. Reaney to be there, but also if it had been possi- ble to have induced Mrs. Reaney to accompany him. (Applause.) They were, however, look- ing forward to an opportunity of welcoming Mrs. Reaney some day in the future, when he hoped they should have Mr. Reaney and his better half both there together. (Ap- plause.) He (Mr. Yonge) might perhaps say, that look- ing at things all round in connection with Wycliffe, he was disposed to take just now a very hopeful view in- deed. He believed that there was a better spirit among them now than there had been for some little titre past— a more cordial and a more free and sympathe.ic He thought that they believed in one another a little more than perhaps they once did, and that they agreed with one another a little more earnestly than once they did; and that was a matter, without making any un- due reflection upon days past, for which they might be very thankful to God. (Hear, hear.) He hoped that as the new year passed onward they should have increas- ing evidence that the work of God was reviving in their midst, and that a deeper interest was being taken in things spiritual and divine. It bad been their privilege quite lately to receive into their church membership a considerable number of friends, Whe had for the first time made that open profession of their faith. They were „sad also that others were coming forward to say what God had done for them. That, by itself, was a matter for which to be satisfied, and from which to gather hope for the future. (Applause.) He thought they had found from a second experiment that there was nothing like a sixpenny tea. (Laughter and ap- plause.) He supposed it would be hardly possible to get a shilling out of them any more for a tea Meeting unless it should happen to be that the money was wanted for some particularly good cause, and then he thought Wycliffe people wor Id not mind responding to that call. (Hear' hear, and loud applause.) Mr. W. H. WALLINGTON then sang "The stowaway" in his very expressive style, and was rewarded withvery hearty applause. Mr. W. Rigby followed e:th a humo- rous recitation, which was highly enjoyed by the mail- one). A pleasing duet on the violin by Mr. Pearon and on the p ano by Mrs. Lane was the next item, after which Mr. W. Rigby followed with another capital reci- tation cleverly delivered, for which he was warmly encored. A vocal duet by Mr. W. Brown and Mr. W. H. Wallington si as also given. Theeßey. G. S. REANRY, who was received with loud applause, next gave a short address. He remarked that the meeting that night seemed to him to be good in qua- lity, and certairly very good in quantity. He had seen worse meetings in that hall, but he had never seen a better, so far RS attendance was concerned. He congra- tulated Mr. Yonge, and the audience also, on having so sucassfel and happy an anntial meeting. He had never seen that room look mo p beautiful than it did that night; he was afraid all the art in the world would make it look altogether beautiful, but it was very useful. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) On looking around taat night he thought they looked very well, and a happy sort of peo- ple, and their minister especially so. Some ministere never recommended the ministry either by preaching or anpeararce, but Mr. Yonge was not one of that sort— he was one of the cheeriest, brightest, and jol- liest sort of men. They all knew that when Yonge, of Wan ingtort, came on they should hear something worth listening to. on, hear.) Mrs Reaney said that if he met anyone she knew he was to say that she was very well, and that she sent her very kind regards to all of them. (Applause.) He was glad to see such signs of prosperity. He did sometimes come across churches where they 'did not see signs of pros- perity. Somehow or other there were some deacons who .did not seem to agree with ministers, some minis- ters who did not agree n ith deacons, and some congrega- tions did not agree with anybody. (Laughter.) Hav- ing told a story ef a deacon, Me. Reaney went on to say that they sometimes preached to dead men out of a dead book when they oaght to preach to livine men and women. Childrenthatwerealivewereof moreinterest to him than apostles that were dead. He sometimes complained of his brethren—not of Mr. Yonge nor in- deed of northern ministers generally—but of the London men that they were so antiquarian in their religious notions. They always believed that the times that wete gone were the best. When in Lon- don he found as a rele that the brightest things he could say was of memories of Lancashire. (Applause.) He prayed God that when he left London He would send him back to Lancashire, and he was glad that he had got within five-and-twenty minutes of War- rington. He was ("lad that his first speech outside his , own place was in the old Wycliffe school, and he should not be surprised if he even had an apportunity of getting , into the old pulpit again. (Applause.) He always was noted for the soundness of his doctrine, and he had , now arrived at even deeper depths of soundness. (Laugh. , ter.) There were a great many vacant pulpits up and . down the land, and all over the country they heard , people say, "Can you find us a man." Yes, it was a man, not a parson. He should advise them to stick close by their man, for of all the difficult things in the world that he kneveof at the present day it was to get a par- son who preached downrialit evangelical truth, and at the same time touched those deep humanities of our nature which he thought in the present day were developing themselves in the Christian Church, where there was a helpful spiritual life somewhat after the fashion of their meeting that night. (Applause.) Mr. Reaney then spoke in favour of young people enjoying themselves in cheerful and social ways, and concluded by expressing the hope that when he had been as long at Cavendish Chapel as Mr. Yonge had been at Wycliffe he might have as good a gathering as they had that night. (Loud applause.) . A humorous sketch was then enacted, the performers being Messrs. W. RoberLs. J. Haynes, T. Wallington, J. Dunbavand, and J. Knowles. A recitation by Mr. H. Spencer and a song by Miss N. Roberts having been ad- mirably rendered, . Mr. J. S. GARLAND moved a vote of thanks to those , who had done so much towards making that night's entertainment a success. He congratulated Mr. Yong() on that the 11th annual tea meeting that had taken place during his pastorate of Wycliffe Church, and he urged upon thosa present to second the efforts of their minister. (Applause). Mr. WasroArcrit seconded the proposal in a few suit- able words.
The Rev. J. Yoe, iri gupporting it. referred to the corning departure of the Rev. W. R. Parry for Peasley Cross. Mr. Parry had made himself very much respec-

The resnllttion of thanks was then carried, and another. song Ms ing been sung by Mr. W. H. Wallington the plea.sant g.‘„nering was brought to a close with the sing mg of the doxology.

div.head: LIBERAL SOIREE AT WIDNES.
div.p: LIBERAL SOIREE AT WIDNES.

The first annual soirée in connection with the Widnes Division Liberal Association took place in t'se Baths Assembly-room, on Wednesday evening, arid was a most encouraging success. The proceedings commenced with a tea party, at which about three hunt:red persons were present. The tables were presided over by Mrs. and Miss Wareing, Mrs. Kershaw, Mrs. S. Sadler, Mrs. O'Keeffe. Mrs. Taylor, Mrs. Showan, Mrs. and Miss Dainteth, Mrs. W. Sadler, Mrs. W. R. Clark, Mrs. and Miss Hewitt, Mrs. Ireland, Miss Martindale, Mrs. and Miss Ward, Mrs. Cane, Mrs. Bray, Mrs. Fairclough, Miss Priestnall, Miss Young, Mrs. McElroy, and Mrs. Bailey. Afterwards an entertainment was given under the presidency of Mr. C. Carey, who delivered a brief speech, in which he referred with gratification to the large number present. A novel feature in the pro- gramme was an "Essay Bee," in which short essays on "Home Rule" were read by working-men; and it proved an unqualified success. The idea had originated with Mr. H. B. Shores. the indefatigable secretary of the association, and he had made the arrangements. Each essayist was limited to five minutes, in which to read his paper, and the inducement held out Was two prizes, the first, a beautifully-mounted and handsomely gilt-framed portrait of Mr. Gladstone; and the second, the newly- published work on "Ireland's Disease," by Mr. Phillipe Daryl. At the outset the audience were asked to select a juryoLfive gentlemen to officiate as judges; and the following were chosen: Mr. J. W. Wareing, Dr. O'Keeffe, S. Sadler, T. Showan, and T. J. Peters. The essayists were Mr. G. E. Quirk, Mr. .1. Marsh, Mr. H. Fairciough, Mr. F. Cane, and Mr. E. Catto ; and each paper possessed many points of merit.—At the conclu- sion of the proceedings the " jury " retired to consider their verdict, and on returning into the room Mr. Wareing said they, had to exress extreme regret that Mr. Quirk had disqualified himself. His paper was unquestionably one of great merit—(hear, hear)— but, unhappily for himself, the time occupied in ie; de- livery was eleven minutes. The jury had concluded that Mr. Marsh was entitled to the first prize—(applause)—and Mr. Cane to the second prize. (Applause.) The only regret the jury experienced was that they were not able to give each essayist a prize —(hear, hear)—but he hoped those who had not been successful that evening would be prize winners on the next occasion. (Applause.)—Mrs O'Keeffe then grace- fully presented the prizes to the successful competitors. In the interirals between the reading of the essays songs were given by Miss Dainteth, Dr. O'Hagan. Mr. P. Hey-es, and Mr. J. Morrison.—ln conclusion the Chairman moved, and Mr. Morrison seconded a cordial vote of thanks to those who had aided _in any Way at the tea party and entertainment. The motion was carried with acclamation, and the audience separated highly delighted with the entertainment.

div.head: RUNCORN UNION RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN UNION RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse, Dutton, on Tuesday afternoon. There were present Colonel Ashton (chairman),. the Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs. Mclntyre, Aaron, Whitlow, Hadfield, Brandreth, Parr, Knowles, H. Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk), Dr. Adams (medical officer), and Farrington (inspector of nuisances). MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

The quarterly report of the medical officer of health (Dr.. Adams) was read. It appeared that during the quarter ending December 31st, 1887, the registrar's re- turns recorded 118 births and 99 deaths in the four regis- tration sub-districts of the Runcorn Union. Of the births, 67 were males and 49 females. The birth-rate was 5.8 per 1,000 per quarter, or 23.2 per 1,000 per annum, compared with 133 births, or a birth-rate of 6.6 per 1,000, or 28.4 per 1,000 per annum in the correspond- ing quarter of 1888. Of the deaths 57 were males and 48 females, the death-rate being 4.95 per 1,000 per quar- ter, or 19.8 per 1,000 per annum, compared with 80 deaths, or a death-rate of 4.0 per 1,000 per quarter, or 18*0 per 1,000 per annum in the corresponding quarter of 1888. Of the deaths 17 oc- curred in persons under one year of age, eight n per- sons between the ages of 5 and 80, and 34 in person of of 60 and upwards. The causes of death were set forth in an annexed tabular statement, and it would be observed tha'c, measles accounted for six deaths, typhoid fever for four, and croup for one among zymotic diseases, whilst diseAstes of the chest accounted for 26 deaths, or rather more taan 25 per cent, of the total. 2

APPLICATION FOR lIR.BAN POWER. Mr. Aaron proposed that an application be made to the Local Government Board to declare that the provisions in force in the Urban district should be in force in the contributory place of Weston to the same extent as such powers are now in force in Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship. He said that the cost of the application would be practically nothing,—Mr. Brandreth seconded this proposal.--Mr. Aaron also gave notice that he would move that day fortnight that a committee be formed to frame building bye-laws.—Mr. Fladlield asked if the new powers would at all affect the buildings already erected ? —Mr. Aaron replied that the buildings.to be erected in the future would only be affected: He wished they could touch the buildings erected in the past.—The proposal was then agreed to,

Dr. Adams reported that il-;;;had been an outbreak of fever near Frodsham Bridge, but up to thepresent the origin of the outbreak had not been traced. This was the principal business. , PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the members of the• above Board was held at the Workhouse, Whiston, on Thurs- day. • There were present Mr. J. Fisher (chairman), the Rev. Dean Finegan, Messrs. W. Tyrer, C. 13. Johnson, T. Radek, W. B. Long van, E. Syder, J. Kenwright, H. Hulme, R. A. Graves, J. Wareing, W. Middlehurst, J. Ranson, J. Jackson, J. Whalley, J. Burchall, and Mr,. S. H. Hartley (clerk). Tint INISA'FFS.—The Workhouse Master reported there were 540 inmates 4n the Workhouse this week, 525 last week, and 524 in the corresponding week last year.—Mr. Wareing thought it Nyould be advisable to know from what distr'ct the increase came, as it was most extraor- dinary, considering that pauperism was decreasing all over the country, as they won e told.—After some further conversation, the Clerk promised to obtain a return showing the number of cases from each relieving officer's district each week during the last 12 months.

APPOINTMENT OF NllRSES.—Communications were read from the Local Government Board sanctioning the ap- pointment of Mary Palmer and Ellen Dodgson as nuis4s at the wo-:khouse. Ts SaccrittiY OF OFFICERS.—The Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board inquiring whether the Guardians of the Prescot Union had called'uporotheir inquiry officers to give sectirity for the faithful discharge of Oar duties. He added that he had'. replied to the lette: as directed by the Finance Committee. REGISTRARS OF Maanienas.—The Clerk reported that he had received from the clerk to the Leeds Union a copy of a memorial which that Union had sett* to the Local Government Board, praying then ito introduce a bill to place the appo;ntmenf of registrars of marriages with 'the guardiaiis instead of, as at present, with the superintendent registrays.—The Clerk added that he Mr. Hartley) was superintendent registrar for that Caton, and he had appointed union officers to the posts, and from none of the appointments did he receive a far- thing. He had appotited the men he thought best quali- fied and best calculated to suit the requirements of the district. It was decided to let the mtition lie on the table.

RE,-lEF.—The Clerk stated that the paupers in receipt of relief on the Ist of January, 1888, in the workkouso andinfirmary were 528, in the industrial school, Liver- pool, there were 159, at Pantasaph and West Derby Orphanage 40, in hospital and other institutions 17, making a total of 724; against 726 last year. The out- door relief lists contained the names of 2,556 persons, and there were five non-resident paupers. Lunatics in asylums numbered 206 persons. Eleven paupers were receiving medical relief that were not included in the above, making a grand total of 2,778, against 2,379. The total number of persons receiving relief altogether was 3,502, against 3,105. TILE PPOPOSED It:rename OF SALARY.—In accordance with notice of motion, Mr. Jackson moved that the salary of Mr. Stuart, relieving officer, be increased from £l2O to £l3O per annum. Ile said Mr. Stuart had been seven years in the service of the Board, and it was five years since he received an increase. SQ long as they had officers doing their duty he thought they ought to be re- warded for merit. —Mr. Buckley seconded the motion.— Mr. Kenwright objected to the increase. They could have hundreds of applications for the post at the present salary.—Mr. Middiehurst did not think there were special reasons for increasing Mr. Stuart's salary.—The Rev. Dean Finegan did not think it advisable to grant the increase, and as a representative of the VVidnes Rate- payers' Association he intended to vote itiminst the motion.—Mr. Jackson asked the members of the Board not to be coerced on the tnatter, and left it to them to say whether a relieving officer's duties would not increase during a period of fiVe years.—Mr. Jackson and Mr. Buckley only voted for the motion, which was lost. This concluded the business.

SIR M. HICKS-BICACR AT BRISTOL.-Sir Michael Hicks- Beach addressed a meeting at Bristol on Tuesday night, and said that unless we could remove Ireland from her present situation and moor her off the harbour of New York ire would never get rid of Great Britain's responsi- bility for Irish affairs. The idea of Home Rule was en- veloped in a kind of benevolent flumme7, but sentimen- tal gush was not a good guide in arranging the relations of nations. The gravest symptoms of the Irish difficulty were popular sympathy with law-breakers and the anti- English feeling,so prevalent amongst the populace. Ile hoped that in the next session local government,fmance, and retrenchment would occupy attention.

div.head: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.
div.p: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.
[FROM 011111 OWN CORRESPONDENT.] 23, Old Broad-street, E.C. . .

The course of the stock marirete is on the whole lather favourable than otherwise, in some directions there be- ing decided firmness; but it cannot be said there is much, if any, improvement as regards business. There is a disposition to take a more cheerful view of affairs abroad, owing to the pacc speech of the Czar; but the caution exercised by operators is in no way relaxed. This unsatisfactory state of things checks speculative business, and notNedistanding occasional re-assuring statements received from abroad must continue to do SO.

Home rails are on the whole firm; prices at the time of writincs being decidedly better. Hull and Barnsley have been most dealt in show;ng as much as a difference of 2 during the day. The S. E. Railway fund shows signs of becoming more bitier as the time approaches for the half-yearly general meeting, which is to be held on the 26th inst. Mr. W. Abbott has been selec- ted as the champion of the opponents to the policy of Sir E. Watkin and the present board. Mr. Abbott claims to have sufficient support to remove Sir E. Watkin from his position as chairman. Whatever may be said as to the proposed attempt to oust Sir E. Watkin, there can be no question of his ligh-handedness, and the fact remains that at a time when trade is un- deniably improving the South Eastern working expenses have increased, while the revenues from passengers, from goods, and from steamboats all continue to show a decrease.

Further, the attempt to compel the Brighton Company to hand over property of which they have have been left in undisturbed possession for a generation past will be ' persisted in. This not only means war to the knife with the Brighton Company, but seems to imply a somewhat supine neglect of the shareholders' interest for the forty I years duns> which the claim has been suffered to lie dormant. Is for the Ckatham Company, and the Folkestone traffic an action is still pencling ; in other , words, the shareholders" money is to be spent in the hope that the House of Lords will reverse the unanimous and unhesitating decision of the cor-ts below. , Copper shares are the centre of interest just now, laq,' I it is an interest of a theoretical kind, consisting mairif of watching the market. The drop in copper &ring the past week is regarded as the result of manipulations, but Rio Tintos are nevertheless flatter. A dispobition is evinceil upon the part of outside holders to take profits, although the market still believes in a further rise. Doh Feciros are firm at about 1. Centennials re- main unaltered at 1 3-16, with a marked tendency to rise further. Some inquiry is being directed to the tin markets, and some new companies dealing with tin !mines are on the eve of production. It is not, possible to believe in a tin corner working so successfully as the I copper corner recently did.but more will be known about , the subject shortly. Gold Hills are commanding some , attention, one broker haNing bought 10,090 at 4s. They Icertaarly appear cheap at this price. In reference to the great Burton Beer Company, the Issue will be made by the barking firm of Messrs. Scott and Co., Cavendish-square. Two of the partners of the , firm, viz., the Earl of Fife and Mr. Horace Farquhar, have taken the whole of the debentures " firm."

Earl Spencer, speaking at a meeting on Thursday of a Northamptonshire Board of Guardians, strongly depre- cated the tampering with county boundaries. He said some hard-hearted people might laugh at sentiment, but sentiment had a good deal of influence in this world. THE TORIES AND Hotta RULE.—On Monday night, Mr. Shaw-Lefevre addressed a large meeting of Liberals at Tunstall, in the Potteries, and replied to theattack made upon him by Lord Salisbury at Liverpool. He contended that there was every reason to believe that Lord Salis- bury was implicated in the negotiations of Lord Carnar- Ivon, Lord R. Churchill, and other leading members of the Tory party in 1884-5 in favour of some form of Home Rule. lie .did not state this as a charge against the Tory leaders, as he believed they would have acted wisely if they had gone in for a policy of that kind ; but he did look upon it as a misfortune that at a critical period they abandoned the idea of legislation he spoke of, and went in favour of a policy of coercion. In man), cases Lord Salisbury had shown a great proficiency in making statements consistent enough with truth to satisfy his own conscience and vet conveying a totally opposite meaning from the truth to his hearers, and ho left it to moralists to say what was the right destription of language of that character. In conclusion, he asserted from his personal observations that the -policy of coercion, so far as it had been tried, was a total failure.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

- - - - --- Sir Robert J. Buxton, 'Bart., formerly. Conservative M.P. for South Norfolk, died on Friday. Mr. Smith had an interview lasting four hours and a half with Lord Salisbury at the Foreign Office yes. terday.
Duiing a football match at Winchester, on Friday, Captain Hornby, of the Rifle Brigade, had his leg broken.

A block of buildings in Monk-street, Bradford, oc- cupied by several warehousemen, was destroyed by fire on Friday. The damage amounts to £4,000. Mr. Hector McLean, of New College, late captain of the Oxford University Boat Club, died on Friday of Typhoid fever. Mr. McLean twice rowed in the University Boat Ttace. The adjourned inquest on Dr. Cross was resumed at Cork, on Friday. Berry, the hangman, did not appear, and the jury refused to find a verdict, and adjourned the inquiry sine the. The authorities of Bolton have issued a notice request- mg the sparing use of water by the inhabitants, SS there is no record of the reservoirs ever have been so low at this period oZ the year. _ _

Mr. Alexander Blane, M.P. was arrested on Friday morning at Armagh, charged with inciting tenants in Donegal not to pay rent. Mr. Blane was removed to DoLegal for trial before a Crimes Act Court. About one o'clock on Friday morning Waterheddings Mill, Oldham, was discovered In flames, and before the arrival of the fire brigade the roof of one of the main buildings had fallen in. The origin of the fire is un- known. ARREST OP ANOTHER PRlEST.—Father McFadden, of Gweedore, who took a prominent part in defending the tenants in certain ejectment proceedings on the Hill estate in-county Donegal, was arrested late on Thursday night at Armagh.

-A partial strike of mill-workers took place at Dundee. I on F, iday. The principal employers met, and decided I that the present condition of the jute trade did not warrant an advance of wages. An extensive strike is therefore expected. RELEASE OF MR. O'BRIEN, M.P.—.A Tullamore corres- pondent says that Mr. William O'Brien, M.P., was re- leased from Tullamore Gaol at eleven o'clock on Friday morning,- and he proceeded to the residence of the parish priest, followed by a crowd. He was presented later in the day with an address by the local branch of the National League. The banquet to Mr. O'Brien, M.P., at Mallow, has been postponed until Thursday next. EXTRAORDINARY MAIL BAG ROBBERY.-011 the Irish mail bags being landed at Greenock from the steamer .Plligator, on Friday morning, it was found that the mail bag from Belfast to Edinburgh was missing. The bag was found lying in a corner of the steamer with the bottom cut out and empty. Five small bags have since been found along the shore, west of the steamboat pier, ' but they were empty. The steamer arrived at Greenock at four o'clock in the morning, and the theft must have I been committed in the darkness. Several bank cheques, bills, and other documents have been washed ashore at Greenock. A young man called at Greenock General Post Office on Friday afternoon and presented for pay- ment five postal orders which had been issued at Belfast and neighbouring towns. The suspicions of the post office clerk was aroused, and, on the young man being closely quesemned, he confessed that, along with another man, he cut open the mail bag on the steamer Alligator, and st6e the letters containing the postal orders. He was‘at once arrested, and then gave his name as Samuel Woods.
FIRE IN LONDON.-FOUR PERSONS BURNED TO

div.head: DEATH.
div.p: DEATH.

_ A disastrous fire occurred on Friday morning at a chandler's shop in Hutchinson-street, Hounsditeli' Lon- don. 'Mrs Phillips, Mrs Salzedo, Miss Sophia Salzedo, her daughter; and Moedecai Salzedo, German Jews, were turned to death. Five others were severely in- jured. The flames wer6discoversd shortly before three o'clock on Friday morning by Police-constable Webber, but he could not penetrate to the first floor, the occu- pants of which jumped from the windows into sheets help by neighbours, but these gave way, and five per- sons received severe injuries. The inmates of the upper floor already named perished before the firemen reached them. The flames were subdued whilst spreading to the adjoining houses. The origin of the fire is not known. The condition of the five injured people is not very seri- ous, and two of them were expected to leave the hospital on Friday. The dead bodies were removed to Golden- square mortuary, whilst Fanny, Maurice, Henry, and Lily Phillips were taken to London Hospital. It was at first rumoured that Fanny Phillips had succumbed to her injuries, but it turns out to be incorrect. Consider- able excitement prevailed in the district, and the narrow streets were crowded with people discussing the terrible event.
A TERRIBLE CALAMITY.-4,000 WORKMEN DROWNED.

A "Standard" Shanghai telegram says :—A body of four thousand workmen, whilst engaged under the com- mand of several Mandarins in making a breakwater to stem the course of the Hoang Ho floods, have been engulfed by a sudden rush of water. Very few of them escaped.
SENSATIONAL SUICIDE WITH A RED HOT POKER. '

The Falmouth correspondent of the Central News tele- graphs that Rear Admiral Lewis Hutton Versturme, a retired officer, aged 62, committed suicide on Thursday night, in a most determined and shocking manner. The gallant officer and his wife were sitting together in the drowing-room of their house, last evening, when one of the . servant maids was alarmed by dreadful groans. She immediately ran to the dram ng-room, and there found Admiral and Mrs Versturme both on the floor. The lady •Xfas in an unconscious state, but the admirtff writhed about the floor and groaned continuously. In his hand he grasped a small brass ti,•awing-room poker, with which he had evidently inflicted SOW kind of wound on his body: The servant rushed from the house screaming, and alarmed Dr. Bullmore who lived near. On his ar- rival he found Admiral Versturme in terrible pain, and on examining the body discovered the unfortunate officer had thrust the poker, red hot, irito•his bowels in three or four different places. Everything possible was done to alleviate the sufferer's agony and to save his life, but he expired on Friday moring. Mrs Versturme is still in a prostrate condition and has not yet been able to make a statement respecting the sad affair. It is, however, con- jectured that the admiral was seized with a sudden frenzi, and, seizing the poker from the fire, wounded himself three or four times before his wife could prevent him, and that on seeing her husband fall apparently dead to the floor, she fainted away before she could even give an alarm.—lt is stated that the admiral was re- recently disappointed in not receiving an expected legacy. .

RESIGNATION OF MR. THOMAS STONE.—IN the course of a discussion at the monthly meeting of the Newtori Improvement Commissioners on Monday afteriumn it was mentioned that Mr. Thomas Stone, of Newton Park, a highly respected member of the Board, had resigned. After the public business of the Board had been transac- ted the Board held a committee meeting, and one of the members was instructed to wait upon Mr. Stone with the view of inducing him to retain his seat. THE QUEEN AHD PARLIAMENT.—It is now announced that the Queen will not open Parliament in person. Her Majesty will remain in England until after the com- mencement of the session, but will leave for the con- tinent immediately afterwards. There is no truth in the statement that the Queen has taken a villa at San Remo. Her Majesty intends to visit Florence in the •spring, and will occupy the Villa Pulmieri, which has been placed at her disposal by the Dowager Countess of Crawford. Goon TEMPLARY.—The members of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars held their weekly session on Monday evening, under the presidency Of Brother John Taylor, W.C.T. There was a good attend- ance. Arrangements were made to join the Ashton Excelsior Lodgein an entertainment in the Wigan Public Hall. BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON. THE MARGARINE ACT, 1887. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that every dealer in Margarine, whether wholesale or retail, and whether as manufacturer, importer, consignor, consignee, commission agent, or otherwise, must conform to the following regula- tions, viz. :—Every package, whether open or closed, contain- ing Margarine must be— (a) Branded or durably marked " Margarine" on the top, bottom, and sides, in printed capital letters not less than finch square. (b) If exposed for sale by retail there must be attached to eacri parcel so exposed, in such manner as to be clearly visible to the purchaser, a label marked in printed capital letters, not less than I.l;inches square, "Margarine." (c) Every person selling Margarine by retail (except in a packet duly branded, or durably marked, as aforesaid) must in every case deliver the same to the purchaser in or with a paper wrapper with the word " Margarine" printed thereon in capital letters not less than of an inch square. Every person found guilty of an offence against the Act will be liable on summary conviction as follows For a first offence to a penalty not exceeding £2O. For a second offence not exceeding £5O. For a third or any subsequent offence not exceeding £lO9. Dated this 29th day of January, 1888. WM. MY. BROOK. Town Clerk.
